40ab7a0a4028.title: Code node review
40ab7a0a4028.content: Skill code-node-review: Review the knowledge graph’s CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the tools graph and schema definition nodes under schemas/ — for the joins a reader cannot see: that a node declares what it is, that what it names resolves, and that the mechanism it describes is the one that actually runs. Named by: Code node review .

8e1e9c3cccd6.title: What you are reviewing, and why it is not ordinary code review
8e1e9c3cccd6.content: Two node kinds: . | node kind | lives in | declared by | says | . | Tool | tools/<id>/<id>.json (the tools graph) | "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" | one concrete mechanism that exercises a skill | . | Schema definition | Zod modules under the tools layer’s schemas/; their generated JSON Schemas under schemas/kinds/ here | the module and its exported types | the shape of a content object, and its own place in the KG | . They are graph nodes that happen to be code. Ordinary review asks whether the code is correct; this asks whether the node is correct — whether it declares what it is, whether its references resolve, and whether the mechanism it advertises is the one that runs. A file can compile, pass its tests, and still be a broken node.

afd7f2d43993.title: Tool nodes
afd7f2d43993.content: A skill states a capability generically; a Tool carries the concrete mechanism (skills-and-tools). Review a Tool node for: . | It names the skills it satisfies, and they exist. A Tool naming no skill is unreachable from the capability it implements; a Tool naming a skill that does not exist is a dangling edge check-tools can catch but a reader cannot. | The mechanism is the one that runs. A vendor, CLI, binary or endpoint in a Tool must be the one the pipeline actually invokes. A Tool describing an aspiration is worse than no Tool: it answers “how is this done here?” wrongly and with authority. | IRIs are minted, not written out. toolTypeIri forms I/O type IRIs against the layer’s canonicalUrl at load. A hardcoded IRI silently breaks when the publication base moves, and nothing fails at build time. | Coverage is a finding, not a score. Not every skill has a Tool node. A skill with no Tool is a gap worth naming in review; it is not a defect in the skill. | .

bcbedc4098dc.title: Schema definition nodes
bcbedc4098dc.content: Reviewed as nodes, the recurring defect is a file that does not say what it is: . | The node declares its own kind. kg (skill front matter), bean-defs (work item front matter) and workflow-state ($schema) declare themselves. schemas/*.ts largely does not — @module names the path rather than the node type, some files carry none, and *.test.ts files sit in the declared directory without being schema nodes at all. A consumer then tells them apart by filename, which is a coincidence of the current layout rather than a contract. | A widened type is a widened contract. Adding a field to a shared schema changes every instance of it, including in downstream folios. Ask what happens to a folio that does not set it, and whether the mirror (JSON Schema, the Python side, the interchange schema under tools/) moves with it. | A REMOVED field needs a reason in the file. The tools layer’s schemas/content/translation.ts carries a comment where roundTripQA used to be, saying what it held and why it went. Without that, the next author re-adds it in good faith. | Defaults are policy. profiles defaults to every profile while adapters narrows — because narrowing silently stops criteria running and a wrong pass is believed where a wrong fail is argued with. When you review a default, review which way it fails. | .

669cbafe0ff3.title: The audits to run, and what they cannot tell you
669cbafe0ff3.content: bun run cat check:tools # Tool nodes: declared skills resolve bun run cat kg:audit # the KG joins, per node, into kg-qa/ sidecars bun run typecheck # a malformed schema module fails here by design . kg:audit writes a sidecar per node rather than printing and exiting, so “this has been broken since it was drawn” and “this broke in the change under review” are distinguishable. Read the sidecar, not just the summary. What no audit can tell you: whether the mechanism a Tool describes is the one that runs, and whether a schema field means what its name suggests. Those are the two things a human or agent reviewer is for, and why this is a skill rather than a check script alone.

826eb37d2864.title: Where this runs in a process
826eb37d2864.content: review-code.bpmn (Process_CodeReview) is this skill’s subprocess. It is called, not inherited: an actor already acting as a reviewer descends into it and takes on the code-reviewer lane for that call path only, so the skills are the union along the path rather than a permanent widening of the outer role. review-task.bpmn is the generic entry that routes a change to this subprocess, to the narrative one, or to both. The feature-request process calls it too — crdm-requirements.bpmn audits the code nodes an implementation adds before an MVP goes to staging, because a Tool or schema node shipped in an MVP is the version stakeholders start building expectations on.

dbaad5247d1a.title: Do not
dbaad5247d1a.content: . | Do not review a Tool node without checking what it claims to invoke. The failure this catches is a node that documents a mechanism nobody wired. | Do not approve a schema widening whose mirrors you have not looked at. | Do not treat a clean check:tools as coverage. It verifies the Tools that exist; it says nothing about the skills that have none. | .

6e61feae6a60.title: The language you communicate in
6e61feae6a60.content: Skill communication-language: Determine the language an agent SPEAKS IN — the language of a turn, as against the language of content. Covers the four inputs and their order, why a model’s own languages are never the answer, the boundary between speaking to the person and writing durable artefacts, where the determination is recorded so a sibling session does not re-ask, and when to re-ask. Named by: Hand back to the discussion .

d6fbe7acb709.title: Why this exists
d6fbe7acb709.content: The language of a turn is a determination to make, not a default. The skills and the corpus are in English; an agent that answers in English without asking has let a default stand in for a decision. Content language is a separate question, owned by translation-manager. Determine it regardless of context. Mirroring the language of the request fails for the person who writes a terse instruction in one language and wants the report in another, or who can type a language more easily than they can read a wall of it.

c310978214a2.title: Make the determination before the first substantive turn
c310978214a2.content: Beside the other opening steps — the session-start sweep and opening-brief. The sweep prints the interaction preferences first, before the work plan.

0003fb6fa527.title: Four inputs, and the order is not negotiable
0003fb6fa527.content: | rank | input | where it lives | . | 1 | the person’s stated preference | cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, per user | . | 2 | the language of their own turns | the conversation | . | 3 | the model’s declared languages | bootstrap/models/models.json | . | 4 | the layer’s defaultLocale | its translation-sources declaration (defaultLocale, default en) | . A stated preference wins outright. It is the only input that is a decision rather than a signal, and a person who has said it once must not be asked again (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7, Redundant Entry); for a user who types with difficulty, asking again is not a small cost. Their own turns rank above the model’s languages. The model’s languages are an INPUT, never the determination: a model strong in a language the person cannot read is worse than the fallback. Rank 3 can only suggest that a pairing may be better served by something other than the corpus’s language; it never selects one on its own. Only human-validated entries are read at all. validatedLanguages() in bootstrap-tools/schemas/model-registry.ts returns nothing for self-reported or unverified, because a model’s own claim about which languages it handles well is a generated assertion about a generated system. self-reported is not a weaker human-validated; it is a different kind of claim.

ecd4f46f59e1.title: The boundary: SPEAKING versus WRITING
ecd4f46f59e1.content: The rule above governs what you say to the person. It does not govern what you write into the repository. | artefact | language | . | chat replies, questions, status reports | the determination | . | commit messages, PR bodies, issue comments | the layer’s source language | . | code comments, skills, work items, schemas | the layer’s source language | . | folio CONTENT | translation-manager, not this skill | . The reason is the reader: a commit message or issue comment is read by reviewers and later agents, not only by the person in this session, and one person’s preferred language would narrow who can read the record.

4462a68ecd9a.title: Record it where a sibling session reads it
4462a68ecd9a.content: cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, in the user’s entry, beside profiles: . "someone@example.org": { "profiles": ["low-dexterity"], "language": "fr", "note": "…", "source": "stated by the user" } . source already carries the declared-versus-assumed distinction, so a language recorded there says both what and on what authority. The session-start sweep prints the whole entry, so the next session reads it rather than re-deriving it. Never write a preference the person did not state. The file is context — read at session start, never written by a process. An inferred language recorded as though stated is worse than no record, because the next session will not re-ask.

4467d7d0f40b.title: When to re-ask
4467d7d0f40b.content: . | Never, on a recorded preference, unless the person changes it. | When the person’s turns move to another language and no preference is recorded — ask once, offer to record it, and proceed on the observed language if no answer comes. | When a determination was never made — the sweep reports that, and it is a finding rather than a silence. | .

893bdce9fe5c.title: What “could not determine” looks like
893bdce9fe5c.content: defaultLocale, said out loud. An agent that falls through to rank 4 says so once rather than presenting the fallback as a choice, because an unknown rendered as a determination is indistinguishable from a real one.

bd46c4ff4682.title: Related
bd46c4ff4682.content: . | interaction-modality — the FORM a question takes; this is the LANGUAGE it takes. Both are read from the same file. | translation-manager — the language of content, which this skill does not govern. | bootstrap-tools/schemas/model-registry.ts — why a model’s own word is not evidence. | .

c09a428c23df.title: Compiled Artefact Cache
c09a428c23df.content: Skill compiled-artefact-cache: The general pattern for caching expensive compiled artefacts (Lean .oleans, FHIR ASTs) across builds. Defines branch-based storage, validity checking, exit code protocol, safety guards, and the restore→build→contribute loop. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Review and publish a folio, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . This skill documents the generalisable pattern for caching compiled artefacts (such as Lean caches and FHIR ASTs). It is the shared contract that specific implementations (e.g. lean-cache-restore and ig-ast-delta) adhere to.

9620b661e939.title: The restore→build→contribute loop
9620b661e939.content: The cache is not a maintenance chore but the output of every authoring session. Every session should leave the cache warmer than it found it: . restore ──▶ draft / edit ──▶ build ──▶ contribute ▲ │ └───────── next agent starts here ─────────────┘ .

8b3d40b61953.title: Branch-based storage
8b3d40b61953.content: Artefacts are stored on orphan branches named for their package and toolchain (e.g. lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain>). This keeps the repository clean while persisting large derived outputs across builds. A branch that keeps every seed grows by what each seed’s writer changes. Write seeds by git-friendly-churn: the same bytes when nothing changed, and a stable path for each file, so a new seed costs deltas, not copies.

05b8f6b86fd9.title: Validity checking (3-valued)
05b8f6b86fd9.content: The validity of a cache is not a simple boolean. It relies on the CompiledInputsSchema defined in the content core’s schemas/materialization.ts. Validity is checked BEFORE use via compiledValidity() and returns one of three states: . | valid: The cache matches the current inputs (e.g. toolchain, source revision, input digest). Restore and build. | stale-inputs: Identifies exactly which input changed. The cache cannot be used as-is; restore for the current toolchain instead, or build cold. | cannot-tell: The cache record lacks required input fields. Never a pass. Build cold or find the missing inputs first. | .

7af3c5d11035.title: Exit code protocol
7af3c5d11035.content: Scripts managing the cache must adhere to a standard exit code protocol. Branch on these codes rather than grepping the output: . | Code | Meaning | Next | . | 0 | present / restored / published | proceed | . | 1 | miss — no such branch | build cold, then contribute | . | 2 | usage or environment error | stop the run, read the message, do not fallback to full build | . | 3 | found but unusable (corrupt, won’t link, wrong toolchain) | repair or reseed | .

a91332f9defb.title: Safety guards
a91332f9defb.content: When contributing a build back to the cache, it must be safe to run unconditionally. The contribution is refused unless it passes these guards: . | Non-empty: There must actually be artefacts to cache. | Own-package: Artefacts must belong to the package itself, not just its dependencies. | Trace coverage: There must be sufficient metadata (e.g. >90% traced) for the build tool to use the cache effectively. | No-shrink: The new result must not be materially smaller than the incumbent cache, preventing partial builds from destroying a fuller cache. | . For cold starts, seeding the cache uses a test-branch staging approach: the cache is seeded to a -test branch, and a restore is verified from a clean clone before touching production.

490c5a68989f.title: The warm-start principle: Cache the intermediates, not just the output
490c5a68989f.content: The core value of the cache is that an expensive step’s intermediate outputs survive across builds. The pattern is: a cache branch carries not just the final output but also the intermediate build artifacts that prevent the build system from re-deriving them: . | cache type | final output | intermediate artifacts | what they prevent | . | Lean | .olean files | .trace files | Lake rebuild + eviction | . | FHIR AST | AST JSON + edges | txcache/ (tx.fhir.org expansions) | Publisher re-hitting tx.fhir.org for every ValueSet | . input-cache/txcache/ goes on the fhir-ast branch alongside the AST files. Preserving these intermediates is what makes subsequent incremental builds (such as those in ig-incremental-build.bpmn) fast: a warm build with cached packages and terminology runs several times faster than a cold one.

45bd416db89a.title: Instantiations
45bd416db89a.content: | Aspect | Lean Cache (lean-cache-restore) | FHIR AST (ig-ast-delta) | . | Artefacts | .olean files, .trace files | Per-resource AST JSON, dependencies.json, txcache/ | . | Inputs Schema | CompiledInputsSchema | CompiledInputsSchema | . | Key Inputs | toolchain (Lean version), sourceRevision | toolchain (Publisher version), sourceRevision, inputDigest | . | Storage Branch | lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain> | fhir-ast/<ig-package-id> | . | Service Script | lake-cache.sh (9 verbs) | ig-cache.sh (7 verbs) | . | Refreshed by | an agent’s lake-cache.sh contribute | a reusable workflow of the IG layer, on a runner (the Publisher needs Java and a 10 GB heap), which each IG repository dispatches; a site build refuses an AST that is not valid | . | Cone Engine | Lake’s .trace-based dependency graph | SUSHI’s fsh-index.json (forward: file → resource) + fsh-cone.ts (reverse: who uses this file) + AstPlanCli | . | Incremental | lake build (only stale modules) | IncrementalBuildCli (cone rebuild loop) | .

785792d3dc58.title: The file-to-resource mapping comes from the toolchain, not from us
785792d3dc58.content: Do not reimplement what the compiler already knows. SUSHI already writes fsh-generated/data/fsh-index.json on every run — the authoritative mapping from source .fsh file to output FHIR resource, with source locations. The AST exporter copies it into the AST directory; the incremental planner reads it there. No modification to SUSHI is needed. fsh-cone (a Tool node, declared by the FHIR IG layer) provides the reverse half — who depends on a file — so a changed RuleSet- or Alias-only file (which produces no resource itself) can be traced to the resources it affects. These two maps together give the planner a complete cone. Without fsh-index.json the planner can only plan a full build; with it, a single-file change rebuilds only the resources in its cone, which is a small fraction of an IG.

98a660c2a288.title: Complete initialization
98a660c2a288.content: Process_CompleteInitialization · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A SUB-PROCESS of initialize-harness, called after a harness is installed and also when the location turns out to be a layer instantiating the chosen harness already. It is how an agent — the one that installed the harness, or one dispatched for exactly this with nothing but this diagram and the declaration — makes sure EVERY initialization step is done. THE STEPS ARE NOT LISTED HERE. They are named by the declarations: the layer’s <name>.json and every declaration it needs, read from the sibling checkouts. A declared directory is a step (it exists); a declared asset is a step (the file is there); a dependency’s <name>/docs/bootstrap/initialization.md is a step (it was followed); the root README and the sections it opts into are steps; the repository a declaration names makes the site steps — a Pages workflow, a gh-pages branch, Pages switched on, the address answering. A harness above bootstrap names more in the same way — a work-plan store it declares as a directory is a directory step — and bootstrap does not need to know which. The skill initialization-steps has the table. IDEMPOTENT BY CONSTRUCTION. Every step is CHECKED before anything is done, and a done step is left alone, so running this twice changes nothing the second time. Nothing is replaced: a step that would overwrite what somebody wrote is a step for a person, not for the agent. FOUR STATES, NOT TWO. done; not done; could not determine — the check could not run (no forge CLI, no network), which is NEVER reported as done; and stated — the declarations name it but nothing can observe it (reading and following instructions), exactly as a stated precondition is never reported as satisfied. THE PRIMARY STEP IS DRAWN, not left in the list: A_CheckDocuments, the harness’s JSON Schemas and JSON-LD at the IRIs they name, checked first after the declarations are read. Everything after it — directories, README, the site — is either how those documents are reached or how a person reads about them. WHERE TOOLS ARE AVAILABLE, a toolset may perform the same checks (initialization-steps); otherwise the agent reads files. The diagram is the same either way. NO work-plan element on any activity, and isExecutable is false, for the reasons initialize-harness gives. i i i i i i i i i Actors: Bootstrapping Agent .

f859014f05e7.doc: compute-QA: are the computations and witnesses sound?
f859014f05e7.title: compute-QA: are the computations and witnesses sound?
f859014f05e7.content: Process_ComputeQA · strict (defaulted) · 6 step(s) . Run qou’s compute-QA gates over computations/ and its witnesses, and publish one verdict per gate to the qa-reports branch. WHY ONE PROCESS. The gates used to live as inline steps in four workflow files, so nothing named them as a set, and the order an agent ran them in locally was whatever it remembered. They are now one table (scripts/compute-qa.py) and this one diagram; the workflows call the table, and each step carries a # bpmn-node: back-reference here. THE COMMANDS DID NOT CHANGE. Each gate runs the exact command the workflow step ran, with the same exit-code handling: a strict gate fails on a non-zero exit, a warn or advisory gate never fails the run and its output is the report; when it exits non-zero its verdict is WARN rather than PASS, so a finding is not recorded as green. Measured on main before the move and after it, every gate’s exit codes and output are identical. QA IS AGENT-OWNED; CI IS A BACKUP. These workflows are dispatch-only (owner directive 2026-06-30, Actions billing), and several have never run. So the normal way through this process is an agent running python3 scripts/compute-qa.py before it commits, not CI. The lane says who runs a gate, not where. THREE OUTCOMES. A gate whose script cannot start (a missing module or binary) is UNKNOWN and never a pass. A failing self-test fails its gate whatever the gate’s mode, because a detector that has stopped matching its known positive reports everything clean. VERDICTS ARE NOT COMMITTED. Each gate writes test/results/compute-qa/<gate>.json, which is gitignored and is the layout bun run qa:publish reads. No rendered diagram — run bun run cat render:bpmn.

8ad1ac5e76eb.title: Which harness, and where
8ad1ac5e76eb.content: Skill confirm-harness: Narrow the harnesses and locations this could be, then have the Requestor settle it. Takes a list; returns at most ONE harness. It needs a person: the Requestor settles it, never the agent. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are the Bootstrapping Agent. You may narrow; only the Requestor may decide.

ff8dae515b6b.title: The contract
ff8dae515b6b.content: |   |   | . | in, from the Bootstrapping Agent | 0 or more harnesses · 0 or more locations | . | out, from the Requestor | 0 or 1 harness · 0 or more locations | . At most one. A list of two harnesses is not an answer, and you may not break the tie yourself. Zero is a real outcome, not a failure to try again: it ends the process, logged.

7df4f37c9dc6.title: Building the list you go in with
7df4f37c9dc6.content: Harnesses. The default is bootstrap itself. Add any the context already names: “please set up <owner>/<repo> here” in a discussion names one, and so does any Harness built on bootstrap that the Requestor mentions. Locations. Is this already a git repository? Were one or more URLs to repositories supplied? Both are Knowledge Graph Data Stores and the difference is only how you reach them — the git CLI, or a forge’s API. Assume a remote repository is read-only (read-from). Having push access to a remote git repository is never evidence that you are meant to modify it, and never makes it written-to. When a remote Knowledge Graph is supplied, two modes are open — and the Requestor chooses which: . | keep it here (read-from) — build and render from the remote Knowledge Graph in this repository, with whether to materialize its content locally or reference it in place asked as its own question; or | put a harness on the remote repository (written-to) — instantiate the harness in that remote repository itself. Nothing is written to a remote repository without the Requestor’s explicit permission for that repository. | .

f1a0c620a468.title: Asking
f1a0c620a468.content: Before you ask, say where you are — Initialize a harness, determining the harness and repositories, as the Bootstrapping Agent, asking the Requestor — and if you cannot tell that the person in front of you is the Requestor, ask that first (human-agent-discussion). Ask through human-agent-discussion: context, the candidates as options, your recommendation, and, said before the question, that there is no default: with no answer, the process stops. Ask once, with what you found, and make it answerable by picking: . What should this become? I can see (list). If it is none of those, name the repository — owner/name. If they answer with a kind — “a paper”, “a guideline” — that is not an answer yet: tell them which harnesses you know of and ask them to pick one. A kind is a property of the harness they name, and you read it from that harness rather than asking for it separately.

2309e4648935.title: Do not guess
2309e4648935.content: A wrong harness does not fail. It succeeds at being the wrong thing, and every consumer that reads the declaration believes it. So when you cannot get an answer: say the process needs one harness, log the failure, and stop.

a11b021b9aae.title: A confirmation can be waived — by the person who is owed it
a11b021b9aae.content: Skill confirmation-waiver: A human may waive a confirmation they are owed — for a session, for a process run, or until a stated time. Covers what a waiver is made of, where it is recorded (the context graph, never the work plan), the gates that can be waived and the rules that cannot, why every waiver carries an expiry, and the one thing an agent may never do: grant itself one. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Several rules here stop an agent and hand a decision back: merging to main, removing a durable artefact, spawning a swarm, closing a work item whose evidence the session could not re-derive, re-entering a process it fell out of. The person who is owed a confirmation may give it in advance, for a stated scope. That is the same decision, made earlier, by the same person — never an agent making an exception for itself.

f5c4814446e0.title: A waiver is five fields, and none is optional
f5c4814446e0.content: | field | what it carries | why it cannot be omitted | . | granted_by | the person, by the identity the repository already knows them by | a waiver with no grantor is an agent’s own decision wearing a hat | . | quote | the grantor’s own words, verbatim | the agent’s paraphrase is the thing under suspicion; a summary can widen a scope without anyone noticing | . | gate | which gate class is waived (below) — never “everything” | a blanket waiver is indistinguishable from no rule, and nobody can audit what it covered | . | scope | session:<id>, process:<instance-id>, or until:<ISO-8601> | an unscoped waiver outlives the situation that justified it | . | expires | a timestamp, always | same argument bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) makes for a block: a waiver with no expiry cannot be told from one nobody remembered to withdraw | . A waiver missing any field is not a waiver, and the gate stands. An agent that finds a malformed one asks, exactly as if none existed.

d45e725cf4c7.title: The gates that can be waived, and the rules that cannot
d45e725cf4c7.content: A waiver relaxes a rule whose text is ask first. It can never relax a rule whose text is never. Never delete a work item is such a prohibition: no waiver reaches it, and the non-destructive move (scrapped, with reasons) is always available. | gate class | the rule it relaxes | waivable | . | merge-to-main | merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — the owner’s authorisation for each merge (and crdm-requirements-workflow §Phase 6) | yes, for green heads only: a head in a repository with no CI is never covered | . | bean-close | bean-coordination §”When you cannot re-derive it yourself” — the ready-to-close batch | yes | . | deletion | deletion-requires-confirmation — report and wait | yes, per artefact class, never blanket | . | swarm-spawn | swarm-management — asked every time, per swarm | yes, with the agent count and model level named in the quote | . | process-reentry | process-state — confirm before re-entering | yes | . | issue-close | issue-working — an agent never closes an issue on its own say-so | yes; the waiver names the issues | . | agent permission grants | agent-permissions — a person grants what a coding agent may do | no — never self-granted, and granted per permission | . | hand-edited agent config | harness-projections — consent per change to .claude/settings.json and the like | no — consent is per change | . | work item deletion | todo-manager, never delete a work item | no — a prohibition, not a gate | . | fabricating evidence | anywhere a rule says re-derive rather than quote | no | . A never that somebody wants waived is a change to the skill that owns it — not a waiver.

09274bfe1078.title: Where a waiver lives — the context graph, never the work plan
09274bfe1078.content: A waiver is context: read at the start of a turn, consulted by whatever gate is about to fire, and never produced by the work it governs. That is the context layer as content-context-and-state-graphs defines it, so a waiver is a node under memory/waivers/ — the same graph an agent’s durable memory lives in. Not beans/. The work plan is state: it records what is being worked on and where it got to. A waiver is not work, has no Done-when, and must be readable by a gate that fires before any work item is opened. The work plan is also branch-local, so a session-scoped waiver filed there could be invisible to the session it was granted for. Not the interaction node (memory/interaction.json) either: that is read at session start and never written by a process, and a waiver is granted mid-session.

eb3a011dd705.title: Consulting one — the three-state read, as everywhere else
eb3a011dd705.content: Before a gate fires, look for a waiver in scope. There are three answers: . | A valid waiver covers this gate, in scope, unexpired → proceed, and say in the turn report which waiver you are acting under, quoting its words. A waived action is still an announced one. | No waiver → ask, exactly as the gate’s own skill says. | Could not determine — memory/waivers/ unreadable, a malformed node, a clock you cannot trust → ask. A gate that cannot read its waivers has not been waived. | . An expired waiver is kept, never deleted, as a scrapped work item is: the record of what was permitted, to whom and when, makes the next grant reviewable.

e781e39e99c0.title: What an agent may never do
e781e39e99c0.content: . | Grant itself a waiver. A waiver whose quote is not the grantor’s own words does not exist. If you are composing the sentence, you are the grantor, and you may not be. | Widen one. session: does not reach the next session; process: does not reach a sibling layer; deletion for build artefacts does not reach content. When the scope does not plainly cover the case in front of you, it does not cover it. | Infer one from tone. “go ahead”, “yes”, “do it” discharge the gate they were said to — that is an ordinary confirmation, and it needs no waiver node. A waiver is a standing grant over future gates, and it is recorded only when the owner says something that plainly is one. | Treat a waiver as a reason to skip the work. merge-to-main waived still means green CI and no conflict; bean-close waived still means the evidence is quoted in the work item. A waiver removes the asking, never the doing. | .

fa75bb408e51.title: Checked, not trusted
fa75bb408e51.content: bun run cat check:waivers reads every node under memory/waivers/ and fails on a missing field, a gate outside the table above, a scope that names a non-existent session or layer, and a waiver over a non-waivable rule. It reports expired waivers as inert, never as findings — they are history. The check reads the same table this skill publishes, so a gate class without a row is refused and the vocabulary cannot drift into “everything”.

131bb0fac54a.title: Acquisition is the step before ingestion
131bb0fac54a.content: Skill content-acquisition: Getting a resource INTO the graph in the first place — accepting one offered unprompted, or asking for one and then asking for it to be uploaded. The channels are plural and open: uploads/ is one, the conversation is another. Runs before document ingestion, which begins only once a file has landed. Named by: Content acquisition . document-ingestion.bpmn begins at StartEvent_Dropped — “a file lands in uploads/“. This skill covers everything before that drop: noticing something is needed, asking for it, telling somebody where to put it, seeing it arrive.

0724ea73cf4d.title: Channels are plural, and the set is open
0724ea73cf4d.content: | channel | what arrives | what it is good for | . | uploads/ | a file, dropped or committed | PDFs, images, anything binary or large | . | the conversation | a link, a quotation, a narrative description | anything a person can say faster than they can find | . Do not treat uploads/ as the acquisition mechanism. It is one, and the most visible, which is why it gets mistaken for the whole. A description given in chat is an acquired resource: it has a source, it can be wrong, and it belongs in the graph with its provenance exactly as a PDF does. Anything added later — a connector, a watched mailbox, a forge issue with attachments — is another row, with no change to this skill.

150f21ab97f2.title: Two directions, and the unprompted one is easy to forget
150f21ab97f2.content: Unprompted. A person offers something with no ask: they drop a file, paste a link, or describe a paper. Accept it. Do not tell them to wait for a step, and do not make them follow a process to hand you something they already have. Record what it is and where it came from, then route it — a file to ingestion, a link or a description to whatever will resolve it. Prompted. Work has reached a point where a resource is needed. Then: . | Say what is needed and why, specifically enough that somebody could go and find it. “The WHO guideline this chapter cites” is findable; “more sources” is not. | Ask for what they can give, and name both forms — a link, or a description in their own words. A person who cannot find the file often knows exactly what it is, and a description is an acquired resource, not a consolation prize. | Only then ask for an upload, with the place to put it — see below. | Say what happens if they do nothing, per decision-comparison and interaction-modality §4.1: which is usually that the work proceeds without the resource and says so. | . Asking for all of it at once is what turns a request into a form. Asking for the upload FIRST is worse: it demands the one thing they may not have, before the cheaper answers have been offered.

2b9bbb58f24e.title: Never write the upload URL by hand
2b9bbb58f24e.content: Use bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/upload-url.ts [branch], which composes it from the declaration. A declared path is relative to its scope: with no scope, { id: "uploads", path: "uploads/" } resolves under the layer (e.g. cat-harness/uploads/ in an index checkout), while a forge URL needs it relative to the repository. Pasting the declared path into /upload/<branch>/ drops the layer segment and mints a 404. Every failure is named rather than guessed. No origin remote, a non-GitHub forge, a declared-but-absent queue — each returns a reason and a remedy, because a URL is believed and somebody sent to a wrong one cannot tell it from an empty directory. When it cannot resolve, fall back to the conversation: that is what the other channel is for.

450fe8be91e5.title: After the ask — watch, do not poll the person
450fe8be91e5.content: A resource may arrive minutes or days later, and chasing is how an agent becomes noise. uploads-watch covers noticing an arrival; the rule here is only that the person is asked once, and the next thing they hear is either the work continuing or a report that it could not.

7baa9a1d7be4.title: What acquisition does NOT do

1098e1a17c33.content: This skill analyses the full knowledge graph of the monograph at three coupled levels: . | Block graph — Every content block under folio/quantum-observable-universe/ is a node. 6c9975b302bd.title: Heuristics
6c9975b302bd.content: The skill applies the following heuristics, each producing a severity- ranked finding: . H1 — Forward references (severity: HIGH) . A forward reference occurs when block A uses block B, but B appears later in the document than A. These cause readers to encounter concepts before they are defined. A block’s position is its (chapter_number, section_index, block_index) tuple in document order. forward_ref: A (pos P_A) uses B (pos P_B) where P_B > P_A . Ideal: 0 forward references. Acceptable: ≤ 5 (architectural cycles across categorical/archimedean wall). Flag for action: > 5. H2 — Cross-chapter coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . A cross-chapter edge occurs when block A in chapter C₁ uses block B in chapter C₂ (C₁ ≠ C₂). Count cross-chapter edges per chapter pair (C₁ → C₂): . | Edges going forward (C₁.number < C₂.number): normal; blocks in early chapters depend on later chapters’ content → may be a problem (forward reference by chapter). | Edges going backward (C₁.number > C₂.number): normal; later chapters build on earlier ones → fine. | . Flag: chapters with more than 10 cross-chapter forward edges. H3 — Cross-section coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . Same as H2 but at section granularity within a single chapter. Report any section pair where ≥ 3 blocks reference each other across section boundaries. Ratio metric: cross_section_edges / total_edges_in_chapter. | Ratio < 0.20: well-structured | 0.20–0.40: moderate coupling | 0.40: high coupling — restructuring likely needed . | . H4 — Section too sparse (severity: LOW) . Sections with fewer than 3 content blocks (excluding intro prose) risk fragmenting the narrative. They are candidates for merging with an adjacent section. Threshold: < 3 non-prose blocks. Exception: Intro/overview sections (first block is prose). H5 — Section too dense (severity: LOW) . Sections with more than 18 content blocks are hard to navigate. Threshold: > 18 blocks. Suggestion: Split along natural dependency boundaries within the section. H6 — Isolated blocks (severity: LOW) . A block with no uses[] edges (other than prose/intro) and no block in uses[] of other blocks is isolated. It may belong to a different section or chapter, or may be dead content. H7 — Remark / example ratio (severity: INFO) . Sections where remark + example blocks outnumber provable blocks (definition + theorem + lemma + proposition + corollary + conjecture) by more than 2:1 may have too much interpretation and too little formal content — or vice versa.

b48d23e0ef34.title: Lean 4 Subgraph Heuristics (L1..L6 — Process_GraphDetanglement)
b48d23e0ef34.content: In addition to prose heuristics H1..H7, scripts/lean-kg-detangler.py and scripts/lean-best-practices-lint.py enforce six Lean subgraph invariants derived from Process_GraphDetanglement: . L1 — Unassigned-first completeness (severity: CRITICAL) . Every library .lean module and every resolved import edge must be classified (unassigned_library_modules == 0, unassigned_resolved_edges == 0) BEFORE evaluating cross-edge or cut-edge counts. Zero cross-edges over an unjudged subset is never read as clean. L2 — Strict zero-QOU.* boundary on Tier-A & Tier-B Reservoir libraries (severity: CRITICAL, BP008) . Pure-mathematics modules in Tier-A (MathlibExt) and the 6 Tier-B Lean Reservoir community lean_lib packages (HeckeTemperleyLieb, TwistedFrobeniusHopf, ToricConicOpt, CompactQuantumMetrics, QCalculus, BraidKnotOctonion) MUST have zero upward import QOU.<Model> edges into QOU physics/framework modules. Resolve any community_to_qou_cut_edges via the four detanglement moves: prune an unused import, merge mutually-defining helpers, factor the pure base definition downward, or reclassify a misbucketed target. L3 — Subgraph condensation acyclicity (severity: HIGH) . Both the module-level import graph and the inter-lean_lib condensation graph must be strictly acyclic (0 Tarjan SCCs of size > 1; imports point monotonically toward lower architectural layers L0 Mathlib → L1 MathlibExt/UGB → L2 QCalculus → L3 TwistedFrobeniusHopf → L4 ToricConicOpt → L5 CompactQuantumMetrics → L6 HeckeTemperleyLieb → L7 BraidKnotOctonion → L8..L15 QOU.<Chapter>). L4 — Synonym-directory anti-sprawl & Open-PR Fixup (severity: CRITICAL, BP009) . folio/quantum-observable-universe/lean/ is isolated under Q3 Option 1 (7 top-level community [[lean_lib]] roots + 12 canonical QOU/<Chapter>/ subgraphs; 0 loose QOU/*.lean files). Never create ad-hoc synonym directories under QOU/ or lean/. New pure math goes directly to MathlibExt/ or one of the 6 Tier-B roots (see lean-mathlibext-curator.md); new QOU model Lean goes to QOU/<Chapter>/. When rebasing a pre-migration branch or open PR, run nice -n 15 python3 scripts/apply-lean-reservoir-migration.py --fixup-branch to relocate legacy QOU/<OldDir>/ modules and rewrite imports/lean.refs deterministically. L5 — §7c Base-ring & empirical wall alignment (severity: HIGH, BP005 / BP006) . Tier-A/Tier-B community libraries and pre-wall chapters stay over generic {R : Type*} [CommRing R] / [Field R] / [LinearOrderedField R] with zero decimal literals, Float, CODATA, or substrate_q. Concrete (R := ℝ) evaluations live exclusively post-wall. L6 — Root & lean.ref reachability (severity: MEDIUM) . Every .lean module should be reachable either from its lean_lib root aggregator (QOU.lean / Tier-B root) or from a live .ts lean.ref / chapter sibling import (scripts/lean-root-coverage-audit.py + scripts/dead-lean-pointer-audit.py).

If a block spans two chapters’ topics, split it (see PR5). PR2 — Forward-reference & upward-leak avoidance . A new prose block must appear after all blocks it uses[], and a new .lean module must import only same-or-lower architectural layers (BP008). PR3 — Section density bounds . When adding blocks to a section, check the count stays within 3–18 blocks. If adding would exceed 18, split the section first (H5). If a removal would drop a section below 3, consider merging (H4). PR4 — Cross-chapter dependency direction . New blocks should depend backward (on earlier chapters), not forward. If a new block in Ch 3 needs to use something from Ch 7, either: . | Move the dependency to Ch 3 first, or | Place the new block in Ch 7 instead. | . PR5 — Topic-coherent blocks . After any block move, section split/merge, or directory rename, update docs/reorganization-map.md with the change. 90f1c3c06f9a.title: Workflow
90f1c3c06f9a.content: Step 1 — Parse the content tree . Read the paper manifest quantum-observable-universe.ts to enumerate chapters. For each chapter, read its manifest to enumerate sections and their block lists. Assign each block a document position (chapter_number, section_index, block_index). For each block .ts file, extract: . | label, kind, uses[], interprets, proofs[], examples[] | . Step 2 — Build the block graph . Build an adjacency map: . edges[(from_label, to_label)] = edge_type # "uses"|"interprets"|"proof"|"example" . Index every block’s document position: . position[label] = (chapter_no, section_idx, block_idx) . Step 3 — Build the chapter/section graph . For each chapter pair (C₁, C₂) count directed edges from blocks in C₁ to blocks in C₂: . chapter_edges[(c1_num, c2_num)] += 1 . For each section pair within the same chapter, count cross-section edges: . section_edges[(s1_label, s2_label)] += 1 . Step 4 — Apply heuristics . Run each heuristic (H1–H7) and collect findings. Each finding has: . | severity: HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / INFO | heuristic: H1–H7 | description: human-readable explanation | blocks: list of involved block labels | suggestion: proposed action | . Step 5 — Generate visualisations . Two DOT/SVG outputs (via Graphviz): . 5a. Chapter/section graph (/tmp/content_chapter_graph.svg) . | Nodes: chapters (large boxes) containing sections (small boxes) | Edges: weighted directed arrows between sections | Color: red = forward cross-chapter edges, orange = high cross-section coupling, gray = normal backward dependencies | . 5b. Block graph heat-map (/tmp/content_block_heatmap.svg) . | Nodes: blocks (grouped by chapter/section in clusters) | Edges: forward references only (red), cross-chapter edges (orange) | Isolated blocks highlighted in yellow | . Step 6 — Report findings . Print a ranked report (HIGH → LOW → INFO): . ## Content Graph Analysis: quantum-observable-universe ### Summary - Total blocks: N | Chapters: N | Sections: N - Total block edges: N (uses/interprets/proof/example) - Cross-chapter edges: N | Cross-section edges: N - Forward references: N ### HIGH — Forward References (H1) - block A (ch1/sec2) uses block B (ch3/sec5) ← B defined later Suggestion: move B earlier, or add stub to ch1 ### MEDIUM — Cross-Chapter Coupling (H2) - Ch4 → Ch1: 14 forward edges ← Ch4 blocks depend on Ch1 Top offending blocks: ... ### LOW — Sparse Sections (H4) - sec:my-section (Ch3): 2 non-prose blocks Suggestion: merge with adjacent sec:other-section ### LOW — Dense Sections (H5) - sec:hadrons-knot-composites (Ch4): 20 blocks Suggestion: split into "Hadron operations" + "Quark structure" . Step 7 — Interactive suggestions . After the report, offer the user a numbered menu of actions they can approve: . What would you like to do? [1] Move block X from sec:A to sec:B [2] Split sec:large-section into two sections [3] Add a new section "Preliminaries" in Ch3 to absorb forward refs [4] Merge sec:sparse-1 and sec:sparse-2 [5] Show detailed block graph for chapter N [6] Re-run analysis after changes [0] Done . For each approved action, make the minimal changes to the .ts manifest files. Step 8 — Implement approved moves . For a block move (action [1]): . | Remove the block name from blocks[] in its current section. | Add the block name to blocks[] in the target section at the correct position (after its uses[] dependencies). | Re-run the analysis to confirm improvement. | . For a section split (action [2]): . | Ask the user to name the two new sections and choose a split point. | Rewrite the chapter manifest with two section({...}) entries. | Move blocks to the correct new section. | . For a section merge (action [4]): . | Combine the two blocks[] arrays in document order. | Remove the merged-away section from the chapter manifest. | . Always show a before/after energy comparison: . Before: energy=142, backward_edges=12, sparse_sections=3 After: energy=87, backward_edges=4, sparse_sections=1 .

56477235b5a1.content: Findings and a decision — two things, not one. See decision-audit and schemas/sdlc/qa-review.ts. | Findings — one per observation, each carrying the axis this reviewer can speak on: blocking | suggestion | praise for a person, critical | major | minor for a checker. Neither defaults into the other, and praise has no machine equivalent. | A decision — approve | request-changes | reject, naming every finding it weighed and every one it overruled. Approving over an open critical or blocking finding without overruling it is a reported problem. | .

ebdd5048f85c.title: Translations are reviewed in their own loop
ebdd5048f85c.content: A content review judges the source text. A translation of it is judged string by string in translation-adjudication: anyone proposes from the review page or a block’s 🌐 pane, and an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates. Approving a source change does not approve its translations. When the change rewrites source text, those strings go stale and re-enter that loop; that does not hold back the content review.

ff2f45b986cb.title: Running CI, not just assuming it
ff2f45b986cb.content: A local build runs on a warm cache, your toolchain and your flags; CI runs cold on its own. A local green is evidence about your machine, not about the branch. Push, then dispatch the workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <workflow>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and record run URL + conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. If dispatch is refused for lack of actions: write, say so in the PR and give the command a maintainer should run. Also check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): a workflow nothing dispatches can sit red on main while the content it checks stops building.

9578eace9d27.title: A green build only covers what the target reaches
9578eace9d27.content: Before reading “build green” as a claim about the corpus, check what the build target actually compiles. Build systems often default to narrow roots: the target compiles its root plus whatever that root imports, not every source in the directory. Where sources are found and what is built are separate settings. The check is cheap in any build system — count build artifacts against sources. A ratio far from 1 means the green is scoped, and any corpus-wide number read off that build — open-obligation counts, coverage, warning totals — is an undercount by construction. Say what the build covered, not just that it passed.

cc3dfba541b3.title: Where the results go — not into a commit
cc3dfba541b3.content: A test run’s results are derived: re-running the plan over the same tree and data reproduces them. They are kept where every derived QA result is kept — the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by the commit they were computed on (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/), written by bun run cat qa:publish (the CI job qa-publish) and read back with bun run qa:fetch. Do not regenerate a results file in order to commit it. Two things a test run produces are not derived, and they stay on main: . | A reviewer’s judgement of a case — an SME or QC reviewer’s verdict, an agent’s adjudication — goes to test/attestations/ (qa-attestations/v1), because no re-run can reproduce it. | A certification — an accountable decision taken on a plan’s rollup — also stays on main, beside the attestations, and is then signed through qa-report-signing (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | . “Regression comparison” against a previous version is a comparison against its stored results: --against <ref> on a gate, or qa:fetch --ref for a report. A previous version with no stored entry is UNKNOWN — say so; never read it as “no regressions”.

a0f48d713228.title: /continual-progress — trackable, always-PR’d, continually-committed work
a0f48d713228.content: Skill continual-progress: Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Sibling agents and the author can only coordinate with work they can see. This skill makes every in-flight task trackable in real time: the PR is open from the first commit, progress lands as a stream of small pushed commits, and the PR body carries a live status checklist. It is the visibility complement to /coordinate (which triages across PRs); this one governs how your own PR stays legible while you work.

d2b39867e141.title: The four invariants
d2b39867e141.content: . | Always have an open PR (from commit #1). Branch, make the first (even stub) commit, push, open the PR — before further work. The PR is the durable, visible artifact; the chat session is ephemeral. Never accumulate work on a local branch with no PR. (Operationalises AGENTS.md “Branch + PR workflow” rule 2.) . | Commit + push small, coherent increments — continuously. Each logically distinct change is its own commit (a single fix, a single module, a single proof). Push after each commit (or every 2–3 if moving fast). A watcher should be able to git log your branch and see a legible, bisectable trail — not one giant drop. Target: no more than ~20–30 min of work between pushes on a long task. | Keep a live status checklist in the PR body. Maintain a - [ ] / - [x] checklist of the task’s sub-parts in the PR description (or a pinned top comment), updated as each increment lands. A sibling or the author should be able to read the PR body and know exactly what is done / in-flight / remaining — without reading the diff or asking in chat. | Post brief intent — on your PR and overlapping siblings. One short intent line on PR-open (“doing X on <files>; will touch <scope>”); a one-line comment on any sibling whose scope overlaps (“starting <theme> on <files>; flag conflicts”). Don’t stream comments — update the checklist (invariant 3) for routine progress; comment only for genuine coordination (overlap, a blocker, a handoff-relevant finding). Defer to /coordinate for the full cross-PR triage protocol. | .

a64be888b256.title: Why — the failure modes this prevents
a64be888b256.content: . | Stepped-on work. A branch that hoards uncommitted work collides with siblings the moment it lands. Continual push surfaces intent from minute 1 so siblings triage around it. | Lost work on session reclaim. Cloud sessions are ephemeral; an uncommitted change vanishes when the container is reclaimed. Push it. | Opaque progress. “What’s the status?” should be answerable from the PR body, not a chat scrollback. The checklist is the source of truth. | Un-takeoverable tasks. If you go idle/blocked, a sibling can pick up a continually-committed, checklist-annotated PR; they cannot pick up an opaque local branch. | .

a42e9cbf60d7.title: Checklist (run this as you work)
a42e9cbf60d7.content: . | PR open? If not: branch → stub commit → push → open it now. | Anything uncommitted older than ~20–30 min? Commit + push it. | Does the PR-body status checklist reflect the current state? | Any sibling whose files I just started touching un-notified? One intent line (not a stream). | Blocked or going idle? Update the checklist + a one-line “blocked on X / handoff-ready” note so a sibling can continue. | .

3233aaad7e14.title: Relationship to other skills
3233aaad7e14.content: . | /coordinate — cross-PR triage (scope map, sibling intent, cherry-picks, ledger). continual-progress keeps your PR legible so /coordinate (yours or a sibling’s) has something to triage. | AGENTS.md “Branch + PR workflow” — this skill operationalises rules 2–6 (always-PR, microcommit, push-often) as a runnable checklist. | /todo-manager — the session work-plan; the PR-body status checklist (invariant 3) is its externally-visible projection, so a watcher needs no access to the session’s TodoWrite. | .

db5e1a0127ee.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
db5e1a0127ee.title: Contributor feedback on a working draft
db5e1a0127ee.content: Process_ContributorFeedback · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A document is still being written, and the Authoring Committee gives feedback on it in a shared Contributor Feedback sheet. This is what happens to ONE change set, one row of that sheet: a member starts it with a title, the sections it is about and their feedback; the agent proposes a direction; an Editor lets the agent edit; the agent makes the edit in the row’s one pull request, whose staging preview shows what changed; the committee answers on the row; and an Editor lets the agent merge. If the row’s feedback changes after the agent wrote its proposal, the proposal is marked stale and the row’s Ready for agent goes back to No, so the agent proposes again and an Editor decides again. The sheet’s colours follow the lanes: Blue for the committee, Green for the agent, Orange for the Editor. Skill: review-sheet-script. i i i i i i i i i Actors: Authoring Committee · Authoring agent · Editor · QA reviewer (independent) .

56f7472ebc54.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
56f7472ebc54.title: Lanes — who acts
56f7472ebc54.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Authoring Committee | authoring-committee | The people writing the document with the editor: contributors, each with their own Contributor Feedback column (Blue). They start rows, give feedback and answer the preview. They recommend; they do not set the Ready columns. | . | Authoring agent | authoring-agent | Writes only Green cells and the Agent tab. Proposes a direction for each row, edits the document in the row’s one pull request once an Editor says so, and merges it once an Editor says so. | . | Editor | editor | The one lane that decides, through the Orange Ready columns, which only the people in the sheet’s EDITORS list may set. Ready for agent lets the agent edit; Ready for merge lets it merge. | . | QA reviewer (independent) | qc-reviewer | Whoever runs the QA gate: an agent session that did not write the row’s pull request, or a person. Never the authoring agent’s own session. Writes only QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab. | .

3387238260f1.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
3387238260f1.title: Steps
3387238260f1.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Start a change-set rowTask_StartRow | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | A member adds a row on the Contributor Feedback tab: a title, the Selected Sections it is about (a dropdown from the document’s table of contents) and their feedback in their own Blue column. The script gives the row its Change-set id and links each section. | . | Propose a directionTask_Propose | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | Reads: the row (Title, Selected Sections, the Contributor Feedback columns, Disposition) and the sections it names. Writes: a proposed direction in Feedback (agent) (Green), and the row’s feedback basis on the Agent tab, so the script can tell when the feedback has moved on. A question for people goes in Feedback (agent) as a Decision needed block with options and a recommendation, and the row’s Agentic status becomes Needs human; a chat card may repeat it, but the sheet is the record. An answered question leaves the feedback: its decision is added to the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab, shown in Disposition (agent), whose decision history is appended to and never removed. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for agent to YesTask_ReadyForAgent | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor agrees the direction and sets the row’s Ready for agent (Orange) to Yes. Person-only: the agent never sets it. | . | Edit the document in the row’s pull requestTask_EditInPullRequest | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | One row, one branch, one active pull request: the agent edits on the row’s branch and opens its pull request, or updates it when the row comes round again. A closed pull request the committee wants back is reopened, or replaced by a new one on the same branch; earlier ones stay listed in Agentic status. Agentic status (Green) says where it is, and Staging review opens the preview’s what-changed page. Before the preview is staged, the agent writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab: one line per feedback item, starting from the people’s Blue Disposition, after an optional Overall statement; the sheet shows it in Disposition (agent) and flags any item without a disposition, or one that differs from the people’s. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Review the preview and answerTask_AnswerPreview | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | Members read the preview and answer in their Blue columns, or leave them as they are when the change is right. They record the row’s Disposition (Blue): Pending, Accepted, Partially accepted, Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope. | . | QA gate: check dispositions and PRTask_QaGate | QA reviewer (independent) | review-sheet-script | Reads: the change set’s Disposition (change set), the people’s Blue Disposition and feedback, the pull request’s diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every feedback item has one disposition; that each agrees with the people’s Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted item has the change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope item has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab, first line “Passed <head sha>: …” or “Failed <head sha>: <why>”, and QA report (change set), the report’s link. The sheet shows the gate under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for merge to YesTask_ReadyForMerge | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor sets the row’s Ready for merge (Orange) to Yes once the QA gate has passed for the pull request’s head commit. Person-only. Set earlier, the agent does not merge until the gate passes, and its feedback says so. | . | Merge the pull requestTask_Merge | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | The agent merges the row’s pull request, and Agentic status says merged. The change set’s Dispositions blurb, as it stands when Ready for merge is set to Yes, is the summary: it goes into the merge, and closes the change set’s issue. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Close the change set: the issue, then the sheet rowTask_CloseChangeSet | Authoring agent | review-sheet-agent-columns | Closing is one step with two tools, GitHub and the review sheet. The agent closes the change set’s issue on GitHub, with the merge or the reason it closed unmerged, then records Agentic status Closed (or Change merged) on the Agent tab through Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn). The sheet script then hides the row and strikes the whole row through (“make sure complete changeset rows are hidden so not cluttered and that text of that whole row is crossed out”). The agent never hides or strikes a row by hand, and never deletes one: reopening the issue and writing a new status shows it again. Hiding and striking are formatting only, which the review-log watcher ignores. A change set closed without a merge, at a person’s request, takes this step too. | .
