24187193e35b.title: Decision methodology selector
24187193e35b.content: Skill decision-methodology-selector: Given a decision context, select the applicable methodology from the methodology graph. Reads the graph’s applies-when declarations, matches them against the context, and returns the ranked applicable methods with rationale. Extends methodology-adoption’s four-question protocol with quantitative method-selection criteria from the MCDM literature. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Options analysis, SWOT situation analysis . Input: a decision context — what is being decided, how many alternatives, how many criteria, available data, time constraints, stakeholder count, reversibility, uncertainty level. Output: a ranked list of applicable methodologies, each with: . | the methodology name and its graph-node id | why it fits this context (matched applies-when) | why it does NOT fit the alternatives (matched not-for) | complexity rating | data requirements | .

b15f67aa6ba1.title: Relationship to methodology-adoption
b15f67aa6ba1.content: methodology-adoption carries the protocol — four questions asked in order, the first yes decides. This skill carries the implementation: given that the protocol routes the decision to a category (computable, evidence-grading, decision-record, decision-analysis), which specific methodology in the graph serves that category best for this context? . methodology-adoption names the lane; this skill names the runner.

ead78ba858bd.title: Decision context schema
ead78ba858bd.content: A decision context has these dimensions. Not all are required — an agent provides what it knows and the selector grades against what is declared. | dimension | type | when it matters | . | questionType | "computable" \| "evidence-grading" \| "decision-record" \| "decision-analysis" | Always — from methodology-adoption §”Choosing which applies” | . | alternativeCount | number | MCDM methods scale differently | . | criteriaCount | number | AHP pairwise comparisons grow as n² | . | criteriaWeightsKnown | boolean | Some methods derive weights, others require them | . | dataType | "quantitative" \| "qualitative" \| "mixed" | Aggregation methods need numbers | . | stakeholderCount | number | Group methods (Delphi, ANP) vs solo | . | timeConstraint | "minutes" \| "hours" \| "days" \| "weeks" | Eliminates complex methods | . | reversibility | "reversible" \| "costly" \| "irreversible" | Higher stakes → more rigorous method | . | uncertainty | "low" \| "moderate" \| "high" \| "deep" | Bayesian methods for deep uncertainty | . | sequential | boolean | True when decisions recur or adapt over time | .

b684554fe52f.title: Method families and when to use them
b684554fe52f.content: 1. MCDM aggregation methods . When: multiple alternatives scored against multiple criteria, quantitative data available, goal is a ranking. Source: Wang & Rangaiah, “Multi-Criteria Decision-Making: Aggregation-Type Methods” (arXiv:2509.06388). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | SAW (Simple Additive Weighting) | First pass, well-understood criteria, all benefit-type after normalisation | Criteria on incomparable scales without good normalisation | Low | . | MEW (Multiplicative Exponent Weighting) | Criteria with exponential importance differences | Any criterion value is zero (product collapses) | Low | . | AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) | Weights unknown, need stakeholder consensus on priorities | >9 criteria (pairwise comparisons explode: n(n-1)/2) | Medium | . | ANP (Analytic Network Process) | Criteria have interdependencies (feedback loops) | Simple independent criteria (overkill) | High | . | COPRAS | Benefit and cost criteria naturally separated | All criteria same direction | Medium | . | MOORA | Quick ranking with ratio normalisation | Need for weight derivation (requires pre-set weights) | Low | . | FUCA | Alternatives close in score, need tie-breaking | Very few alternatives (<3) | Medium | . | WASPAS | Combines SAW + MEW for robustness check | When SAW and MEW agree (no added value) | Medium | . 2. Probabilistic / sequential decision methods . When: decisions recur, data arrives over time, exploration-exploitation trade-off matters, experiments are costly. Source: Kristiadi, “Introduction to the Analysis of Probabilistic Decision-Making Algorithms” (arXiv:2508.21620). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Multi-armed bandits (UCB, Thompson sampling) | Repeated choice among options with unknown payoffs | One-shot decisions | Medium | . | Bayesian optimisation | Expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions, few evaluations | Cheap evaluations (just try them all) | High | . | Tree search (MCTS) | Sequential decisions with branching outcomes | No natural tree structure | High | . | Contextual bandits | Payoff depends on observable context | Context is not available or not meaningful | Medium | . The source backs bandits and Bayesian optimisation only: the ingested version has no tree-search chapter and does not mention contextual bandits, so those two rows are UNSOURCED. 3. Social / behavioral decision methods . When: multiple stakeholders, group consensus needed, behavioral biases must be accounted for. Source: Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology” (arXiv:2607.20636) — for grit-aware evaluation only. Delphi and nominal group technique come from the group-consensus literature and are UNSOURCED here. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Delphi method | Expert consensus without groupthink | Time pressure (<1 day) | Medium | . | Nominal group technique | Structured brainstorming → voting | >15 participants | Low | . | Grit-aware evaluation | Decisions requiring sustained investment | Reversible/low-stakes | Medium | . 4. Classical decision methods — UNSOURCED . When: well-understood problem structure, textbook applicability. No source in this repository. Nothing in library/ covers cost-benefit analysis, decision trees, game theory or expected utility, and no methodology node renders any of them. The rows below are textbook recall, not adopted method — see §”What this does NOT cover”. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Cost-benefit analysis | Monetisable outcomes, policy decisions | Non-quantifiable values | Low | . | Decision trees | Sequential binary/multi-way choices with probabilities | Too many branches (>50 leaves) | Medium | . | Game theory / minimax | Adversarial settings, zero-sum contexts | Cooperative settings | High | . | Expected utility | Single decision under known probability distributions | Deep uncertainty, unknown distributions | Low | . 5. Hybrid / distance-based MCDM — UNSOURCED . When: reference-point comparison (ideal solution), outranking rather than scoring. No source in this repository: the ingested MCDM source covers aggregation-type methods only, not outranking (ELECTRE, PROMETHEE) or distance-based (TOPSIS, VIKOR) methods. The rows below are textbook recall — see §”What this does NOT cover”. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | TOPSIS | Ranking by distance to ideal/anti-ideal solution | Criteria weights uncertain (use AHP first) | Medium | . | ELECTRE | Partial ordering, incomparability is valid | Need a total ranking | High | . | PROMETHEE | Preference functions on each criterion | All criteria are simple linear | Medium | . | VIKOR | Compromise solution for conflicting criteria | Stakeholders refuse compromise | Medium | .

2a24cfe5d94f.title: What this does NOT cover
2a24cfe5d94f.content: |   | methods | backed by an ingested source | . | §1 MCDM aggregation | 8 | yes — mcdm-aggregation | . | §2 probabilistic | 4 | 2 of 4 — bandits and Bayesian optimisation | . | §3 social / behavioural | 3 | 1 of 3 — grit-aware evaluation | . | §4 classical | 4 | no | . | §5 distance-based / outranking | 4 | no | . | total | 23 | 11 | . An unsourced row is not thereby wrong: these are standard methods and their guidance may be good. It means nobody here has read a source for it, no methodology node renders it, and methodology-adoption’s “never adopt a method by naming it” applies. The selector returns a FAMILY, plus prose. MethodologyRecommendationSchema requires methodologyId — the methodology’s name from its front matter — so a recommendation must name a node in the methodology graph. The graph’s nodes are families and adopted processes (mcdm-aggregation, probabilistic-decision-analysis, adequacy-for-purpose-modelling, kepner-tregoe, dmn, swot, madr, raci/rasci, …); no individual method in the tables above has a node. So the selector returns a methodology node that exists and names the within-family method in rationale, as prose. The 23 rows are material for that prose, not a menu of returnable answers, and no individual method gets a node. | methodologyId is always resolvable. Every value the selector can emit is a node in the graph, so a consumer that follows the id finds a document. Never invent an id for a method: an id that names no node sends a consumer to a methodology that does not exist. | An unsourced row may still be named in prose, and must be named as what it is. “Of the distance-based family, TOPSIS is the usual first reach — note that nothing in this repository’s library covers it” is honest; “use TOPSIS” as a returned recommendation is not. | A request that lands wholly outside the sourced families gets a refusal, not the nearest fit. SelectionResultSchema carries the explanation for when no methodology fits. An agent asking for an outranking method is told none is adopted here. | . These families are entirely absent, even as recall: ambiguity and robust decision-making (maximin under unknown distributions), real options, voting rules and social choice, multi-objective optimisation proper (Pareto fronts rather than scalarisation), and satisficing / bounded-rationality methods.

1cc1c24fc675.title: Selection algorithm
1cc1c24fc675.content: function selectMethodology(context: DecisionContext): MethodologyRecommendation[] { // Step 1: Route via methodology-adoption protocol const lane = routeByQuestionType(context); // Step 2: Load methodology graph nodes const nodes = readMethodologyGraph(); // Step 3: Classify each node against the context const classified = nodes.map(n => ({ ...n, matchTier: classifyFit(n, context), // primary | secondary | excluded rationale: explainFit(n, context) })); // Step 4: Return primary matches first, then secondary. Excluded are named // but NOT recommended — per methodology-adoption, refusals are stated. return classified.sort((a, b) => tierOrder(a.matchTier) - tierOrder(b.matchTier) ); } .

d37b85009dad.content: . | Never blend. The output is one or more methods, each whole. A composite is a house method that §methodology-adoption forbids creating here. | Name refusals. Each recommendation names the paper or standard the method comes from. | Report no-match. d36cacc7d11e.title: Deep document research
d36cacc7d11e.content: Skill deep-document-research: Answer a question from a corpus this folio already holds, iteratively, and stop on a stated condition. The four roles, the two stopping conditions and why both are load-bearing, the granularity choice, and the three things this repository must NOT adopt along with the method. Named by: Deep document research . Renders methodologies/doc-researcher.md — Dong et al., arXiv:2510.21603v1 — as something an agent here can run. Read the methodology node for what the paper claims and what it measured; this is the part you act on. It assumes a corpus, and does not build one. library-ingestion acquires and files; ingest-* derives structure; the L1 completeness gate says whether an entry is fit to use. This begins after all three.

37b5bd5b5cb4.title: The loop, and the only two ways out
37b5bd5b5cb4.content: plan → [ search → refine → evaluate ] → report ↑ | └── σ < τ and t < T_max . Stop when σ ≥ τ, or when t = T_max. Both, always. | Threshold alone never terminates on a question the corpus cannot answer, and a corpus that cannot answer a question is the normal case rather than the exception. | Cap alone stops an answerable question early, and the answer it returns looks exactly like a complete one. | . A loop with only one of them is not this method. Say which one you stopped on. An answer that hit T_max is an answer with known gaps; one that reached σ ≥ τ is not. A report that does not distinguish them hands the reader a confidence nobody established.

6568182b766c.title: The four roles are four QUESTIONS, not four programs
6568182b766c.content: |   | asks | . | plan | which documents could possibly bear on this, at what granularity, and what are the sub-questions? | . | search | what does the corpus return for this sub-question at that granularity? | . | refine | of what came back, what is actually relevant and not a duplicate? | . | report | what does the accumulated evidence say, and where can a reader check each claim? | . One actor may perform all four. The deep-researcher role is one swimlane because a role is an accountability, not a step: somebody stands behind the synthesis. Do not read the paper’s four agents as four roles.

cd4f774f48cc.title: Choose the granularity per question, and say you chose
cd4f774f48cc.content: The method’s substance is that a corpus parsed at several granularities lets a LATER step pick. A broad question is answered from summaries; a specific one from chunks. Picking once, in the pipeline, answers every future question the same way — which is the condition this method exists to escape. This checkout is not there yet. l1-blocks.ts produces blocks and sections exist; there is no summary level and no per-query choice. Until there is, say which granularity you searched rather than implying the corpus offered one.

5bb15fc3f22a.title: Three things NOT to adopt with it
5bb15fc3f22a.content: . | Machine descriptions as fact. The paper converts figures to text with a VLM and uses the output. Here an agent’s description is a draft and only a person confirms it (apply-image-verdicts.ts, cat-harness-tools schemas/content/narrative.ts): “an uncited narrative is indistinguishable from a transcription of the source.” Search over drafts if you must — and never report a draft as what the figure shows. | A sufficiency function you invented. The paper gives σ a symbol and a threshold and never says how it is computed. If you need one, propose it and have it adjudicated; do not bury a judgement in a number. | The paper’s numbers. 50.6% and “3.4× baselines” were measured on the authors’ own benchmark over their own 304 documents. They say nothing about this corpus. | .

ba1d4b59cae0.title: Say what you did not find
ba1d4b59cae0.content: The one failure this method makes easy: an iterative search that ends quietly looks identical to one that succeeded. Report the sub-questions that returned nothing, and whether that means not in the corpus or not found by this search. Those are different, and only the first is a fact about the folio.

3753b8e9af10.title: Deletion requires explicit confirmation
3753b8e9af10.content: Skill deletion-requires-confirmation: An agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. Report what would go, with sizes and ages, and wait for the user to say so. Covers what counts as durable, the non-destructive move for each kind, and the rule that a workflow whose shape deletes something counts as a deletion nobody decided. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, A harness’s default rendering, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . One rule: . An agent does not remove a durable artefact on its own initiative. It reports what it would remove — with sizes, ages and what each one is — and waits for the user to say so. The rule is about the gap between an agent decided this was no longer needed and a person decided it: the second is cheap to obtain, and the first is never recoverable from the outside. A waiver is not an exception to it. The owner may grant the deletion gate in advance — for a session, a process run, or a named artefact class — and that grant is the person deciding. The agent never supplies the decision itself. A waiver carries the grantor, their verbatim words, one gate class, a scope and an expiry; one missing field means there is no waiver (confirmation-waiver). A deletion waiver is never blanket — a grant over build artefacts is not a grant over content — and it never reaches a work item: never delete a work item is a prohibition, and scrapped, with reasons, is always available.

6036ca1488a3.title: Why removing something is not the inverse of creating it
6036ca1488a3.content: A deletion destroys the evidence that it happened. A wrong file is visible and gets fixed; a removed one looks exactly like “there was never anything here”. The person who pays is not the person who acted. A sibling session, a reviewer following a link, the next agent — none can tell a deliberate removal from an accident. A scrapped work item records that something was considered and rejected; a deleted one leaves a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. The same holds for a staging preview, a witness or a library source. Asking is nearly free and reverting often is not. Confirming costs one line in a report and one word back; a wrong deletion costs whatever it took to produce the thing, and may never be discovered. This skill is the general rule; the work item rule in todo-manager (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) is one instance of it.

e3ad308d28c4.title: What counts as durable
e3ad308d28c4.content: The test is not “is it committed” and not “is it large”. It is: . Could somebody other than me want this later, and would they be able to tell it was removed on purpose? . If the answer to the first is yes and to the second is no, it is durable. Durable — confirm before removing: . | artefact | why | the non-destructive move | . | a work item (beans/defs/*.md) | records that something was considered; ids are referenced from commits, issues and other work items | set status: scrapped with the reasons; beans archive MOVES resolved ones | . | a todo (todos/items/*.md) | it is a person’s outstanding work, not an agent’s | ask the person; an agent may neither close nor remove one | . | a staging preview (branches/<slug>/ on the publish branch) | it is the artefact a human assesses a rendered change from — unless the PR merged, when the main site now shows the same thing | merged → removed automatically; the merge IS the confirmation. Otherwise: while the PR is open, the staging:cleanup label applied by a person; once closed unmerged, a feature-staging.yml dispatch with cleanup_slug + a matching cleanup_confirm, since the label cannot reach a closed PR | . | a published page on the site | a URL somebody has linked or bookmarked | say what would 404 and let the owner decide; a redirect is often the answer | . | a QA verdict or witness | the previous answer is what separates “this broke today” from “this has been broken since it was written” | regenerate it in place; never remove it to make a sweep clean. Its record is the commit-keyed entry on the qa-reports branch; an entry there is removed only by qa:prune’s declared retention, never by hand | . | a QA attestation (test/attestations/**) | a judgement — agent, human or baseline pair — that no regeneration can reproduce | never removed to clear a finding; a stale one is re-judged, and the new judgement replaces it through its writer | . | library / uploads content | every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through library/; a file in uploads/ reads as absent to every consumer while still on disk | move it forward through the pipeline, or ask | . | a workflow instance (beans/workflows/*.json) | it is where a running process got to; a sibling session is reading it | complete or discard the instance through the engine, which records the fact | . | a branch, tag or ref somebody else pushed | it is the only copy of work that is not on main | leave it; say it looks finished with | . Not durable — rewrite or remove freely: . | scratch files in a scratchpad or temp directory, and anything you created this session that nothing else has seen; | build output: _site/, _kg/, dist/, node_modules/, test-results/; | a generated artefact being rewritten in place by its own generator. The distinction is in place: writing a fresh kg-qa sidecar over the old one is regeneration; removing a sidecar whose subject you could not load is a deletion, and a false pass besides. | . Three cases sit on the line and all resolve the same way — ask: a file you believe to be an orphan, a directory you believe to be empty, and a file whose only reference you have just removed, because in each the belief is exactly what would be wrong if you are wrong. Establish which layer owns a node before you propose removing it. In a multi-layer layout a file that looks orphaned here may be declared from somewhere else (placement).

6785b4ae4d55.title: What to do instead
6785b4ae4d55.content: Report, do not act. The report is the deliverable: . | Name every artefact. Assert by naming, never by counting — “4 previews are orphaned” is a statistic; “branches/<slug> (36.8 MB, last deployed 11 days ago, its PR merged) matches no open pull request” is something a person can answer. | Give the size and the age. | Say what is lost if it goes, in terms of what would differ — a 404 on a link, a reviewer unable to compare, a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. | Recommend one option and mark it as your recommendation, then say what happens if they say nothing — the frame interaction-modality §4.1 requires of every handed-over decision. | . Prefer the move that keeps the record: scrapped over deleted, archive over remove, redirect over 404, regenerate over unlink, a label over a workflow step. When the user does say so, do exactly that and no more. A confirmation to remove one thing is not a confirmation to remove the class it belongs to. If the scope is ambiguous, ask again. A standing confirmation for a class is the owner’s to give — never an inference. The worked case is the staging preview cap: the owner’s standing confirmation covers removing the oldest previews beyond a total size budget (3 GB), so the stage job removes them without asking per preview. A class confirmation covers the class as the owner last stated it; changing the rule is theirs. It does not waive the record: each rotation names the artefact, its age and its size — in the commit message, the job log and a removed render-log entry — and retires its staging-preview.json into branches/_retired/ rather than deleting it. It covers rotation over the cap and nothing else on the branch. See staging-review §”The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off”.

ce6f641581a1.title: A workflow whose shape deletes something
ce6f641581a1.content: A deletion nobody decided is still a deletion that requires confirmation. A publish step that clones the publish branch, removes everything on it and copies the new build in (a full replace with no kept files) deletes every artefact other workflows put there — for example every open PR’s staging preview — with no step anyone wrote with that intent, silently, and against any explicit retention rule elsewhere. Since there is nobody to ask at push time, the workflow must not be shaped that way: restore what it does not own (e.g. branches/) into the publish directory before the push. A removal policy needs a removal that can actually be confirmed. If the only sanctioned remedy cannot reach the artefacts a report names (a label on a PR that is already closed), the person is left with unsanctioned options. Give the confirmation somewhere to go — e.g. a dispatch whose confirmation input repeats the slug, and which re-evaluates liveness at removal time rather than trusting the report. A report that names live work invites a deletion. “No open pull request” is not “abandoned”; check recent activity before naming a candidate.

1bef2faa84d4.title: Name the instrument that produced the list
1bef2faa84d4.content: A candidate list must say where it came from. If a committed check computed it, quote the check’s finding and name the check. If you built the list by hand, say so, so the person can see they are being asked to act on a derivation rather than on a measurement. A hand-derived list SHORTER than the instrument’s is a harmless miss. One that is LONGER extracts a permission the instrument never justified — for example a slug rule re-implemented inline that names live previews of open PRs as orphans. So do not re-derive what a committed check already computes (goal-review rule 2, stated there for the reviewing side).

292b5a47950a.title: Applying it to your own code
292b5a47950a.content: Does anything you are writing remove something as a side effect of doing something else? A full-replace publish, a --prune, a cleanup step, a cache eviction, a git rm that globs. If so, name what it removes, in the code, and make sure a person chose it. If it is a sweep, does it act or does it report? A checker that finds accumulation reports it: every finding’s action names something a person does, as in bun run cat health, whose workflow opens an issue and removes nothing.

6d6d08cf712b.title: Checklist
6d6d08cf712b.content: . | Is the thing durable by the test above? If unsure, it is. | Is there a non-destructive move — scrap, archive, redirect, regenerate, label? Prefer it, and say you preferred it. | Have you named each artefact, with its size and age and what is lost? | Does the list say which instrument produced it — or, if you built it by hand, does it say that? | Have you given a recommendation, and said what happens on silence? | Did the user confirm this removal, rather than a similar one? | Does any code you wrote remove something as a side effect? Say so in the code, and check a person chose it. | .

c109247512ae.title: Delivery Summary
c109247512ae.content: Skill delivery-summary: Post-delivery summary with server restart command and viewer links . Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . The links are the delivery; the report is not optional (2026-08-25). Everything below is packaging — restart command, viewer links, sibling file list. It sits alongside the substantive report of what you found, never in place of it. A summary that lists five links and says “done” has delivered the artifacts and dropped the finding. What the report must carry — claim, evidence, implications, options, and a recommendation marked as judgement — is specified in AGENTS.md §User accessibility → “Terse ≠ compressed”. Read it before writing this section. After completing a feature or edit (i.e., after pushing changes), provide: .

ba5793f659ae.title: 1. Server restart command
ba5793f659ae.content: A single copy-paste block to fetch, switch to the branch, pull, and restart: . git fetch origin <BRANCH> && git switch <BRANCH> && git pull origin <BRANCH> && ./scripts/start-folio-assistant.sh --http . Replace <BRANCH> with the actual branch name you pushed to.

9e33786fa73f.title: 2. Content block change links
9e33786fa73f.content: This is the most important part. List every content block that changed, with a clickable viewer link and a short explanation of what changed. How to find changed blocks . Extract labels from changed content .ts/.md/.lean triples (a .md-only edit is still a block change): . # Collect changed content files (any sibling triggers the block) changed=$(git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only -- \ 'content/**/*.ts' 'content/**/*.md' 'content/**/*.lean' \ | grep -v '/rendered/' | grep -v 'schema/' | grep -v 'pipeline/') # For each, resolve to the sibling .ts and pull the label for f in $changed; do ts="${f%.*}.ts" [ -f "$ts" ] || continue label=$(grep -oP "label:\s*['\"]\\K[^'\"]+" "$ts" 2>/dev/null || echo "") [ -n "$label" ] && echo "$ts|$label" done | sort -u . Link format . The viewer runs on localhost:<viewer_port> (from lean-mcp.config.json). Each block links via its label anchor: . http://localhost:8080/assistant/#<label> . Presentation format . Group by chapter. Use a markdown table with columns: Block (clickable link — ALWAYS to the .md file), Siblings (GitHub blob links to .ts/.lean/etc. that also changed), What changed (1-line description). Rule: the Block column always links to the .md file. Sibling links (.ts, .lean, .tex) appear in a separate column and only when that sibling was actually modified in this delivery. | Block | Siblings changed | What changed | . | def:quantum-universe | ts · lean | Updated notation from λ to ∫_A | . | prf:dq-squared | — | Added first SVG render | . Viewer anchor links (http://localhost:8080/assistant/#<label>) may be included as an additional row-end column when the folio-assistant is running locally, but the .md blob URL is the canonical reference. GitHub blob links — ALWAYS PROVIDE, ALWAYS .md FIRST . For every created or modified file, include a direct GitHub blob URL using the pattern: . https://github.com/litlfred/qou/blob/<branch>/<relative-path> . The primary link for a block is always the .md file. Sibling files (.ts, .lean, .tex) are listed only if they were actually modified. Never make the .ts or .lean the primary clickable link for a block reference — readers want narrative first. This applies to all file kinds: .md, .ts, .lean, .tex, config files, etc. Never report “created/edited foo.md” without also giving its clickable GitHub blob link on the pushed branch. If the branch is not yet pushed, say so explicitly — do not fabricate a URL that will 404. Categorize changes . Explain the nature of changes — don’t just list files. Common categories: . | Narrative edit: .md content was modified | Re-rendered SVG: notation/style change caused SVG hash update | New SVG render: block got its first rendered SVG | Structural change: label, uses[], lean ref, or kind changed | New block: entirely new content block added | . Remote/deployed links . For remote/deployed builds: . | GitHub Pages: https://litlfred.github.io/qou/ | Draft preview (feature branches): https://litlfred.github.io/qou/drafts/<branch>/ | .

e59b95170ccb.title: 3. GitHub links
e59b95170ccb.content: Always provide: . | File blob links: https://github.com/litlfred/qou/blob/<branch>/<path> for every created/modified file (see §2, “GitHub blob links — ALWAYS PROVIDE”) | Commit links: https://github.com/litlfred/qou/commit/<hash> for each commit | Branch diff: https://github.com/litlfred/qou/compare/main...<branch> | .

468d42990c9c.title: 4. Decisions you leave with the author (STRICT, 2026-08-29)
468d42990c9c.content: A summary is one of the places agents hand the author a decision, and the commonest way to do it badly is a closing one-liner: “the one thing waiting on you is whether to do X”, or a **next** bean entry that names a choice and nothing else. Naming a decision is asking a question, so it owes the same frame as an AskUserQuestion — see AGENTS.md §”NAMING A DECISION IS ASKING A QUESTION”. In a delivery summary that means, for each decision you raise: . | What is being decided, in words that do not assume the reader watched you work. Expand every identifier on first use. | The options, each with what it means / costs / risks / commits to. | The default — what happens if they say nothing. Usually the honest answer is “nothing changes”, and saying so lets them defer with confidence. | The blast radius in real terms — which files, which producers, which published numbers. “Three consumers” is not a blast radius; naming them is. | Your recommendation, marked as judgement rather than finding. | . If you are not willing to spend those words, do not raise it in the summary. Leave it in the bean, where the author reads it on their own schedule. An unframed decision in a summary is worse than no mention: it occupies the author’s attention while withholding what would let them act, and it hides how cheap the item might be to ignore.
