76805839411b.doc: Publish a folio's Lean render with the harness chrome
76805839411b.title: Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome
76805839411b.content: Process_LeanDocsPublish · strict · 4 step(s) . Build a folio’s Lean render — the doc-gen4 HTML of the Lake packages the folio holds — keep it on its own branch store, and publish it inside the folio’s site with the harness navbar and rail. The visualiser is the Lean KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH viewer (owner, 2026-11-19: “use thin html and dynamic loading”): lean-kg-publish turns doc-gen4’s per-module declaration data into one viewer page and JSON shards the page loads on demand. doc-gen4’s static HTML is a non-default fallback only. Three places, and each step says which it reads and writes. The SOURCE is the Lake packages in the folio’s own tree (folio/<paper>/lean/), never moved. The RENDER lives on a branch store the folio declares (a directory of graph typology lean with source: { kind: "branch", keyedBy: "tip" }, on a branch under cat/folio-assistant-sci/), mounted at the declared path by state:mount exactly as beans/ is; it is never committed to the folio’s main. The PUBLISHED pages are the site’s route named by that declaration’s coverage.visualiser (_site/lean/index.html → lean/). The build is a Lake run over the folio’s warm olean cache: expensive, and able to damage the cache (a Lake build over an untraced restore evicts it), so it sits with the Lean toolchain and refuses rather than risks. Its output is pushed to the branch store (branch-store.ts push --id <id>), so a site build needs no Lean toolchain at all: it mounts the store and rails the render, a file pass that cannot touch the cache, after the site is built and before the chrome check and deploy. A site rebuilt without a Lean change starts at the mount. Only End_Ready publishes: a refused guard, a failed build, a store that did not take the push, a mount that failed and an unrailed page are each reported as such, never as a complete site without Lean docs. i i i i Actors: Lean toolchain · CI/CD Pipeline .

b2e62a1001ef.doc: Publish a folio's Lean render with the harness chrome
b2e62a1001ef.title: Steps
b2e62a1001ef.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Build the doc-gen4 render over the warm cacheTask_Build | Lean toolchain | lean-html-docs | Tool lean-html-docs (adapters/paper/lean/lean-docs-build.sh --lake-root <pkg> --lib <Lib>). Reads the SOURCE, the folio’s Lake packages. Refuses while another lake/lean process holds .lake/, refuses over a restored tree with no traces, checks or restores the warm cache, enables the sentinel-commented doc-gen4 require for this build only, then lake -R -Kenv=dev build <Lib>:docs. Output: <pkg>/.lake/build/doc-data (the per-module declaration data the viewer is made from) and <pkg>/.lake/build/doc (the static HTML, kept only as the fallback): working directories, not yet anything a site reads. | . | Write the KG render to the Lean branch storeTask_Store | Lean toolchain | lean-html-docs | Tool lean-kg-publish (adapters/paper/lean/lean-kg-publish.ts --doc-data <pkg>/.lake/build/doc-data --site <checkout> --route <store path> --no-rail) writes the viewer page and its data/ shards into the mounted store’s path (the folio’s declared lean graph, e.g. lean/), then bun folio-assistant/cat-harness-tools/scripts/branch-store.ts push --id <id>. The store is tip-keyed: the branch tip IS the current render, with a root manifest.json (state-manifest/v1); the push splices onto the tip and never forces. The render is never committed to the folio’s main. | . | Mount the Lean branch storeTask_Mount | CI/CD Pipeline | lean-html-docs | bun run cat state:mount (or branch-store.ts mount --id <id>) at the start of the site build, as for beans/: puts the branch tip on disk at the declared path. Reads the RENDER; writes nothing to the branch. A site build of a folio whose Lean did not change starts here. | . | Publish the render at its route, railedTask_Publish | CI/CD Pipeline | lean-html-docs | A site step of the folio’s declared build (site.build.siteSteps). Reads the mounted RENDER, writes the PUBLISHED pages at <site>/<route>/, the route the declaration’s coverage.visualiser names: the KG viewer and its data/ shards are copied as they are, and the site build’s own rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts --foreign-site, which runs after every site step) puts the harness rail on the viewer page, so the rail’s assets are the site’s and nothing extra lands at its root. Fallback, when the store holds doc-gen4’s static HTML instead: Tool lean-render-publish (adapters/paper/lean/lean-render.ts --docs <mount path> --site <site> --route <route> --no-rail) stages it without Lake’s bookkeeping, marks its iframe navbar and find/ redirect rail-declined and adds the layout shim. The document site’s ∀ panel links each declaration to the viewer opened at it, <route>/#/m/<Module>/<name>. | .

13d879f1572b.title: lean-formalization
13d879f1572b.content: Named by: Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . Skill id: lean-formalization · Package: authoring-math · Named by authoring-a-paper.bpmn step 6 · Formalise in Lean, in the Lean toolchain (lean-mcp) lane. Take a block whose assertion is a formal mathematical claim and give it a .lean sibling that Lean 4 accepts. This skill is the entry point, not the manual. The formalisation work itself is covered in depth by folio-paper-adapter, which carries the Lean and proof skills. This says which of those to open and in what order; do not stop here.

0059b161f58b.title: When this applies at all
0059b161f58b.content: Only in a paper folio. The seven block kinds whose assertion is formal — definition, theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, conjecture, proof — are the paper profile, and content_profile_check refuses them in a document folio on every content_validate. If you are reaching for this skill in a document folio, read folio-document-adapter/normative-statements first: what you probably want is a labelled prose block, not a theorem. definition requires lean. The rest expect it. example, remark, algorithm and simulator declare an optional lean field that the paper profile permits and the document profile forbids.

d64fa958f9b7.title: The order to work in
d64fa958f9b7.content: | step | skill | why it is first | . | 0 | lean-environment-setup | A formalisation attempt against a toolchain that will not build is not a measurement of anything. | . | 0b | lean-cache-restore | Restore the Mathlib cache before building, or pay tens of minutes for what a download gives you in one. | . | 1 | lean-generation | Produce the declaration. This is the skill that actually writes Lean. | . | 2 | lean-build-fix | When lake build fails, work the error rather than rewriting the statement to make it compile. | . | 3 | lean-proof-review | Does the Lean say what the prose says? A green build does not answer this. | . | 4 | proof-verification | Record the status honestly — see that skill for what counts as done. | .

01e59fbd0113.title: The failure this skill exists to name
01e59fbd0113.content: A compiling declaration is not a formalised claim. The two ways it goes wrong are both invisible to lake build: . | Vacuity — the statement is true because its hypotheses are unsatisfiable, so it asserts nothing. lean-proof-vacuity-audit is the check. | Drift — the Lean statement is a weaker or different claim than the prose it sits beside. proof-narrative-lean-equivalence is the check, and lean-witness-audit is how you evidence that a declaration is inhabited. | . Run both before you call a block formalised.

be60cc98e5c2.title: uses[] is editorial and must not come from Lean
be60cc98e5c2.content: The block’s uses[] is what a reader must have read to follow the block. The formal dependency graph is machine-derived from lean.ref and is a different graph — the two diverge legitimately in both directions, because a proof invokes simp lemmas nobody reads about, and a theorem is motivated by an example it never cites. Never populate uses[] from Lean. It destroys the signal every ordering metric in the corpus is computed from. lean-formal-graph is how you look at the formal side; content-graph is how you ask impact questions across both.

56652c8c2658.title: Adopted methods for formalising, and where they live
56652c8c2658.content: Three external methods for Lean formalization are adopted as methodology nodes in the science layer, folio-assistant-sci/methodologies/, each citing a paper held in folio-assistant-sci/library/. They are the method; the skills above are how this platform performs it. Read the node when the question is the one it names: . | node | read it when | . | blueprint-driven-formalization | deciding who writes dependency and completion status, and splitting a target into nodes a prover can attempt one at a time | . | process-driven-autoformalization | testing a candidate Lean statement (compile it WITH a proof — a one-sided filter, never evidence of faithfulness), or generating prose from Lean | . | bidirectional-agentic-autoformalization | organising an agent run over a whole paper, and reviewing the output by informalizing it back without the source | . Each node states what its paper measured and did not, and what this platform refuses from it. The refusal most likely to be breached: running out of attempts is never a reason to write an axiom (see sorry below).

4d425b250b89.title: sorry
4d425b250b89.content: skills/requirements/lean-verification.json states it as a SHALL: every sorry carries a reference to the proof obligation it stands for. An unannotated sorry is indistinguishable from an abandoned one. proof-triage and proof-gap-audit are how you work the backlog of them down.

539833c8b9c5.title: Lean HTML docs — a folio’s Lean render, from its branch store to its site
539833c8b9c5.content: Skill lean-html-docs: Build a folio’s Lean render (the Lean knowledge-graph viewer made from doc-gen4’s declaration data for its Lake packages), keep it on the folio’s branch-mounted Lean store, and publish it under the folio’s site wrapped in the harness navbar and rail. Use when a folio’s Lean docs are missing, stale, or published without the harness chrome, or when declaring the Lean store a folio mounts. Named by: Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . What renders a folio’s Lean 4 formalisation is doc-gen4, not this platform. The platform’s job is to keep that render, and to put it inside the folio’s published site with the same navbar and rail every other page carries, so a reader moves between the paper, its graphs and its Lean without leaving the harness. Three places, and each step reads one and writes the next (owner, 2026-11-19: “lean repo branch”, “needs to be mounted”): . | what | where | who writes it | who reads it | . | the source: Lake packages, their modules, the declarations a block’s lean.ref names | the folio’s own tree, folio/<paper>/lean/ | authors | the build (§1) | . | the render: the Lean KG viewer and its data/ shards (doc-gen4’s static HTML only as a fallback) | a branch store the folio declares, under cat/folio-assistant-sci/, mounted at a declared path (§Declaring the store) | the build, by branch-store.ts push (§2) | state:mount, then the publish (§3) and the document site’s ∀ links | . | the published pages | the folio’s site, at the route its declaration names (lean/) | the publish (§3), a site step | readers | . The render is never committed to the folio’s main: it is derived, large, and regenerated, so it lives on its branch the way the work-plan lives on cat/cat-harness/beans. The process processes/content/lean-docs-publish.bpmn governs the order: . | step | Tool / command | runs | cost | . | build | lean-html-docs | adapters/paper/lean/lean-docs-build.sh | Lake; thousands of modules for a Mathlib package | . | make the KG render | lean-kg-publish | adapters/paper/lean/lean-kg-publish.ts | seconds | . | store | branch-store.ts push --id <id> | cat-harness-tools/scripts/branch-store.ts | a splice onto the branch tip | . | mount | state:mount | cat-harness-tools/scripts/state-mount.ts | a checkout of the tip | . | publish | a site step | the folio’s site.build.siteSteps (fallback: lean-render.ts) | a copy, railed by the site build | . The commands below write <owner>/<repo> and <paper> for the folio’s own values: <owner>/<repo> is GITHUB_REPOSITORY in CI, else the checkout’s origin (the rule scripts/lib/paper-env.sh and defaultBlockActions follow), and <paper> is the document directory under folio/. Nothing here names a repository.

c4fb57bfb064.title: 1. Build the render — never on someone else’s cache
c4fb57bfb064.content: # from the folio's checkout root bash folio-assistant/folio-assistant-sci/adapters/paper/lean/lean-docs-build.sh \ --lake-root folio/<paper>/lean --lib <Lib> \ --platform folio-assistant --restore . The script refuses, rather than risks, three things — read its header for the evidence behind each: . | another lake/lean process running: two Lake processes on one .lake/ race on the same oleans; | a restored tree with no traces (.lake/RESTORED-NO-TRACES): :docs is a Lake build, and Lake rebuilds an untraced olean, evicting the cache; | no warm cache, unless --allow-cold: Mathlib from source is 30–60 minutes before doc-gen4 starts. | . doc-gen4 stays out of main’s lakefile (it adds heavy modules to every build). A folio comments its [[require]] between --- BEGIN doc-gen4 / --- END doc-gen4 sentinels; the script uncomments them for the build and restores the lakefile on exit. It never runs lake update, so the folio’s lake-manifest.json must already list doc-gen4 at that rev. Start with --dry-run: every guard runs and the lake command is printed.

dbf6d36bde5d.title: 2. Make the KG render and keep it on the branch store
dbf6d36bde5d.content: THE visualiser is the Lean knowledge-graph viewer (owner, 2026-11-19: “use thin html and dynamic loading”): doc-gen4 still elaborates, but what is kept and published is one viewer page plus JSON shards it loads on demand, made by lean-kg-publish from doc-gen4’s per-module declaration data (.lake/build/doc-data/declaration-data-<Module>.bmp). Write it straight into the mounted store, then push the store: . bun run cat state:mount # or: branch-store.ts mount --id <id> bun run folio-assistant/folio-assistant-sci/adapters/paper/lean/lean-kg-publish.ts \ --doc-data folio/<paper>/lean/.lake/build/doc-data --site . --route <store path> \ --modules <Lib>,… --content-root folio \ --repo <owner>/<repo> --ref <sha> --content-prefix folio/ --no-rail bun folio-assistant/cat-harness-tools/scripts/branch-store.ts push --id <id> . | file | what | . | data/index.json | modules, declaration counts, chunk counts, a content hash per module | . | data/names.json | every declaration name, for search; fetched on first search | . | data/m/<Module>.jsonld | the module node, imports edges, one node per declaration with formalizes edges to the blocks whose lean.ref names it | . | data/m/<Module>.<k>.sig.json | rendered signatures, 500 per chunk, fetched as cards scroll in | . Measured on qou: 3,011 modules, 53,565 declarations, 651 formalizing a block, 171 MB in 6,005 files, 13 s. The 12,804-declaration QOU.BraidKnot.AllKnownIsotopesUniqueness opens on a target declaration in about 2 s (it was a 55 MB HTML page in the static render). doc-gen4’s style.css styles bare body/header/nav/main; the publish step keeps only its custom properties and signature rules, scoped under .lkg-sig, so it cannot lay the viewer out as a doc-gen4 page or reach the rail. The store is tip-keyed: the branch tip IS the current render, with a root manifest.json (state-manifest/v1), and the push splices onto it without ever forcing. A site build that follows needs no Lean toolchain and no warm cache: it mounts the store.

4e777167753f.title: 3. Publish it at its route, with the rail
4e777167753f.content: A step of the folio’s declared site build (site.build.siteSteps, a package script whose last argument is the built site), so stage-local.ts runs it for the folio. It reads the MOUNTED store, never a Lake build directory, and copies the viewer and its data/ to <site>/<route>/, the route the declaration’s coverage.visualiser names. The site build’s own rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts --foreign-site), which runs after every site step, puts the harness rail on the viewer page, so the rail’s assets are the site’s own and nothing extra lands at the site root. With the store not mounted the step has nothing to publish and must say so, not succeed quietly. The document site’s ∀ panel links each declaration to the viewer opened at it, <route>/#/m/<Module>/<name>, using the render’s data/names.json to find the module (folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-lean.ts); a declaration the render does not list gets no link.

b24a3b10dadb.title: 4. Fallback: doc-gen4’s static HTML
b24a3b10dadb.content: Not the default. When a store holds doc-gen4’s static render instead (.lake/build/doc, copied without Lake’s .hash/.trace bookkeeping), the site step stages it with lean-render-publish: . bun run folio-assistant/folio-assistant-sci/adapters/paper/lean/lean-render.ts \ --docs <store path> --site _site --route lean --modules <Lib>,… --no-rail . (without --no-rail it runs the rail pass itself, --platform <index root>, and is a standalone publish.) What it adds before the rail runs, each for a measured reason: . | leaves out Lake’s .hash/.trace bookkeeping (4,646 files in qou’s July render, more files than pages); | marks doc-gen4’s iframe navbar and its find/ redirect <meta name="folio-navbar" content="none">, or a second rail is drawn inside the sidebar of every page; | adds a layout shim, keyed on the rail being present: doc-gen4’s header and sidebar are position: fixed, so the rail’s body padding does not move them and the rail covered the sidebar (measured in Chromium: sidebar at 7.8 px under a 56 px rail; 63.8 px with the shim). | . --modules keeps only the named module roots. Without it the folio publishes Mathlib’s docs too — qou: 4,193 pages, 533 MB, 347 s to stage and rail; pruned: 34 pages, 29 MB, about 5 s. Pruning repoints every link into a dropped module to the community mathlib4 docs, and says what that costs: those docs are built from their Mathlib, not the folio’s pin, and doc-gen4’s search index still lists pruned declarations, whose hits 404. Choose it knowingly. The script ends by asserting that every staged page is railed or declined the rail; a page with neither fails it. The ∀ panel then links doc-gen4’s page for the declaration, read from the render’s declarations/declaration-data.bmp. Cache the doc-gen4 output, iterate per branches/ branch . The doc-gen4 run is the expensive part (qou: about 2 h 20 min on 4 cores, 15,151 Lake jobs). Its output is cached on an orphan branch, e.g. qou’s lake-cache/qou-docgen4-v4-24-0 (doc HTML with Lake .hash/.trace, doc-data, and doc-gen4’s own build; ~160 MB in two parts, MANIFEST.json). Restore it after the olean cache and lake -R -Kenv=dev build <Lib>:docs re-renders only modules whose traces changed. For a branches/ branch, publish an overlay against the main graph: . … lean-kg-publish.ts … --base https://<site>/lean/data . Only modules whose content hash differs from the base are written, plus data/overlay.json; the viewer loads changed modules from the branch and the rest from the base. A branch with no Lean change writes no module files.

394ae19d9080.title: Declaring the store
394ae19d9080.content: A folio declares its Lean render as a directory of graph typology lean whose content comes from a BRANCH, mounted the way beans/ is, and names the site route it is published at as its coverage.visualiser: . { "id": "lean-docs", "path": "lean/", "scope": "repository", "source": { "kind": "branch", "branch": "cat/folio-assistant-sci/lean-docs", "keyedBy": "tip" }, "graphTypologies": ["lean"], "coverage": { "visualiser": [{ "ref": "_site/lean/index.html", "title": "Lean" }] } } . | path is where state:mount puts the branch’s files, and it is gitignored: the render is never committed to main. The branch mirrors the checkout, so the render sits under lean/ on it as well. | coverage.visualiser is the route the publish step writes (_site/<route>/), and the route the document site’s ∀ panel links each declaration’s rendered page under (folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-lean.ts, which reads the render’s declarations/declaration-data.bmp from the mount). | The source is NOT declared here: it is the Lake packages already under folio/<paper>/lean/, which the folio’s folio graph holds. | . The kind is defined in folio-assistant-sci’s typologies/lean.json, so the folio’s platform pin must reach a folio-assistant-sci that has it: an unknown graph typology makes the whole declaration fail to parse. A folio’s site recipe that keeps an earlier lean/ on its publish branch (site.build.keep) publishes that copy instead of the mounted one: drop lean from keep once the store holds the render.

43bd3f3b3371.title: What this is not
43bd3f3b3371.content: . | Not the formal-edge graph. Elaborated dependencies between lean.ref declarations are lean-formal-edges. | Not the warm cache. Restoring and seeding oleans is lean-cache-restore (the lean-cache Tool); this skill only refuses to damage it. | .

eaf05b438bb5.doc: Is the generated Lean in sync with its generators?
eaf05b438bb5.title: Is the generated Lean in sync with its generators?
eaf05b438bb5.content: Process_LeanRegenerateAndDiff · strict (defaulted) · 2 step(s) . Check that the Lean text a script in this repository writes is still exactly what that script writes. Two files carry such text: every knot block of QOU/Knot/GeneratedGluing.lean (from scripts/gen-gluing-lean.py) and the depth-3 corner column BokutShiaoCornerDepth3 in UGB/GrobnerShirshov/HeckeCompletion.lean (from scripts/gen-hecke-corner-column.py 3). WHY IT IS STRICT. These are proofs. If a generator and its output part company, a Lean file that compiles is carrying certificates nothing in the repository produces, and the next regeneration silently changes a proof. The check is cheap (about nine seconds) and writes nothing, so strictness costs nothing. THREE OUTCOMES, NOT TWO. A generator that cannot run, most often because SnapPy is not installed, is UNKNOWN and never reported as in sync. That is the parity rule the witness-parity Tool already follows. WHAT IS NOT CHECKED, AND WHY. The depth-2 column BokutShiaoCorner (section 4ad) was written by hand first; the generator was checked against it by re-deriving the same words and rules, not the same text. Measured 2026-10-05, the two differ on 964 lines while proving the same thing, so a textual diff there would report drift that is not drift. The module header of GeneratedGluing.lean and its closing end line are hand-written too, and are excluded from the comparison for the same reason. DRIFT IS A DECISION, NOT A FIX. When the regenerated text differs, either the generator changed (and the Lean should be regenerated) or the Lean was edited by hand (and the generator should learn the edit, or the edit should go). Which one is right is a judgement about a proof, so it goes to the author; the agent does not overwrite either side. No rendered diagram — run bun run cat render:bpmn.

dc9173987f18.title: Lean toolchain — the role’s contract
dc9173987f18.content: Skill lean-toolchain-contract: The contract the lean-toolchain role is held to: what a Lean toolchain must answer when a paper folio’s formal half is built, and what it must not be asked. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . lean-toolchain in scenarios/roles.json is played by a mechanical actor (actorKinds: ["system"]; today scenarios/actors/lean-mcp.json). A role played by a machine is still a role, and its skills are its contract: the responsibilities it must perform, which a test can hold it to. This is that contract.

2c3aa65635a3.title: What it must do
2c3aa65635a3.content: . | Elaborate and check the formal half of a paper folio, and answer only what Lean can answer (the role’s own description). A judgement about whether a proof is good belongs to proof-review-agent, not here. | Build with lake build and exit 0 with no compilation errors when the project is sound — req:lean-verification#lean-compiles, which the lean-toolchain capability (scenarios/capabilities/lean-toolchain.json) declares it satisfies. | Be detectable: lean --version answers on a machine that has it (the capability’s detection). Where it does not, the lean-mcp capability is the declared fallback, with the Lean running server-side. | Report what it ran, not only that it passed: the lean-build Tool (tools/lean-build/lean-build.ts) writes a committable lean-build-status.json every run, so a green build is distinguishable from one nobody ran. | .

4d268fb6867b.title: What it is not asked

Sorry tracking (req:lean-verification#sorry-tracking) is verified by inspection, by an actor that can judge; this role reports diagnostics and proof state. | To run in this repository. The test in tested-by: holds lines 2–4 to what this repository declares — the capability, the requirement statement it satisfies, its detection and fallback, and the lean-build Tool’s status output — and does not run lake build. | .

23912e88721a.title: Library ingestion — the basic flow
23912e88721a.content: Skill library-ingestion: The BASIC ingestion flow every asset takes: an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/<slug>/ if it is materialized. The two entry points (a drop in uploads/, or materializing an asset a remote graph lists), what happens to the upload afterwards, and why content-type methods refine this flow from above rather than living in it. Command: bun run cat ingest. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . uploads/ and library/ are two stages of one pipeline. uploads/ is the incoming queue — raw files as dropped, not L1 and not greppable as corpus. library/<slug>/ is where an ingested asset lives, and every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through it. Why that bites: the corpus-grep checklist searches library/ only, so a file still in uploads/ makes a clean grep mean “nobody has done this” when the source is right there. That is how a held result gets re-derived.

c79628ce9027.title: The flow — four steps, and no content-type decision
c79628ce9027.content: cat-harness holds only the basic, high-level ingestion workflow, with very little process context assumed: the uploaded asset’s extracted metadata goes into the KG, and the asset into library/ if materialized. library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (Process_Ingestion) is that flow, executable: . | Accept — the bytes reach the declared uploads/ queue by a declared route (upload-routes; names per upload-naming; arrival noticed by uploads-watch). | Extract metadata into the KG — asset-extraction: a container’s INDEX goes in, its contents do not unless asked for. | Materialized? — the state vocabulary is schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts: referenced, materialized or unknown, with no default. | Place in library/<slug>/ — this skill. A referenced asset is still catalogued: its record says where the bytes are and that we hold none. | . The flow calls no subprocess and decides nothing about content type. Which reader a PDF needs, what a complete L1 entry holds, how images or datasets are described — those are refinements, and they live in a layer above this one. The mechanism is inversion: a higher-layer process CALLS Process_Ingestion as its first step and continues with its own work. Nothing here names a refinement, because there is no BPMN extension point in the corpus and a harness process naming a higher one would be an upward edge. methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest is a harness caller of the same flow.

998ab43f006c.title: TWO entry points
998ab43f006c.content: Things enter the library through uploads/ → library/ document ingestion, or through materializing an asset listed in an external KG that a dependent harness declares. |   | drop | materialize | . | the source is | a file somebody put in uploads/ | an asset listed in a remote graph a dependency declares | . | decided first | how it is read (a refinement’s choice) | the five gates, and a purpose | . | entry | bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE | materialize-remote.bpmn | . Neither is a shortcut past the other. A materialized asset still arrives as bytes that have to be read, so it re-enters at exactly the point a dropped file does. Materialization adds what happens before there is a file: may we hold it, what does holding it cost, for what purpose, and what if the source goes away. Entry one is bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE (--dry-run says what it would do, and why). Entry two starts from remoteGraphs in a layer’s declaration (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts, RemoteGraph): assets listed there are referenced — we know they exist and where, and hold none. materialize-remote.bpmn asks purpose (working or archival), then the five gates, then fetches; the asset lands in library/ with its provenance and fixity, and a refusal leaves the node referenced rather than failing. A reference is not a fetch: the KG viewer follows a remote graph to show its hierarchy without materialising anything — navigable without being held. Who owns which half . | This layer owns the basic flow and the reading CODE — the pdf-* rungs, ingest-document.ts, notebook-structure.ts. Reading bytes is platform work, and OCR stays here. The method that chooses among them is a refinement above. The flow itself cannot move up: uploads and library are graph typologies this layer declares, and a flow above would make the harness’s own library writable only from a layer above it — a wrong-direction, and circular, dependency. | The remote half’s gates belong to the content layer above. Only the state vocabulary lives here; the five gates, the purposes and the record binding them stay with the layer that owns content, because each gate is a decision about content. A harness that cannot hold content must not own the vocabulary for deciding to acquire it. | The large-datasets package owns the question before both (library/skills/large-datasets/): how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset (source-descriptor.ts). Neither entry point can start until something says what is out there. | Further down the tree, a dependency’s declared remoteGraphs is what makes the second path reachable at all, inherited the way directories are. | .

534b309d8abb.title: A held PDF gets its page-1 cover BEFORE the upload is retired
534b309d8abb.content: The picture of a PDF entry is library/<slug>/cover.png, page 1 rendered by pdf-cover.py — never its first figure, which can be any picture from deep in the document. With no cover, the entry shows the book glyph. | A new ingest writes it: ingest-document’s cover arm runs last. | An entry without one gets it from bun run cat library:covers. Run it in the checkout that holds the PDF (the composed index, whose uploads/ may be another repository’s), and commit the cover into the repository that holds the entry. | Run it before the upload is retired. Once the PDF moves to fsh-guts/uploads/, library:covers no longer finds it and skips the entry as “not held”. | bun run cat library:covers:check fails on a held, unwithheld PDF that has no cover. | .

d3f1411964c1.title: After ingestion the upload is RETIRED — never left, never deleted
d3f1411964c1.content: Three places, and only uploads/ is temporary: queued uploads/FILE; derived library/<slug>/, which may not hold the source bytes (check:l1-complete reports an unexpected child); archived fsh-guts/uploads/FILE beside a folio-fsh-guts/v1 sidecar whose movedFrom and movedOn are load-bearing. Never rm an ingested upload: it is the only working-tree copy of the source. bun run cat check:uploads-retired finds unretired ones by sha256 against every declared library, never by filename, and refuses rather than passes when no library records a hash. It reports and never moves anything. Rename an upload before its first ingest — the slug follows the name. The full rule — why the library cannot be the destination, the sidecar convention, the blocking and advisory families, and renaming — is in library-ingestion/uploads-retirement.md.

06750a40b146.title: When an ingested document names what else the library needs
06750a40b146.content: Some documents say what they rest on, by number, in a section the content type defines — and then the library is not complete until it holds those too. The flow above is run again for each, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated once they are in, so a cited source the library HOLDS is described from its own metadata rather than from a one-line reference. The content type owns which section that is, how its citations resolve, and how a cited source is acquired (for instance from a DSpace repository); it says so in its own authoring skill. This layer owns only the rule: the flow above runs once per cited source, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated after.

1e5163155d12.title: A second representation sits DOWNSTREAM of the entry
1e5163155d12.content: A content type may describe an ingested document a second time, in its own schema — a WHO guideline is also an L1 knowledge graph. The library is upstream of L1: L1 points upstream, never downstream. So that representation is derived from the entry and points at the entry’s nodes (the source document, its sections, its blocks); nothing in the library points back, and the entry is never rewritten for it. It inherits whatever sectioning this flow produced, so a better reader here improves it without a change there. Whether a document gets one is recorded on its intake (classifications), by a person, by the process that acquired it, or by a rule — the content type owns which, and its skill says how.

685386e51f4e.title: Liquid templates — layout only, every fact from the graph
685386e51f4e.content: Skill liquid-templates: Authoring a Liquid template in this repository — a README template the subgraph-readmes Tool renders with liquidjs, or a Jekyll include on the just-the-docs site. Where templates live (inside a declared directory, reached through its id), what a template may read (only what the Knowledge Graph hands it), the leading comment the generator reads as the file’s description, includes, whitespace control, escaping, and regenerate-then-commit with the --check gate. Read it before adding or changing any .liquid file or anything under docs/_includes/. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Two engines run Liquid here, and they produce different kinds of output. Know which one you are writing for before you write a line: . |   | README templates | site templates | . | engine | liquidjs, run by bootstrap-tools’ subgraph-readmes (jekyllInclude: true, strictFilters: true) | Jekyll, run by docs-site.yml with the pinned just-the-docs remote_theme | . | lives in | templates/readme/ beside the writer, in the tools repository (bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/) | cat-harness/docs/_includes/ — just-the-docs’ extension points (head_custom.html, footer_custom.html, nav_footer_custom.html) plus our own | . | output | <directory>/README.md, committed, read on GitHub where no Liquid runs | _site/, never committed, published to Pages | . | data | only what the generator passes: subgraph, instance, kg, files, subdirs, summary | site, page, include, and _data/*.json written by the pipeline | . | verified by | bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check — the diff is the output | building the site: rendered-verification, bun run cat preview:site | .

2d157c1e3041.title: Where a template lives
2d157c1e3041.content: Beside the writer that renders it, in the tools repository. The README templates are part of bootstrap-tools’ scripts/ subgraph, at bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/, and the writer finds them with TEMPLATES, a path relative to its own file. A template is part of the toolset: somebody who wants different READMEs uses a different toolset over the same content, and a harness that wants its own layout passes its own templates directory to plan(). They are files OF the scripts/ subgraph, not a directory of their own: a declared directory nested inside another is refused by check:layout-norms. Never an inline template string in a .ts file and never a .liquid file outside a declared directory: a template nobody declared is one no checker looks at, and its README row cannot say what it is.

e9fdbeebfba2.title: What a template may read — and what it must not compose
e9fdbeebfba2.content: A template arranges facts; it never states one. Every word that is not layout comes from a variable the generator read from the Knowledge Graph: the directory’s declared title and description, each file’s own account of itself, a relation a diagram records. No count, URL, name or claim typed into a template — each is a second answer free to drift from the first, which is readme-sections §”Resolve links; never compose them” one level down. | Computation belongs in the generator, where it is tested: counting, grouping, choosing a link target, collapsing a long list. The template sees results (subdirs[].count, summary), not inputs to derive them from. | A missing value is shown as missing, never papered over: {{ subgraph.title | default: subgraph.id }} and “No description is declared for …” are the pattern. The generator records the gap as a QA finding in test/results/subgraph-readmes.qa-results.json (a derived result, stored on the qa-reports branch by qa-publish); the template must not make it look filled. | A new variable is a generator change first. Add it to the object passed to renderFile, list it in the template’s comment, then use it. | .

9e62169aa48f.title: Versions are variables, never numbers
9e62169aa48f.content: A version typed into a template is stale on the next bump. Read it: . | README templates get release: version (every layer declares one), and — for a layer declaring an iriBase — major, agent (for identifiers) and human (for pages), both <iriBase>v<major>/. Empty strings where not declared: test with != "", and show nothing rather than a guess. | Site templates read site.data.harness.releases.<instance> — the same four fields for every layer, written by sync-docs-harness into _data/harness.json under the docs:harness:check gate. | . Link a person to human and name an identifier with agent. They are one address today — every address carries the major only, and the pin, not the address, fixes the exact release (instance-publication §”Release IRIs”) — but the field still says which audience a link is for.

2acfb8af4071.title: The leading comment IS the file’s description
2acfb8af4071.content: Open every template with a {%- comment -%} block. Its first sentence is what the directory README’s “what it is” column shows for the file (describe() in bootstrap-tools/scripts/readme-graph-sections.ts), so write it for a reader of that table — “The file table: files directly in the directory, then its subdirectories.” — and put the variables it reads in the lines after. No comment and the row says only “a template”.

281c22f09786.title: Includes
281c22f09786.content: jekyllInclude: true gives Jekyll’s syntax: {% include files.liquid %}, the file name unquoted and with its extension. An include with no parameters sees the including template’s variables (files.liquid reads files directly); a parameter passed as {% include x.liquid key=value %} is read as include.key, as in Jekyll. Split a template when a part is reusable or when a reader would want its own row for it — not to hide logic.

59af41261feb.title: Whitespace — check the output, not the template
59af41261feb.content: {%- and -%} strip the whitespace on that side of the tag, and that is how a template emits clean Markdown. It is also how a separator the output needs disappears — a stripped space between two HTML attributes makes the page print its own markup as text, past every gate (continual-progress §”A template is not a page”). Strip freely inside a tag’s own lines; think before stripping next to a table row’s newline, the blank line before a heading or table, or an attribute boundary. subgraph-readmes also collapses three or more newlines to two, so do not fight blank lines with stripping.

7ca7091d4253.title: Escaping
7ca7091d4253.content: . | strictFilters: true — an unknown filter is an error, not a silent pass-through. No custom filter is registered. | A value bound for a table cell is escaped before it reaches the template — the generator’s cell() turns | into \| and folds newlines. A new cell-bound field goes through it; a raw | from a file’s description splits the row. | Liquid syntax in prose that Jekyll will build must sit inside a raw block. gen-skill-docs wraps every skill page in one, so a skill may quote {{ }} and {% %} freely — but never the closing endraw tag itself, which ends the block early. A generated README that sits under a site source (cat-harness/docs/, root docs/) may be read by the site build too; if a KG value there can carry Liquid, build the site and look before assuming either way. | .

1dcf8ece63c0.title: An undefined variable is a message, not silence
1dcf8ece63c0.content: Jekyll renders an undefined variable as the empty string and says nothing; strict_variables says something by FAILING the build and by changing what renders (the exception aborts the whole tag, else branch included). docs/_plugins/liquid-undefined-warn.rb does neither: every lookup runs as Liquid runs it, and at the end of the build each path that was ABSENT is printed as a warning with its count and pages, site.data.* first. A lookup inside a condition or under | default is not reported — there the template asked — nor an include’s own parameter (include.x, optional by convention), a field of a variable that is there and nil (its cause is reported once, where it went undefined), or a path liquid_undefined_ignore in _config.yml lists: a THEME’s optional settings, which site-chrome/_config.yml names for just-the-docs. Without those exclusions the report is mostly noise over a few real gaps. FOLIO_LIQUID_UNDEFINED_REPORT=<file> writes the same record as JSON; liquid_undefined: off in _config.yml turns it off. It runs only where plugins do (bundle exec jekyll, as an IG repository’s own site and preview:site build); the github-pages build is safe mode and loads none.

21cd5774f2b6.title: Markers — the platform owns the region, the folio owns the file
21cd5774f2b6.content: subgraph-readmes writes only between <!-- kg:subgraph:begin --> and <!-- kg:subgraph:end -->, creates a README holding just that region when there is none, and leaves an unmarked README alone and reported. The rules are in readme-sections; do not restate them in a template.

d9cd534dea0f.title: Regenerate, commit, and the gate
d9cd534dea0f.content: bun run cat readme:subgraphs # render every declared directory's README + the QA sidecar bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # fail on a stale README or sidecar — CI and the pre-commit hook . Changing a template changes every README it renders; commit them with the template, in one commit. So does adding or removing a file in any declared directory — that directory’s table changed. readme:subgraphs:check runs in code-quality-gates.yml and in cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit; it is part of bun run cat gates.

33641a660b3e.title: Literature search — finding the source a citation points at
33641a660b3e.content: Skill literature-search: Finding the source a node cites but does not hold — memory first, then this repository, then open-access services. Always produce a DIRECT download link. Read before recording that a citation cannot be found, and before appraising any source you have not opened. Its central rule: a blocked network is not a missing document, and the two must never share a report. Named by: Options analysis . A node cites a source. Nothing in any declared library holds it. This skill is the step between those two facts and library-ingestion, which takes over once a file exists. It runs on a measurable trigger, not a feeling: a origin, evidence, source or bibliography reference whose target does not resolve to an entry in any library the layer declares. The methodology graph is where this bites hardest — methodology-adoption requires that an adopted methodology be “external and named”, with “an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body” — and a front-matter string nothing can follow satisfies that requirement only on paper.

a2ad48c9fca8.title: Look in this order, and stop at the first hit
a2ad48c9fca8.content: 1. Memory. The memory graph and agent memory under .claude/agent-memory/. A source located once and found unreachable is worth recording; re-deriving that costs the same search twice and reaches the same wall. 2. This repository. Every declared library and uploads directory, not one of them. A layer may declare several — ask the declaration, do not assume a path. A file sitting in uploads/ is found but not ingested, which is a different finding from not found, and it is the cheapest possible outcome: hand it to library-ingestion and stop. 3. Open-access services. DOI resolution through the publisher, then the open-access aggregators and repositories — Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Crossref, DOAJ, CORE, arXiv, PubMed Central, Zenodo, HAL, and a standards body’s own site where the origin names one. archiving-arxiv and archiving-web-pages cover the fetch once a URL is in hand. Open access only. What this finds is committed into a library in a public repository, so a paywalled PDF is not a candidate whatever its availability to the person searching. When only a paywalled copy exists, that is an outcome to report (below), not a licence to take it. A publisher’s own free-to-read landing page, a preprint, an author copy in an institutional repository and a standards body’s public specification are all fine.

6b3515f605f7.title: Always give the direct link
6b3515f605f7.content: Every outcome carries a direct download link — the URL that yields the file itself, not a search page, not a DOI landing page, not “search for it on X”. A landing page is acceptable in addition, never instead. The person reading this has limited hand function; “you can find it by searching” converts a finished search into their work, which is the whole thing this skill exists to absorb.

e8cd717c8b7b.title: Three outcomes, and the middle one is the point
e8cd717c8b7b.content: There are three, not two, and collapsing the middle into the third is the failure this skill is written to prevent. 1. Found and fetched . The file is in uploads/. Hand to library-ingestion and say which service it came from, so the provenance is checkable. 2. Found, but this agent cannot fetch it . The document exists, its location is known, and something in the way this agent is running stopped the transfer — a proxy refusal, a TLS failure, a robots policy, a rate limit, a login wall, a network the container cannot reach. Report this as a located document, never as a missing one. Say all of: . | what the item IS — full citation: authors, year, title, venue, volume, pages, DOI. Enough that a person recognises it without opening anything. | what it contains, in a sentence, and its extent if known (pages, format). This is what lets the person judge whether it is worth their trouble. | the direct download link, as above. | why the fetch failed, in plain words — “the agent proxy returned 403”, “the publisher requires a login”, “the host is not reachable from this container”. Not “could not retrieve”. | what to do with it: drop the file into uploads/ and the ingest runs. | . Then record it in the work plan as blocked on a fetch, with what it waits on — bean-blocking’s rules apply, expiry included. A network restriction is a fact about this agent, not about the literature. Reported as “not found” it becomes a fact about the world, and the next agent re-runs the identical search, hits the identical wall, and reports the identical wrong conclusion. Worse, a methodology whose source was found and blocked reads exactly like one whose source does not exist, and the first is a five-minute human action while the second may mean the methodology should not have been adopted. 3. Not found . Nothing open-access resolves to it. Say what was searched — the services, not “a search was done” — and what the closest candidates were and why each was rejected. A rejected candidate with no record is a dead end the next agent walks back into, which is bean-coordination’s argument for scrapped over deleted, applied to a search. “Not found” for a source that is merely paywalled is wrong. That is outcome 2 with “the only copies are behind a paywall” as the reason.

a1bde35745e7.title: Never fill the gap with recall
a1bde35745e7.content: Do not paraphrase, summarise, quote or characterise a source you have not opened. Not from training, not from a secondary source, not from an abstract read in a search result, unless the abstract is what you say you read. This is the rule the whole evidence base rests on. A methodology file that renders a method from the agent’s recollection and cites a paper nobody fetched is worse than one with no citation at all: it carries the authority of a reference while resting on nothing, and there is no way for a reader to tell it apart from a faithful rendering. Where a source is read through another — a review paper reporting a primary one — say so at each claim. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: Humphrey, Weihrich, Dealtry, Wheelen & Hunger, Hill & Westbrook, Mintzberg and Dess et al. are all read through one review, every attribution is marked second-hand, and the file says the origin of the method is contested rather than repeating the usual story as fact.

80fabc2aca71.title: What this skill does NOT do
80fabc2aca71.content: . | It does not appraise. Certainty of a body of evidence is evidence-appraisal against the grading system the folio declares, and for a health recommendation that is grade. Finding a paper says nothing about whether it is any good. | It does not ingest. library-ingestion owns uploads/ → library/, and the ingest chooses its own rung. | It does not decide which methodology to use. That is methodology-adoption, which this skill feeds: the evidence behind a methodology is an input to selecting it. | It does not judge whether a gap matters. It reports the gap. Whether a methodology with no reachable source should still be adopted is the owner’s call, and deletion-requires-confirmation’s posture applies — report, with what is missing, and wait. | .

1b980a78be8f.title: Related
1b980a78be8f.content: . | library-ingestion — the next step, once a file exists | methodology-adoption — what requires an origin in the first place, and the selection question this feeds | evidence-appraisal — appraising what was found | evidence-review — separation of appraiser from drafter | bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) — recording outcome 2 so it does not read as abandoned | .

88ef15c64be2.title: Logging what you are doing
88ef15c64be2.content: Skill log-message: Say what you are doing, to the Logger, in a form a reader can act on. Five required fields and one optional body; an incomplete message is not logged. Callable from any task in any process, and required by some. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness, Log a message . You are the author of a log line; the Logger is where it goes. The Logger records and decides nothing, so it cannot know who acted: you supply actor. It is carried out as a sub-process: nobody starts there. A task in another process calls it, and the calling task’s diagram says so; this skill does not list its callers or the process that implements it.

fdb9d11fddd3.title: The message
fdb9d11fddd3.content: Five strings, all required, and one optional markdown body. | field | what it answers | shape | . | timestamp | when | an ISO-8601 instant, e.g. 2026-09-20T14:03:11Z | . | actor | who was acting | the acting actor’s id — never the Logger’s | . | process | inside which process | a process id, e.g. my-process | . | task | at which step of it | a node id within that process, e.g. A_DoTheThing | . | message | what happened | one line, no newline | . | body | the detail, if any | markdown, optional | . All five are required: each answers a question a reader would otherwise guess. body is the one place free prose belongs. A diff, an error, the contents of a file that was not where it should have been. Keep message to the line somebody scanning will read, and put everything else here.

0fa5c2e9ff5c.title: When to log
0fa5c2e9ff5c.content: Optionally, from any task in any process. You need no permission and no element in the diagram: an actor saying what it is doing is always in order. Required where a diagram says so, which it says by drawing the call explicitly — a callActivity whose calledElement is Process_LogMessage. If the diagram drew it, logging is a step, not a courtesy. The difference between the two is only whether the caller drew it. It is the same sub-process either way, and it takes the same six fields.

42e05d8820d5.title: If you cannot complete the message
42e05d8820d5.content: Do not log, and say that you could not. The End_NotLogged branch is a real outcome, not an error path to route around. A line missing its actor or its task still looks like a record, and a reader cannot tell it from a complete one. The same holds if the Logger is unreachable: say so, in the place you would have logged to, and carry on with the task. Logging is not a gate. A failure to log is never a reason to abandon an install.

76297772f39e.title: The one destination bootstrap has
76297772f39e.content: The discussion with the human actor. A Bootstrapping Agent has no log file, no service and no work plan — the only place it can put a line where a person will see it is the conversation it is already in. There is no command: the agent writes the six fields into the conversation. A harness that installs a real log sink adds a Tool for it; this skill still says what a message is.

7862739825a1.title: What this skill is NOT
7862739825a1.content: A log line says what an actor did at a moment; it is not a record of work still outstanding. Logging is also not asking: if a step needs a judgement, that is confirm-harness, and no number of log lines substitutes for it.

be0eed9b1c41.content: Skill logger: The contract a Logger keeps: accept a complete log message, record it unchanged where a person can read it, attributed to the actor the message names. 73991e3c8fac.title: LSI indexing — the platform’s application of methodologies/lsi.md
73991e3c8fac.content: Skill lsi-indexing: Build, read and audit a Latent Semantic Indexing index over a declared prose graph — a library, the skills, the work items, docs — to find units that discuss the same thing in different words, near-duplicates, outlier clusters, and a proposed home for unfiled work. Every output is a proposal; LSI never writes a relation. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . The method is the node, not this file. lsi carries what LSI is, its sources, and the six refusals. This skill says how to run it here and how to read what comes back. Where the two disagree, the node wins.

65b2e7a0c87f.title: When to reach for it
65b2e7a0c87f.content: | you are asking | use | . | “which nodes contain these words?” | graph-search — lexical, exact, no score | . | “has anyone worked this topic in other words?” | bun run cat lsi query "<text>" --instance <i> --graph <g> | . | “is this new bean / section a restatement of an existing one?” | the sidecar’s nearDuplicates | . | “what is this graph about, as a whole?” | the sidecar’s dimensions (read both poles) | . | “is there junk in this library — boilerplate, specimen text, a bad page?” | the sidecar’s narrowDimensions | . | “which epic does this bean / branch / PR belong under?” | bun run cat lsi:epics | . Run the lexical search FIRST. LSI supplements an empty or thin lexical result; it never replaces a lexical hit, and its hits are always reported under their own label (latent only vs lexical+latent) — refusal 1.

2a91cc0e9c32.title: Commands
2a91cc0e9c32.content: bun run cat lsi index --instance <instance> --graph library # build + write the sidecar bun run cat lsi index --instance <instance> --graph library --doc 9789241548960-eng # one document bun run cat lsi query "certainty of the evidence" --instance <instance> --graph library bun run cat lsi:audit # which graphs need one; is each fresh? bun run cat lsi:epics --out <file.md> [--prs <open-prs.json>] # epic-filing proposal bun run cat lsi:near "<planned bean title>" # before `beans create` bun run cat-harness-tools/pipeline/graph-search.ts "<q>" --latent # lexical + graph, THEN a separate latent list . From an MCP host: the lsi_query tool (Tool node lsi-query), with the query as text and optional instance / graph. On a shell the query goes on STDIN (echo "<q>" | bun run cat lsi query --instance <iris-replica> --graph library), because free text never goes on a command line. A unit is the graph’s own chunk: a library section (what ingestion already produced), otherwise one markdown file. Units under 20 tokens are skipped — too little vocabulary to place.

875feb7aebc3.title: Beyond the beans: other graphs in lsi:near
875feb7aebc3.content: lsi:near also searches every graph a layer declares under lsiUnitProviders in its <instance>.json: content blocks (core) and Lean declarations (sci). It prints one list per graph. Scores from two separately built indexes are not comparable, so the lists are never merged into one ranking. Each list starts with explicit references: a block @id or a Lean name written in the query text. These are deterministic and unscored. The latent hits come after them, labelled lexical+latent or latent only. A graph that could not be indexed is shown as not searched, never as “no hits”. bun run cat lsi:near "<planned bean title>" --graphs blocks,lean-decl --root lean-decl=<lean dir> .

59070c9e38bc.title: Cross-document links — a floor, and hubs reported, not penalised
59070c9e38bc.content: bun run cat lsi links --instance <i> --graph <g> proposes links between units of DIFFERENT documents in one graph: each unit’s best other-document match, only at cosine ≥ 0.5 (LINK_FLOOR), with the units that are “nearest” to many others listed as hubs to discount. Most units get no link when the median best match is low, and that is the honest answer. There is no hub PENALTY. A CSLS-style penalty (2·cos − r(a) − r(b)) made ranking worse on reader-labelled pairs (real-vs-spurious AUC 0.96 with plain cosine, 0.75–0.79 with the penalty): a hub is often central because it is genuinely on-topic. The floor is a house number fitted to 15 labelled examples.

035b23da65fb.title: Keywords — the per-unit view
035b23da65fb.content: The weighted matrix says which terms characterise each unit before the index reduces it to k dimensions. keywordsOf(matrix, cols, texts, top, headings) keeps that view: a unit’s (or a pooled set of units’) top terms and two-word phrases, from the same weights. Its first consumer is bun run cat library:keywords (per library section and per document, written as keywords.json and shown in the library viewer). The scoring rules are documented with keywordsOf in pipeline/lsi.ts, and the ingestion skill that runs it says when (skill_fetch l1-document-ingestion, §”Keywords”). Reuse it for any unit set the index covers — work items, chapters — rather than writing a second term weighting.

23470c5a7aae.title: Correspondence analysis — the parallel track
23470c5a7aae.content: correspondence-analysis is a separate method over the same term matrix (pipeline/ca.ts): the SVD of the χ² residuals, so no dimension carries document length or term frequency. bun run cat lsi:epics --method ca runs it on the work item store. It is not significantly better or worse than LSI at filing work items (exact McNemar p = 0.17–0.71), so LSI stays the default. Reach for CA when an LSI dimension 1 has no negative pole, or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — CA’s leading dimensions go to the most distinctive profiles. Pick one per question; never average the two scores.

1f800fe93d1f.title: On ingestion — the index refreshes itself
1f800fe93d1f.content: bun run cat ingest … --promote ends by re-indexing the library it wrote into and printing, for the promoted document only, its near-duplicate section pairs and any narrow dimension it carries. Advisory: an index is not part of L1, so a failure prints “not refreshed — this is not a pass” and the ingest still succeeds. Read the lines while the document is fresh: a narrow dimension on a new document is almost always boilerplate, specimen text or a mis-extracted page, and it is cheapest to mark now.

0bb867de92e8.title: Where to LOOK at an index
0bb867de92e8.content: Its health is in the repository health report: bun run cat health, check lsi-indexes. It lists every declared prose graph that needs an index and lacks a fresh one, with the command that builds it, and each stored index’s narrow-dimension and near-duplicate counts. Its content (the dimensions as two poles, the near-duplicate pairs, the narrow-dimension units) is the sidecar below; read it with lsi query or open the file. bun run cat lsi:viz writes the Indexing evidence page at /cat-harness/lsi/ (/lsi/ is its declared alias). Until cat-harness#1144 it drew the indexes; the owner (2026-11-08) made it the evidence chain instead. For each indexing method (this one, correspondence-analysis, skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation) it shows the held papers it rests on, the skills that declare uses-methodology for it, the Tools that satisfy those skills, and the processes that call them. It also lists the indexing skills that apply no method, such as glossary work and lexical search, as having no evidence yet. So a skill that reads this index (keywords, lsi:near, graph-search --latent) gets the papers as its evidence by declaring uses-methodology: lsi. cat-harness DECLARES the page (visualisers entry lsi, renderedBy: lsi-viewer), so it appears on the navbar and the central Published graphs page with no further wiring. The page is excluded from every index’s units.

cc4b3bc76a04.title: Where the index lives, and what is stored
cc4b3bc76a04.content: test/results/lsi/<instance>/<graph>.lsi.json — the fingerprint, parameters, retained variance, per-dimension pole terms, each unit’s three nearest neighbours, and the findings. Not the vectors: a rebuild is about a second per few hundred units, and a float dump is not reviewable. That path is the working copy, and nothing under it is committed. The record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/). The readers cope with its absence: with no test/results/lsi/ in the checkout, the verdict rebuilds the index in memory and judges that run, writing nothing, and the health check reads the indexes by ref through qa-store (main). Anything but a hit is unknown, never “no index is missing”. The Indexing evidence page is never committed. It is declared under builtAtPublish in cat-harness.json (docs/en/cat-harness/lsi/), because it joins every instance’s methodologies, skills, Tools and processes, so it moves with the index’s pins, not with one commit. It reads no stored index; --detail and --ref are accepted and ignored. A merge strategy does not stop a generated file conflicting, even when the file is reproducible and take-base plus a regeneration converges. An SVD rotation is globally sensitive: one sentence added to one skill rewrites most of a sidecar’s dimensions and neighbours, so there is no small diff to merge. A declared strategy (derived-results/take-base) settles how a conflict is resolved, never whether one arises. Ask of a conflicting generated file “what is this file’s record, and is main it?” Where the answer is no, take the file off main. State graphs are indexed on demand, never stored. The beans graph changes on nearly every commit; a stored index would be stale on every PR and a merge-conflict magnet. lsi:epics rebuilds it each run.

8cfdd26a3a3d.title: Reading a sidecar
8cfdd26a3a3d.content: . | retained — share of ‖A‖²_F the rank-k approximation keeps. It is not a quality score; a low value on a large heterogeneous graph (work items: ~45 %) is expected. | Dimension 1 is usually a margin. Qi et al. (2023): LSA’s first dimensions mainly carry document length and overall term frequency. A dimension with no negative pole is that signature — skip it when reading themes. | dimensions — a dimension is a contrast, so read the positive and negative poles together. Refusal 2: it is not a topic until a person names it. | narrowDimensions — a dimension ≥ 80 % of whose mass sits on ≤ 3 units (or 1 %). Almost always non-prose: Lorem-ipsum layout filler, font specimens, a mis-extracted page. Treat as an ingestion finding. | nearDuplicates — cosine ≥ 0.95. In the work item store these are work items filed twice. A duplicate work item is scrapped with a pointer, never deleted (bean-coordination). | .

92de8262884d.title: The need-an-index audit
92de8262884d.content: bun run cat lsi:audit walks every declared graph of a prose kind across every layer and writes test/results/lsi-need-an-index.qa-results.json (qa-results/v1). | result | means | . | n/a | below the threshold — not judged, which is not the same as fine | . | fail | needs an index and has none, or its fingerprint no longer matches | . | pass | has a fresh index | . The threshold (≥ 100 units and ≥ 20,000 words) is a house number with its basis stated in scripts/lsi.ts; the method gives no corpus-size rule. It reports and does not gate (exit 0), like check:methodology-evidence; --strict exits 1 for a caller that has decided; no CI step runs it yet. The same verdict in the audited record — kg:audit’s tool-downstream-fresh . LSI is the first member of the downstream-tool family. The lsi-index Tool node declares downstream, and every bun run cat lsi index writes a folio-tool-run/v1 record — outcome and input fingerprint, on success AND on failure — under test/results/tool-runs/lsi-index/. The verdict reads three states: . | state | meaning | green? | . | fresh | a successful run’s recorded fingerprint matches the graph now | yes | . | stale | the graph changed since the recorded run | no | . | not-run / failed | no run record, or the last run failed | never | . A sidecar on disk with no run record is not-run: a file is not evidence the run that should keep it current succeeded. kg:audit carries this as tool-downstream-fresh on the lsi-index Tool (minor), one finding per graph, using the same verdict function as lsi:audit. Its finding text carries no counts, so the kg-qa sidecar moves only when a verdict flips. Two chains keep the indexes fresh, so the criterion stays quiet in ordinary work: . | a skill edit — skill:register runs lsi:skills before kg:audit, and CI checks it with lsi:skills:check; | an ingest — --promote re-indexes the library (§”On ingestion”). | . A graph that needs an index and has none is a standing minor finding on the lsi-index Tool, so “needs one and has none” is a fact in the audited record.

07d3d311f05f.title: Epic filing — the qou hierarchy, proposed by evidence
07d3d311f05f.content: The qou project-management skills (todo-manager, session-intent) require every piece of work to sit under a parent work item. lsi:epics proposes that parent for each open work item with no epic, each unmerged branch and each open PR: . | explicit first — a parent: chain that reaches an epic, or a work item id named in a branch’s commit messages (case-insensitive, merge commits excluded); | latent second — cosine to each open epic’s centroid (the epic plus all descendants of every status, each normalised; leave-one-out for the work item being scored). A branch or PR is folded in from its name and commits. | . It prints a calibration line: of the work items already under an epic, how often LSI’s best guess is the current epic (about 59 % against 21 classes, flat across k = 50–250; log-entropy beats tf-idf). Read every proposal in that light. A disputed filing is not a misfiling. A work item filed by symptom (translation catalogues under CI RELIABILITY because they turned main red) may be filed by LSI by subject (TRANSLATION). Both are defensible; which axis an epic means is a decision for the owner, not for the score. Never apply the proposal in bulk. beans update <id> --parent <epic> is done one work item at a time by somebody who read both the work item and the epic.

9866501c0084.title: Materialize on demand
9866501c0084.content: Skill materialize-on-demand: After bootstrap, a person asks for part of a remote subgraph to be held locally. Check what is already here (cache:index), put a number on the ask before anything is fetched, then run materialize-remote. Eviction is a report, never an act. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Bootstrap brings an agent to a working harness. It does not bring the corpus, and must not: a remote source such as IRIS runs to about a million files and hundreds of gigabytes. What arrives is the reference; a person asks, as they come to need it, for parts of subgraphs to be materialized. This skill is that ask. The gates are not here; they are in materialize-remote, once.

55e0c027f037.title: 1. What is already here
55e0c027f037.content: bun run cat cache:index # summary and eviction candidates bun run cat cache:index --all # every copy . Read the columns for what they are: . | column | values | what it means | . | size | recorded · measured · directory · absent | measured is the file now, not when it landed. A directory is counted through its parts. absent is not zero. | . | fetched | a date, or not recorded | only the record’s materializedAt | . | last read | not recorded, always | nothing records reads; file access times are not used, because they are often off or reset by a checkout. | . | freshness | fresh · expired · no-expiry · permanent | from freshness(). no-expiry is a finding: a working copy nobody gave a lifetime. | . If what they want is already held and fresh, stop: point them at it.

dd6ba91c5437.title: 2. Put a number on the ask BEFORE anything moves
dd6ba91c5437.content: Asking must not mean hundreds of gigabytes arrive without a number first. Before calling materialize-remote: . | Name the subset in the source’s own terms: its identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning layer’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | Close it over dependencies if the descriptor says the subset is not self-contained (subsetIsSelfContained: false, mathlib). The size that matters is the closure’s. | State the size and its basis: from the descriptor’s enumeration, or a measured listing. If neither gives a number, say that. The SIZE gate refuses on an unknown, and so should this conversation. | Say what it would add to the cache total from step 1. | . Then ask the person, with the number in front of them.

3045ead25b90.title: 3. Materialize
3045ead25b90.content: Run Process_MaterializeRemote. Its five gates decide; this skill does not second-guess them. A refusal leaves the content referenced, with the reason recorded. That is the process working, not failing.

97227a908762.title: 4. Eviction is a report
97227a908762.content: cache:index lists candidates: expired first, then no-expiry working copies, largest first. An archival copy is never a candidate. Nothing is removed by the tool or by you. Show the list with sizes and reasons, and let the person decide (deletion-requires-confirmation).

a88c6efac80a.title: Materializing remote content
a88c6efac80a.content: Skill materialize-remote: Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . One process for every caller that lands remote content locally. | caller | remote source | held locally | refresh | . | the IRIS replica | IRIS | selected items | refresh-materialized | . | bootstrap | a harness | the cat-harness checkout | upstream-pins.json | . bootstrap/workflows/initialize-harness.bpmn fetches a harness that is remote content and lands it locally; upstream-pins.json exists because that copy goes stale. Diagrams: materialize-remote.bpmn and refresh-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Nothing here restates either — where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

f5a080e96366.title: Ask the purpose FIRST
f5a080e96366.content: working or archival, before any gate, because three of the five mean different things under each. |   | working | archival | . | what is kept | derived content — sections, OCR | the original bytes | . | retention | expires; re-fetchable | no expiry, by design | . | sourceLoss | unanswered | discharged | . | fixity | not needed | required | . A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know.

404c80e1f02f.title: The five gates
404c80e1f02f.content: Each is a decision a person makes; none is answerable from a file. A gate that only warns is a gate nobody fails. | Size — what fraction, and what the whole would cost. Refuse when you cannot tell: “three items” with no denominator is not a size answer. | Restrictions — “no restrictions known in context” is a state, not a green light. unknown is never rendered as permitted. | Copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists here and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. | Retention — what expires this copy. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. | Source loss — what survives if the origin goes. Only an archival copy discharges this. Origins do disappear: a regional repository instance can be merged away, taking its handles with it. | .

2fbec28a444b.title: Three states, and no default
2fbec28a444b.content: referenced (it exists, we know where, we hold no bytes) · materialized · unknown. A node that has not declared one is invalid, not unknown — “the author did not say” and “the author said they could not tell” are different facts, and only the second is actionable. A refusal is the process working. The node stays referenced, the graph still knows it exists, and the refusing gate’s basis is recorded so the next agent does not re-litigate it.

6654977eb102.title: Refresh is not re-import
6654977eb102.content: Three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both. A materialized copy edited in place is not a copy — overwriting it destroys work whose existence was never established; check:materialized-fixity detects it. An archival copy is never refreshed. Re-fetching it discards the state it exists to keep. It gets a fixity check instead — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy: restore from backup, never re-download.

0e9883d35579.title: Before you enumerate anything
0e9883d35579.content: cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts answers the question that comes before the gates: how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset. Check subsetIsSelfContained first — when it is false (mathlib), close the request over its dependencies before gating, because the size being gated is the closure’s, not the request’s.
