f1da3ff3e3ce.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
f1da3ff3e3ce.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

74189d37d40f.title: Step 1 — which layer?
74189d37d40f.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

a31811337bf0.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
a31811337bf0.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

95c4d8b6f215.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
95c4d8b6f215.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

f97888d9243c.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
f97888d9243c.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

9d2e35120c92.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
9d2e35120c92.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

a62e7134ee75.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
a62e7134ee75.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

a1e100d747fe.title: Checklist
a1e100d747fe.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

86f83755d7e5.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
86f83755d7e5.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

25ec434e070d.title: The CI workflow is the list
25ec434e070d.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

3834eab11c99.title: bun test green is not the gates green
3834eab11c99.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

7a514df02afd.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
7a514df02afd.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

4796cb7fbcd7.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
4796cb7fbcd7.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

e898ed290578.title: Fast versus full is job membership
e898ed290578.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | . render:bpmn:check and node-views:report are QA reports, not merge gates: their results go to the qa-reports branch and show on each layer’s QA page, and neither is in index-gates.json or always-green. The node-view report needs a built site or a live base, so it is not in the fast set either; its author’s check is node-views:judge --against main, which fails only on a finding new against the baseline.

1209bcaeba9c.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
1209bcaeba9c.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

6d0d00330093.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
6d0d00330093.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

0a2ac7d569df.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
0a2ac7d569df.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

15cc610a92aa.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
15cc610a92aa.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

fef38e5137b3.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
fef38e5137b3.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

518abcda622e.title: 🛑 Role Split: Active merge-steward vs Sibling Sessions (Process_MergeTrain & Process_MergeToMain) — STRICT
518abcda622e.content: This skill composes directly with the platform SDLC merge architecture; read these alongside this file: . | Merge Steward Watch Loop (merge-manager-watch.bpmn): folio-assistant/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-manager-watcher.md | Merge Queue & Merge Train (Process_MergeTrain + merge-overlap): folio-assistant/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-queue.md and folio-assistant/cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-overlap.ts (bun run cat merge:overlap) | Merge to main Gate (Process_MergeToMain): folio-assistant/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-to-main.md | Declared Conflict Patterns & Refusal Hand-Back (Process_MergeRefusal): folio-assistant/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-conflict-patterns.md | Mandatory Swarm Launch Briefing: swarm-sibling-launch.md | . 1. Only the Active merge-steward Merges onto main . | Siblings NEVER self-merge onto main when a merge-steward is active. Only the single session holding the merge-steward lane writes to main (under explicit owner release recorded per merge-to-main.md). | Sibling handoff contract (sibling-session lane): When a sibling finishes its branch and passes local verification (lean-direct-cone.sh -j 1 / lean-library-sweep.py, precision-gates.sh --changed, check-sidecars.sh, voice-leak-audit.ts, two-step witness SHA stamp, 0 dirtied qou-v0t8 contended audit witnesses), it: . | Opens a Ready PR (--base main, using --body-file / shell=False so backticks survive intact) with a linked GitHub issue (Closes #<issue>) and zero unticked - [ ] boxes; | Applies the ready-to-merge label (when authorized by the owner per merge-queue.md §”Ask the user before submitting”) and posts a signed ready: <full head sha> comment on the PR; | Sends the 6-line merge request (PR #<n> + URL, Closes #<issue> + bean IDs, branch + ready: <full head sha>, authored files touched, local gate verdicts, overlap / ordering constraints) to the active merge-steward, then monitors status (never fire-and-forget, and never churn unnecessary rebases while queued far back). | . | . 2. Overlap-Partitioned Merge Trains (>= 2 Ready PRs Queued, Process_MergeTrain) . When >= 2 Ready PRs are queued, the merge-steward MUST NOT rebase, sweep, and rebuild main $N$ separate times sequentially. Instead, execute Process_MergeTrain: . | Overlap Partition (merge-overlap): Run bun run cat merge:overlap (folio-assistant/cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-overlap.ts) over the open Ready PRs to classify authored vs generated/additive paths and partition admissible PRs into mutually independent batches of 4–8 PRs on merge-train/<base>-<n> (broadcasting hold to pushing siblings before assembling/landing the train, and done when finished per merge-manager-watcher.md). | Stack Members & Regenerate Shared Additive Regions ONCE: Merge each admitted member onto merge-train/<base>-<n> in priority/PR order (--no-regen), then reconcile and regenerate additive/generated regions once across the combined train: . | computations/q0_anchor_manifest.json (additive union of producer entries, +0 removals), | folio/quantum-observable-universe/lean/QOU.lean (sorted module umbrella imports), | folio/schema/references.ts + folio/references/*.json (ORDER union + references.bib regeneration when bibliography entries were added), | folio/**/*.qa.json via python3 scripts/qa-sidecar-agent-union.py --against <pre-rebase-ref> --apply (mechanically preserving all agent verdicts whose field_hash still certifies the merged block). | . | Run the Combined Gate Suite ONCE on merge-train/<base>-<n>: . | python3 scripts/lean-library-sweep.py (plus bash scripts/lean-content-sweep.sh <changed content-block .lean> if any content sibling .lean changed — require VERDICT: GREEN, exit 0; exit 8 INCOMPLETE is NOT green), | bun run scripts/run-validate.ts folio/quantum-observable-universe (and bash scripts/check-sidecars.sh), | bun run folio/pipeline/voice-leak-audit.ts (L1–L4 clean on touched blocks), | python3 scripts/compute-qa.py --all --base origin/main (diff/ratchet gates clean; revert any dirtied qou-v0t8 tree-measuring audit witnesses via git checkout -- computations/audits/ computations/*.witness.json). | . | Bisect & Eject ONLY Red Culprits (Process_MergeRefusal): If the combined train fails a gate, attribute (Task_Attribute) or bisect (Task_Bisect) to isolate ONLY the red culprit PR(s). Eject ONLY the culprit(s) — never abort the green members and never edit authored code inside the train — handing each culprit back via Process_MergeRefusal (Merge refused: #<n> <cause> blocking bean + in-place PR status comment), re-assemble the remaining green members on merge-train/<base>-<n>, and re-verify once. | Land in Train Order & Verify Replay (Process_MergeToMain): Land each green member in train order under recorded owner authorisation (merge-to-main.md), NEVER passing --delete-branch (delete_branch_on_merge is strictly forbidden — preserve every local and remote branch), verify EVERY landed member with python3 scripts/verify-merge-replay.py --branch origin/<branch> --merged <merge-sha> (MISSING: 0), run post-merge-rebuild (bash scripts/publish-main-local.sh --deploy) once on the new main tip, and post done. | .

d072a4a7e06a.title: Workflow
d072a4a7e06a.content: Phase 0: Sibling coordination . Before starting the merge pipeline, identify sibling PRs whose scope overlaps this branch’s files: . mcp__github__list_pull_requests(owner, repo, state="open") . For each sibling PR that touches the same files or content domain: . | Post a brief coordination comment: “Starting prepare-merge on # | ; touches . Review welcome if you'd like to check for conflicts before merge." | | Do NOT wait for responses — this is a courtesy notification, not a blocking request. | . Phase 1: /prepare-merge (steps 1–6) . Execute the full /prepare-merge skill (rebase, integrate, one-voice, Lean build, final rebase, request reviews). All steps must succeed before proceeding. 🛑 If the branch touches any .lean, the Lean step is a SWEEP, not bare lean-direct. /prepare-merge §4 carries the reasoning; the short version is that lean-direct against the restored olean cache verifies against a snapshot, so a library signature that moved afterwards leaves the file green and broken at once. That is not hypothetical — descartesWtrace recorded exit 0 and landed on main red (#6751). # If rebasing a pre-Q3 branch that still places/imports modules under legacy `QOU/<OldSynonym>/`: nice -n 10 python3 scripts/apply-lean-reservoir-migration.py --fixup-branch scripts/lean-content-sweep.sh <changed content-block .lean ...> # or no args scripts/lean-library-sweep.py # unified dirty closure across MathlibExt + 6 Tier-B libs + QOU . Both rebuild from source only the modules whose own olean predates their own last source commit, and never invoke lake, so the restored cache is not evicted. Library sweep is 122 s on a 74-module closure; the content sweep is ~50 min for all 261, so pass the changed files when you have them and SHADOW=<dir> to reuse the shadow. Record which one ran, in the PR, in these words — this is the Phase-4 verification gate’s evidence and the distinction it turns on: . | “lean-library-sweep.py: N/N dirty modules rebuilt from source, exit 0” — source-verified. Quote its VERDICT: line. Exit 8 (INCOMPLETE) means no RED but some module TIMEOUT / UNVERIFIED / BLOCKED: that is not a green, so do not write “exit 0” for it (bean qou-tpdg). | “lean-direct against the restored cache, exit 0” — snapshot-conditional. Say so, and say why the sweep was not run. | . A sweep result is container-scoped (the dirty closure is computed against this container’s olean tree) and does not cover the UGB or Fred2005 packages. Do not write either limit out of the PR. Bean qou-56qy. Sidecar conflicts during the rebase. Resolve content/**/*.qa.json to either side as usual for the script entries, then restore the other side’s agent entries mechanically: . python3 scripts/qa-sidecar-agent-union.py --against <pre-rebase-ref> --apply . An agent verdict has no producer — qa-sweep regenerates script candidates and never a judgement — so “let the pipeline re-run it” loses those entries silently. The #5103 takeover dropped 7381 of them that way (qou-tqr9). The script is additive and skips any entry whose field_hash.md no longer certifies the merged .md. Phase 1b: Wait for reviews + status briefing . 🟧 OWNER RULING 2026-11-22: Copilot review is no longer required; audit checks replace it. Verbatim: “co-pilot review is no longer required. We are using audit checks.” Do not request Copilot or wait for it. Phase 1b is now: run the audit checks (lean-direct on changed .lean, scripts/precision-gates.sh --changed, scripts/check-sidecars.sh, run-validate, producer re-runs) and record what ran in the PR. The text below is history. Wait for the Copilot review to land before proceeding. Do NOT skip ahead — the review is the input to Phase 2. Gemini is sunset — never wait on it (2026-08-07). The consumer Gemini Code Assist GitHub integration has ceased all code-review activity; a /gemini review comment is answered only by a [!CAUTION] sunset notice, or by nothing at all. Copilot is the only live external reviewer. Waiting for a Gemini review that can never arrive is the documented stall mode (PR #4456). 🛑 CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (bean qou-426q) — READ THIS BEFORE THE BANNER BELOW. The banner is half right, and the wrong half is the operative one. Measured on #6104, #6116, #6132: . | claim | verdict | . | get_check_runs returns total_count: 0 — no copilot-pull-request-reviewer run is ever created | CONFIRMED | . | therefore zero reviews arrive | FALSE — Copilot reviewed #6104 and #6116 | . The mechanism is UNSETTLED — do not repeat my first explanation. I wrote here that Copilot “delivers via webhook, not check run, so the poll is structurally blind”. That is a candidate, not a finding, and it does not discriminate: total_count: 0 is equally consistent with every other candidate, including simple quota exhaustion. The adjudicated write-up is docs/audits/2026-08-30-copilot-review-works-again.md (bean qou-gwe9, reopened), which weighs three and picks none: availability changed; Copilot reviews on its own trigger rather than on request_copilot_review; or a quota gates it, making the whole thing intermittent. 🛑 THERE IS A QUOTA, and it is easy to exhaust. That audit measured five requests across two repos in ~30 minutes returning “the user who requested the review has reached their quota limit”. Copilot review is a rationed resource, not a binary available/unavailable one. Do not re-request after every push — nothing else in the repo’s docs says this, and it is the operational rule that actually follows from the measurement. Cost, on the record: #6104 and #6116 were merged on the “do not wait” guidance and the reviews landed minutes later, carrying six findings — one a real correctness regression (a tautology introduced into a three-path cross-check, so its printed “should be ≈ 1.0” ratio read exactly 1.0 by construction). Fixed in #6132, after the merge. What to do: do NOT restore a blocking poll on check runs — that half of qou-gwe9 stands and the poll would still see nothing. Instead, subscribe to the PR (subscribe_pr_activity) and expect the review to arrive as a wake. A merge is not gated on a check run that does not exist, but a subscribed session must handle the review when it lands — which, after a merge, means a follow-up PR rather than nothing. Latency is unmeasured (n=2, both within minutes); do not write a specific wait window into this skill on that basis. The original banner follows, and its check-run half remains accurate: . 🛑 MEASURED 2026-08-23 — do NOT run this wait. Copilot never enqueues. n=5 (bean qou-gwe9, AGENTS.md rule 10): on #5474, #5495, #5411, #5459 and #5482 the review was requested explicitly and zero arrived. Critically get_check_runs returns total_count: 0 — there is no queued or in_progress copilot-pull-request-reviewer run, so step 1 below polls for an object that is never created and the 15-minute cap is the only exit. Re-requesting after a force-push does not help (#5459), and the cases span new Lean, a 20-file revert and a .beans/-only change, so the “did not trigger for this file type” reading in step 1 does not survive n=5. Do this instead: request the review once (cheap, keeps the record), then proceed immediately with 0 comments and say so in the briefing — “Copilot: not enqueued (measured, qou-gwe9)”. With CI dispatch-only and Gemini sunset, there are zero live external gates; your own verification is the whole gate, so state what you ran. The protocol below is kept for the day a reviewer is reinstated. Wait protocol (15-minute window — extended 2026-05-31 per author): . | After requesting reviews in Phase 1, poll for Copilot’s check-run status every 30 seconds (up to 15 minutes): mcp__github__pull_request_read(method="get_check_runs", ...) . Look for the copilot-pull-request-reviewer check run: . | "status": "queued" or "status": "in_progress" → reviewer has noticed the PR; keep polling every 30s | "status": "completed" → reviews are in, proceed immediately | No check run after 2 minutes → reviewer did not trigger for this file type (e.g. skill-only PRs with no code); proceed with 0 comments | . | Check that Copilot reviewed the CURRENT head. A review whose commit_id is an earlier commit is stale and does not count — re-request with mcp__github__request_copilot_review and keep polling. (PR #4456 carried a 13-file review against an 85-file head.) . | 15-minute hard cap: if Copilot has not completed after 15 minutes, proceed with whatever comments have landed. Note “Copilot: timed out (15 min)” in the briefing. | . Once reviews arrive (or the 15-minute cap is reached), give the user a concise status briefing: . | PR identity: “#N — title” with clickable URL | Branch: branch-name → main | Scope: files changed, additions/deletions, commits | Review comments received: total count, by reviewer, with 1-line summary of each thread: ``` Review comments (3 total — Copilot: 3): . | [Copilot] line 42 engine.py — threshold mismatch | [Copilot] line 98 engine.py — unused variable | [Copilot] line 173 engine.py — spelling fix ``` | . | Disposition plan: for each comment, state the planned action (accept / modify / reject / escalate) BEFORE making changes — so the user can redirect: Plan: accept 1,2,3; accept-with-modification 4; reject 5 (reason: "classical limit" is the standard term per §7a) . | CI status: green / failing / pending | . The user can reply with overrides (e.g. “reject 4”, “skip 2,3”). If no override within ~30 seconds, proceed with the stated plan. Phase 2: Resolve review comments . After the briefing (and any user overrides), triage each thread: . | Classification | Action | . | accept | Apply the suggested fix, commit, push. | . | accept-with-modification | Apply a modified version, commit with explanation. | . | reject-with-reason | Reply on the thread with the reason (e.g. “intentional — see §X”). | . | escalate | Cannot resolve autonomously — proceed to Phase 3. | . For each resolved thread, commit the fix with message: fix(PR #N): address <reviewer> thread r<id> — <1-line summary> . Push after each batch of resolutions. Phase 3: Structured user questions (only when blocked) . If any review comment requires a judgment call (ambiguous intent, architectural decision, multiple valid approaches), use AskUserQuestion with: . | Rich context per AGENTS.md user-accessibility rules: . | Quote the exact comment + file path + line number | Show the current code vs proposed change (preview) | State trade-offs for each option | Default to multiSelect: true unless choices are mutually exclusive | Prefix with 🟡 | . | Batch questions — collect ALL blocked items into a single AskUserQuestion call (up to 4 questions) rather than asking one at a time. | . Phase 4: Merge (Process_MergeToMain — Active merge-steward Only) . Reminder: Only the active merge-steward executes Phase 4 (or runs it across 4–8 PRs simultaneously via Process_MergeTrain when >= 2 Ready PRs are queued). A sibling session stops after Phase 2/3, applies ready-to-merge + signed ready: <full head sha>, and sends the 6-line merge request to the merge-steward. After all review comments are resolved (or the user has answered all escalated questions): . | Run bun run scripts/run-validate.ts folio/<paper> (and bun run folio/pipeline/voice-leak-audit.ts if folio/ prose changed) one final time. | If the branch touches any .lean, the sweep from Phase 1 must have run on the FINAL head, and its result must be in the PR. A sweep on an earlier commit is not evidence about what is being merged — the final rebase in /prepare-merge §5 moves the branch onto a main whose library may have shifted underneath it, which is the exact mechanism this gate exists for. Re-run it after that rebase, not before. | Check CI status via mcp__github__pull_request_read get_check_runs. Expect total_count: 0 — auto-triggers are disabled repo-wide, so this returns nothing and is not a gate. Never read it as green. | If all green: merge via mcp__github__merge_pull_request with merge_method: "rebase" (default per AGENTS.md §”Branch + PR workflow” rule 8 — replays the structured commits onto main linearly, no merge commit). Rule 8 is authoritative. | CRITICAL: DO NOT DELETE THE BRANCH EVER! If using the GitHub CLI, DO NOT pass --delete-branch. If using the GitHub API, ensure the branch is preserved. | Report the merge SHA + URL. | . Phase 5: Post-merge verification, then coordination . Verify the merge replayed every commit — this phase had no check at all until 2026-09-04, and the failure it misses is on the record. scripts/verify-merge-replay.py --branch origin/<branch> --merged <merge-sha> . A rebase-merge can land 7 of 8 commits and still report success through the API. PR #5111 did exactly that; it was recovered as #5125, and only because someone grepped main for the edited content. Do NOT verify with git diff origin/main <merged-head>. After a rebase-merge the PR’s head becomes main’s tip, so that command compares a commit to itself and returns empty whether or not anything was dropped — strongest-looking evidence, zero information. Whenever the PR is the last thing merged (the normal case for this pipeline) it cannot fail. Ten PRs were merged on 2026-08-15 under an instruction calling it “the strongest check”; bean qou-vtau. Its mirror image misleads too: diffing main against the pre-merge branch head shows every sibling PR that landed in between as though it were yours. The script compares patch-ids — a hash of each commit’s diff, invariant under rebase, where shas are not. Run --selftest if you want to confirm it can still detect a drop; it synthesises one and asserts the patch-id check catches what git diff misses. Two behaviours to read correctly rather than “fix”: . | a commit with an empty diff has no patch-id and is reported separately, not counted as replayed; | a commit whose content changed during the rebase (a conflict resolved differently) reports MISSING by design — it did not replay, and the resolution deserves a look. | . Then coordinate: . | Post a brief update on any sibling PRs that were notified in Phase 0: “PR # merged; updated on main. Please rebase if needed." | Unsubscribe from the merged PR’s activity. | . Then rebuild the published site (owner, 2026-11-23). GitHub Actions is dispatch-only here, so nothing rebuilds the site on a merge. After every merge to main, follow post-merge-rebuild: check out the merged main and run bash scripts/publish-main-local.sh --deploy. If it cannot run (no platform checkout, a failed build), say so in the merge report; do not skip it silently.

b38533e5a6a6.title: Process state — the task you are in, inside the process you are running
b38533e5a6a6.content: Skill process-state: Track where you are inside a running process — which task, in which swimlane, under which role — and recover deliberately when you find yourself outside it. Read before completing a workflow step, and whenever something unexpected interrupts one. Covers what to do about notes and stickies you re-anchored while off-process, which leave no trace in the artefact. Named by: Hand back to the discussion . An agent working a BPMN process holds nested state: a task, inside a process instance, under a role that owns a swimlane. Losing track of the outer level while still acting on the inner one looks like ordinary work and produces changes nobody authorised.

b6a953f04633.title: The three levels, and what each one answers
b6a953f04633.content: | level | answers | where it lives | . | process instance | which run of which process is this? | beans/workflows/ (workflow-state graph in work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)) | . | swimlane / role | am I the actor who may do this? | the lane on the activity; checked by the executor (task-authorization) | . | task | which step am I on, and is it enabled? | workflow_next | . workflow_next reports what is enabled now, which lane owns it, and which skill implements it. workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. Those two are the ground truth; your memory of where you were is not. Name yourself when you complete a step. Pass actor as a declared actor id, not a free-text name: workflow_complete checks that actor against the lane’s role and the ODRL policies before recording anything, refuses a role mismatch or a deny, and writes the verdict into the history. An actor you type is recorded as asserted, not authenticated. Say so rather than presenting it as identity. workflow_gate takes the same actor and target, so ask it before doing the work (task-authorization). The history is checked again afterwards. bun run cat prov:qaqc turns every instance’s history into a W3C PROV-O log and re-runs the same check on each step; claude or a login in actor, rather than a declared actor id, shows up there as undeclared-actor. It is advisory: the findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page, and CI fails only when that page is stale (task-authorization §”The after-check”).

a818ebed1f66.title: Say which process you are in — every turn
a818ebed1f66.content: Claiming a work item says what you are working on. This says where in the process you are working, which is the question a reader cannot answer from an id. Name the process, the lane and the task, and say when you switch: . Process: crdm-requirements, Agent lane · Phase 6 — implement. Completed A_Implement; next is A_Summary. The engine’s “what is enabled now” call (workflow_next) reports the enabled step, the lane that owns it, and the skill that implements it. Say which permission you are acting under. Entering a task in a lane means performing it as that lane’s role, and that needs an ODRL rule that permits it there (permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts: the actor, the action, and the process, task and role as scope). If the answer is unknown or deny, you are out of process for that task: route it to a lane whose actor holds the permission, or stop and ask. The engine enforces this before the task at the deterministic end of the spectrum; at the agentic end nothing stops you, and the QA/QC report over the PROV-O record finds it afterwards (agentic-harness.html#bpmn-execution). Switching processes is the case that matters. Moving between processes changes who is accountable for the next step and which gates apply, and a reader who does not know you switched will assume the old lane’s rules still hold. Naming it is not the same as recording it (advisory) . A turn that is in a process has an INSTANCE under the declared workflow-state graph. Naming the process in prose is the report; the recorded instance in the work-plan store is the evidence. Without recorded instances, a reviewer sweeping a window of merged work cannot classify a single session by lane. workflow_start creates it, workflow_next and workflow_complete advance it, and the state lives in the work-plan store precisely so a sibling session reads the same position — workflow-state.md §”Where running instances live”. Opening or claiming a work item for a process step means starting or resuming its workflow instance: . | Claiming or starting work in a process (code-change-review, merge-train, crdm-requirements, etc.): start an instance with workflow_start passing bean: "<id>" (CLI: bun run cat workflow:start --process <process> --subject <subject> --bean <id>), or resume the running instance that already names that work item. workflow_start writes the process:<Process_Id> tag and Workflow: backlink onto the work item so the visualiser can place the work item on its current BPMN step. | Advancing through tasks: call workflow_complete (bun run cat workflow:complete --id <instance> --task <node> --actor <actor>) as each step finishes so the token moves with the work. | Closing the work item: complete the final step so the workflow instance reaches status: "completed". If a work item is closed (completed or scrapped) while its workflow instance still sits running, run bun run cat workflow:instances --sweep to close stale instances while preserving their history and PROV-O trail (cat-harness#988). | . The session-start sweep reads the work-plan store and reports “no instance recorded” as a FINDING, not as silence, when the directory holds none. A finding is not a failure — plenty of turns are legitimately outside any process — it is the prompt to say which. This rule is ADVISORY: nothing gates on it. Record the instance when the turn is in a process, but no check refuses a merge without one, and none should be added without a new ruling from the owner. It is labelled advisory because a rule called STRICT that nothing enforces teaches readers that the word is decoration, including where it is enforced. The gap is computed, never quoted, because a count written down goes stale with nothing to say so. bun run cat workflow:instances prints today’s count: instances recorded, instances started since the rule, first-parent merges in the same window, running instances whose work item is closed or missing from the store (staleInstances), in-progress work items carrying a process:<id> tag with no running instance (untrackedProcessBeans), and the CI workflows that read the graph. Merges are an upper bound on the instances owed, since a steward’s train, a docs-only fix or a revert may have none. The command reports the gap and exits 0 by default (--strict exits 1 on stale or untracked process work items; --sweep closes running instances whose work item is completed, scrapped, or missing); only a count it cannot make (store unmounted, shallow clone, an undatable instance) exits 2. Arriving without the sweep — a mid-session clone, a project thread . A session that clones a harness repository after it started has no route to this skill: . | the sweep above runs from .claude/hooks/session-start.sh, and a hook runs only when the repository is there at session start; | the workflow_* and skill_fetch tools come from the folio-assistant MCP server (.mcp.json), which starts with the session, so a mid-session clone has neither; | the repository’s CLAUDE.md reaches the agent only once the clone is registered. | . So, when you clone a harness repository after the session started: . | Register it if the platform offers that (Claude Code on the web: register_repo_root), so its CLAUDE.md and skills load. | Run the sweep by hand, from the checkout root: bash .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. It lays the mounts down and prints ## Running processes, the prompt this section depends on. | Name the process before the first edit. A code fix in a layer is sdlc/code-change-review; a repin is sdlc/upstream-version-adoption; a preview is sdlc/feature-staging. A delivery is delivery-summary plus the deep-link rule in feedback-deep-links. | With no workflow_* tools, say so. “Process X, not recorded: this session has no workflow engine” is the true third state. Never write it as recorded, and never leave it out. | . A coordinator that briefs a thread (a project’s coordinator session, a swarm lead, anything that spawns an agent) puts the process, or “none”, the governing skill and the repository in the brief. A spawned thread starts with nothing else that would tell it, and the coordinator’s own memory holds no process rules by design. When the brief is written during a live discussion with a person, it also names the discussion: who is talking with the person, how to reach them, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). That is definitions.discussion of the hand-back-to-discussion input schema, and it is what lets the thread hand its cards, questions and results back instead of leaving them in its own channel.

7f17d01eb32b.title: How to tell you are out of process
7f17d01eb32b.content: You are outside the process if any of these is true, and each is cheap to check: . | workflow_complete refused a step you believed was next. The refusal is not an obstacle to route around — it is the detector working. | You are about to change a corpus file and cannot name the instance that authorised it. scripts/check-corpus-gate.ts refuses exactly this at the commit boundary; discovering it there is late. | workflow_next returns a step in a lane whose role you are not playing. | You cannot say which process instance you are in without looking it up — and looking it up returns nothing, or more than one candidate. | The work you are doing was not in the brief you opened the turn with. An unplanned detour is the most common way this happens, and the least likely to be noticed from inside it. | .

f91bc42c44f8.title: Recovering
f91bc42c44f8.content: When one of the five fires, stop making changes and recover in this order: . | Re-read the instance. work_plan_prime reports every instance’s position next to its work item. State is committed, so a sibling session’s progress is visible too. | Reconstruct from context what you were doing and which task it belongs to. You usually can: the branch name, the claimed work item, and the opening brief together pin it. | Say what you concluded, and confirm it with the user before resuming: . I completed the QA sweep but never completed Task_ReviewFindings, so the instance is still sitting before the editor decision. I believe I am in content-lifecycle instance cl-2f9, in the editor lane, at Gateway_EditorDecision. Confirm before I proceed? . This confirmation is not optional and not a formality. An agent that silently re-enters a process it inferred its way back into is asserting authorisation nobody gave it. The whole point of the swimlane guardrail is that the actor is assigned, not self-declared. The person owed the confirmation may give it in advance for a stated scope — see confirmation-waiver.md. | If you cannot reconstruct it, say so and stop. A wrong instance is worse than none: completing a step in the wrong run records an authorisation that did not happen. | .

6a45a0a3fbe0.title: What you MOVED while you were out of process
6a45a0a3fbe0.content: Steps 1–3 reconstruct where you were. They do not reconstruct what you changed position of, and for notes and stickies that is a separate problem with a sharper edge: . A move is not self-documenting. moveNote (schemas/ui/note-anchor.ts) returns the note with its new anchor and nothing about the old one. A note that has been moved cannot say where it was. So a sticky re-anchored during an off-process detour leaves no trace in the artefact. There is no field to read back, no diff that distinguishes “moved deliberately” from “moved by an agent that had lost the thread”, and — because a move keeps the id — nothing that even looks unusual. The only possible record is what was written to a work item at the time. Work items carry no anchor: a work item is not a thing pinned to a block, it is the record that a pinning changed. workflow/bean-link.ts has the note op that writes it. So, as part of recovery, before step 3’s confirmation: . | Name every note or sticky you re-anchored during the detour, with its anchor before and after. Read them off the work item’s note trail — not off the notes, which no longer know. | If the trail is silent and you moved things, say that. A gap is a finding. “I moved stickies and did not record where from” is recoverable by a person who remembers; “everything is fine” is not. | Do not move anything back on your own judgement. Re-anchoring to undo is another unlogged move, and it is a durable change made to cover one — see deletion-requires-confirmation.md, which is the same rule about a different verb. | . A note carries no movedFrom history. History kept in the artefact being moved is lost when the note is deleted, or moved by a tool that does not maintain the field. The work item is a separate record, which is what an audit trail has to be. Reading a bean back as the trail . A work item is a usable trail when a wrong claim is left in place, with the correction appended beside it rather than replacing it. Read back, the work item shows the premise, the disproof, and the re-scoped work in order, so an agent resuming can see that the original framing was abandoned and why, which is what it needs to avoid re-deriving the same mistake. A work item tidied to show only the correct conclusion reads as though the work had always been aimed there. That is why bean-coordination.md has unwanted work scrapped with its reasons rather than deleted: a record that shows only outcomes cannot distinguish a dead end somebody ruled out from one nobody tried.

51b73c569364.title: What not to do
51b73c569364.content: . | Do not start a fresh instance to escape a confusing one. Two instances for one piece of work is two answers to “was this authorised”, free to disagree. | Do not complete a step to “unstick” the process. Task_ReviewFindings, Gateway_EditorDecision, Task_Commit, Task_AuthorizeRelease and Task_PublishRelease are marked relaxable="false" precisely because they are the steps where skipping is most tempting and most costly. | Do not treat a refusal as a bug. workflow_complete refusing a step is the system telling you your model of where you are is wrong. | .

e077e11c5857.title: Relationship to the opening brief
e077e11c5857.content: The brief you open a turn with (turn-reporting.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) is what makes detector 5 usable: without a stated plan there is nothing for the current work to have diverged from. The two skills are one loop — brief the route, notice the divergence, confirm the recovery.

350a8b25913d.title: The three states, and why the third is the point
350a8b25913d.content: | state | means | evidenced by | . | verified | Lean accepts it, it is non-vacuous, and the Lean claim matches the prose | lean-proof-review + lean-proof-vacuity-audit + proof-narrative-lean-equivalence | . | open | there is a declaration, and at least one annotated sorry | proof-gap-audit, proof-triage | . | could not determine | the toolchain did not run, or the cache was cold, or the build died before any declaration elaborated | lean-environment-setup | . The third is never written as either of the other two. A build that did not run is not a failed proof, and it is emphatically not a passed one. An agent that cannot build must not report “no errors”.

f05b98d215f0.title: What a green build does not tell you
f05b98d215f0.content: lake build answers one question — does this elaborate. It does not answer: . | Is the statement inhabited? lean-witness-audit. | Is it vacuous? lean-proof-vacuity-audit. A theorem whose hypotheses cannot be satisfied is true and says nothing. | Does it match the prose? proof-narrative-lean-equivalence. This is the most common real defect: the Lean is a weaker claim, quantified differently, or over a different structure than the paragraph beside it. | Is the proof substantive? lean-substantive-pass, and proof-conciseness for the opposite failure. | . A block that passes the build and fails any of these is not verified, and recording it as such is worse than recording it open — an open claim gets worked, a falsely-verified one gets built upon.

ed3a75a48147.title: Recording it
ed3a75a48147.content: proof-status-tracking owns the sidecar and its shape. Two of its rules: . | The status is written by the sweep, never hand-edited. | Every sorry carries the proof obligation it stands for (skills/requirements/lean-verification.json, SHALL). An unannotated sorry cannot be told from abandonment. | .

Deciding that a mismatch between prose and Lean is acceptable is not the toolchain’s call — it belongs to the editor, at editing-hci-validation.bpmn’s Task_ReviewFindings, which is marked relaxable="false" precisely so that no policy can route around it.

da97ce6d5beb.title: The documents at their addresses: the primary step
da97ce6d5beb.content: Skill publish-documents: The primary step of initializing a Knowledge Graph harness: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document it names an address for (schemas, vocabulary, diagram vocabulary, graph export, each with its @context) is published AT that address, and the address answers. Checked first, right after the declaration is read. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . A Knowledge Graph harness is its JSON and JSON-LD. Its schemas say what a declaration and every node may be; its vocabulary says what each term means; its graph says what it holds. Each names itself with an IRI: a JSON Schema with $id, a JSON-LD document with @id. An IRI that answers 404 is a broken promise to everything that points at it. So this is the first step checked once the declarations are read, before any directory, README or site step.

1cc944b55421.title: Which documents
1cc944b55421.content: Read from the files, never from a list: . | every JSON file whose top-level $id lies under the declaration’s iriBase is a JSON Schema published at that $id; | every JSON-LD file whose top-level @id lies under iriBase is published at that @id. For bootstrap that is the vocabulary (ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/ns/) and the diagram vocabulary (processes/ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/processes/ns/, the namespace every diagram binds); | the graph export, built when the site is published, at the address its own @id names (bootstrap-graph-publication). | . Each document carries its @context inline, so publishing the document publishes its context. A harness whose documents name an external context publishes that context the same way, at its own IRI. No iriBase, no addresses. A layer that declares none has nothing here to publish, and says so rather than reporting a pass over nothing.

e0fd86e5b4b9.title: Where each goes
e0fd86e5b4b9.content: At the path its IRI names, with iriBase removed. An address ending in / (…/v0/ns/) gets the document as index.jsonld there, with an index.json copy beside it. A .jsonld gets a .json copy with the same bytes beside it, because many hosts serve .jsonld as a download. The .jsonld stays the real one: it is what the @id names.

2aa2f650a947.title: Two checks, four states
2aa2f650a947.content: | step | checks | done | not done | could not determine | . | schemas:staged | the site build puts each document at its address | every one is there, byte for byte | one is missing, or another file holds its address | the build could not run | . | schemas:published | each address answers | every one answers | one answers 404 | 403, 407, 5xx or no answer: that is about the way from here (a proxy, an access rule), not about the address | .

fac8f3adb952.title: The site is the vehicle
fac8f3adb952.content: The documents get to their addresses by the Pages site (publish-site): its workflow stages each one where its IRI says, and lists them all under “Published documents” on the README page (README.html). When schemas:published is not done, the site steps are how it gets done. The site is not the goal: a site that answers while one schema address does not has not finished initializing the harness. Where a toolset is available, its site check (site.ts --check) lists every address and what is staged at it, and init.ts reports both steps first.

f076e36f7231.title: Publish extracted statements with source links
f076e36f7231.content: Skill publish-extracted-statements: The standard step of adding source documents to a folio’s working artifact: every statement extracted from a library source is published readably in the artifact’s own pages AND in the shared extraction viewer, each with a link to its library entry and to the section it came from, and CI fails when the generated pages are stale. Generic across content types; each type’s adapter says only how its pages look. Executable form: processes/library/publish-extracted-statements.bpmn. Named by: Publish extracted statements with source links . A statement nobody can read beside its source is reviewed from memory, or not at all. So whenever source documents are added to a folio’s working artifact (a document, a paper, an implementation guide, a guideline), the statements extracted from them are published where a reader of that artifact will find them, each one linked back to where it came from. This is a standard step, not a per-folio choice. It is the sub-process Process_PublishExtractedStatements, and every process that brings source documents into an artifact calls it: . | caller | when | . | l1-document-ingestion | right after the entry is promoted, which is where it becomes complete | . | authoring-a-document, and each content type’s authoring process | before the artifact is rendered, so a source taken up since ingestion, or a statement changed since, is published too | .

65d29553874a.title: What is published
65d29553874a.content: A statement is a sentence or row captured verbatim from a library entry, whatever kind the extraction gave it: a recommendation, a requirement, a candidate a person has still to rule on. It is published as captured, with its status. This step neither promotes nor edits it. Each statement carries two links: . | the library entry: the entry’s own page in the library viewer; | the section: the section of that entry the statement was read from, labelled with the section’s title and its locator in the source’s own unit, read off the entry’s structure.json. For example “Catch up schedule, slide 7”, “Annex 2, page 41”, “Setup, cells 3–9”. | . The link is a library reference (instance, libraryId, sectionId), so a statement from another layer’s library resolves through that layer’s declaration and never through a relative path. A statement whose section does not resolve is reported, never published without a link: an untraceable statement is the failure this step exists to prevent.

1be56c917ee9.title: Where it is published — both places, from one list
1be56c917ee9.content: | place | what a reader gets | . | the artifact’s own pages | the statements of the sources this artifact draws on, inside the artifact, so a reader need not leave it | . | the shared extraction viewer | every source and every statement extracted from it, whichever artifact uses them, reached from the site’s Sources menu | . Both are generated from one collected list, so they cannot disagree about what was extracted or where it came from. Neither is hand-edited: a person corrects the extraction or the source, then regenerates.

274b94021a8d.title: What the content type supplies, and nothing more
274b94021a8d.content: The step is the same for every content type. What differs is how the artifact’s pages look, and that is the content type’s adapter’s business, declared in its content profile (folio-content-profiles): . | a document (a handbook, policy guidance): pages of the document; | a paper: an appendix or a section of the paper; | an implementation guide or a guideline built as one: pages of the guide. | . The platform layers name no folio, no content type and no level of a guideline. A folio’s own names for its pages (for example “L1 Recommendations” and “Scenario Candidates” in an immunization guideline) are the folio’s, set in its own configuration.

905cf5ef9282.title: Run it
905cf5ef9282.content: bun run cat statements:pages --page <spec>.json [--page <spec2>.json] [--check] . Each page is declared in a committed page spec (folio-statement-page/v1): the statement lists it publishes, the page it writes, its title and introduction, the URL prefixes of the library viewer (entryBase) and of the sources (sectionBase), and the content type’s table look (tableAttr). A spec rather than flags, because those are free text, and free text is never a command-line word. A spec names one or more statement lists (folio-extracted-statements/v1, schemas/extracted-statement.ts): each statement’s id, its text verbatim, its kind and status as the extraction records them, optionally the id of the statement it was derivedFrom (a scenario candidate written from a recommendation names it, and the page shows a “Derived from” column), and its source, a library reference with either a sectionId or the page (or slide) it was read from. With only a page, the section is the one that starts latest at or before it. When several sections start on that page (a one-page poster), the label names only the page. The front matter the PDF rung synthesises (sec-front-matter) is used only when no authored section starts at or before the page. A collector writes the list, and the collector is not core’s. A folio’s extraction has its own format (a guideline’s recommendation rows, a DAK layer’s requirement candidates, a paper’s quoted claims), so the content layer or the folio that owns the format turns it into a statement list. Core resolves, labels, renders and checks. Declare two specs over the same lists, one for the artifact’s page and one for the shared viewer’s, so the two cannot disagree.

12baed7dec3b.title: Staleness fails CI
12baed7dec3b.content: --check regenerates in memory and fails on any difference from the committed pages, and on any link that does not resolve. CI runs it, so a change to an extraction or a library entry that was not republished fails the build instead of leaving a page that says something the extraction no longer does.

b3b727ac3b28.title: Nothing to publish is a result
b3b727ac3b28.content: A referenced source (its licence forbids a copy), a dataset, or a source with no normative content yields no statements. The sub-process ends at “Nothing to publish”, which is a determined zero, recorded as such, not a skipped step.

d8f5516f5746.title: The site: a layer rendered for publication, and its address answering
d8f5516f5746.content: Skill publish-site: Give a layer a site: its Knowledge Graph rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answering. Four checks — a workflow publishes it, the gh-pages branch exists, Pages serves that branch, the address answers. How the rendering is staged and pushed is the toolset’s own process, not this skill’s. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . One abstract step. A layer with a repository is rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answers. How the rendering is staged, committed and checked is the toolset’s own subprocess (its render-to-GitHub-Pages skill and diagram), so this skill stays a list of checks. The site is how the documents reach their IRIs (publish-documents, the primary step), not the goal. Where the README page lands. At <site address>README.html, and the site address itself (index.html) is the landing page: by default a plain redirect to README.html, so a Harness that wants a different front page puts its own index.html or index.md at its root and changes nothing else. A page generated from the layer’s files says so at its top, and its footer points to what it was generated from, never to an editor for the published copy: that copy is replaced on every publish. The site address is the declaration’s iriBase when it declares one, otherwise https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/.

e33bda5d6f1d.title: The checks (initialization-steps)
e33bda5d6f1d.content: | step | done when | . | site:workflow | a workflow commits the rendering onto gh-pages: one under the layer’s own .github/workflows/, or one in the toolset that publishes it from outside. bootstrap’s own workflow writes only its JSON-LD context to gh-pages; its site is published from outside | . | site:branch | a gh-pages branch exists. It must exist before Pages can be switched on; where it does not, the step says how to create it (an orphan branch with a placeholder page) | . | site:enabled | Pages is on, serving gh-pages at /. Only after site:branch passes for this repository (see Order below). Switched on only by an authenticated forge CLI once the branch exists; otherwise the person gets the one step below | . | site:live | the address answers 200, and so does its README page, README.html. 404 after Pages is on usually means the workflow has not run yet. A 403, 407, 5xx or no answer is about the way from here: could not determine, never done | . Order: create gh-pages, then switch Pages on. Never the reverse. site:enabled is not attempted, and not asked of a person, until site:branch has passed for that repository, checked at the moment of asking (a read of the branch, not a remembered publish run). A first publish that is still running, or that failed, has not created the branch. When several repositories are set up together, the ask lists only those whose gh-pages exists now; the others are asked later, once their branch exists, and never ahead of it “for when it appears”. Owner, 2026-11-10: “you need to create gh-pages first … create gh-pages THEN update settings. you make this mistake a lot.” . When site:enabled cannot be done here, it goes to the person through human-agent-discussion, written so it can be followed without opening anything else: . Open https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/pages. Under “Build and deployment”, set Source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). It is free for a public repository. Then re-run the workflow that publishes the site from its Actions tab. If Pages is already on but serves something else, do not switch it yourself: that changes how an existing site is built, so ask. Never silent: a step that could not be checked is said to be unchecked.

52879595921e.title: Refresh materialized remote content
52879595921e.content: Process_RefreshMaterialized · strict · 8 step(s) . Keep a materialized copy of remote content current: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both did — an archival copy is never re-fetched and gets a fixity check instead. One general process, used everywhere. REFRESH IS NOT RE-IMPORT: it needs three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally since, and what to do when BOTH did. upstream-pins.json answers the first for one caller and nothing answers the other two anywhere. An ARCHIVAL copy is not refreshed. Re-fetching it would defeat it: the copy exists to survive the source, so replacing it with whatever the source says today discards exactly the state it was keeping. What an archive gets instead is a FIXITY CHECK — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy. i i i i i i i i Actors: Contributor (human or agent) · Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) .
