78afc665d1be.title: Sub-KG lifecycle — staged here, separated later
78afc665d1be.content: Skill sub-kg-lifecycle: A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . Skill id: sub-kg-lifecycle · Package: graph-management Process: sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn Stages 6 to 13 are drawn as the phases it shares with kg-separation: authorise, move and cut over. A sub-KG created inside a folio or harnessed repository can move to its own repository later: once it is staged for separation, a new repository is created and the staged contents are copied into it.

95e698788646.title: Which skill, this one or kg-separation?
95e698788646.content: | the graph | use | . | holds data — an artefact index, generated pages, a library, a folio — and leaves whole | this skill | . | holds data and the code that writes it, and the two must become a content repository and a tools repository | kg-separation — its fourteen stages, the pair, FR-7 | . | is not yet a graph at all — tangled into its host | graph-detanglement first | . The two share their gates on purpose. Ready to seed? here is the same decision table, seed-readiness-gate.dmn, evaluated by the same command, and the owner’s confirmations here are the same rule, deletion-requires-confirmation. What this skill adds is the part kg-separation does not cover: a sub-KG born in the host, with no tools pair, that leaves in one piece.

fe9bbf33fb87.title: How a sub-KG is born — the intent question
fe9bbf33fb87.content: A content type’s own creation skill asks whether the new thing goes in a new repository or inside this one, and routes here for the second answer. For a folio in general that is getting-started’s add-folio branch. A harness above this one may own a creation skill for its own kind of graph; ask skill_list for it rather than improvising. In-repository is the cheaper default whenever the session is already in a harnessed repository. Every stage up to 6 is reversible with git revert, and nothing outside the repository changes until stage 7. A new repository is the first irreversible, outward-facing act, and this lifecycle puts it behind a confirmation rather than at the start.

3cd46f275a4c.title: The stages
3cd46f275a4c.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and what decides that it is done. A stage is done when its check is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | done when | . | 0 | Brief, claim the work item (opening-brief) | authoring-agent | work item claimed with bun run cat beans:claim | . | 1 | Declare it in place | authoring-agent | the declaration parses; instance-repositories.test.ts green | . | 2 | Grow it in place | authoring-agent | the content type’s own gates | . | 3 | Push generic down | platform-authoring-agent | check:import-direction, check:reference-direction, check:process-bindings add nothing | . | 4 | One import seam | platform-authoring-agent | every climb out of the directory goes through <name>/platform.ts | . | 5 | Rehearse self-contained | build-pipeline | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse | . | 6 | Report what would move | authoring-agent | the report is in the work item (as kg-separation stage 9) | . | 7 | Owner confirms: create the repository | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 8 | Create the repository | administrator | it exists, empty, and was read before writing | . | — | Ready to seed? | build-pipeline | seed-readiness-gate.dmn answers settled | . | 9 | Copy the staged contents in, with history | authoring-agent | a reviewed PR on a branch of the new repository | . | 10 | Re-point the declaration | platform-authoring-agent | the host is green consuming the new repository | . | 11 | Verify on a fresh clone | build-pipeline | the new repository’s gates green from git clone in an empty directory | . | 12 | Owner confirms: delete the in-repo copy | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 13 | Cutover commit | administrator | one commit, revertable (as kg-separation stage 13) | . 1 · Declare it in place . A directory <name>/ at the host’s root, with <name>/<name>.json: . { "name": "<name>", "repository": "<owner>/<name>", // the PLANNED home; IRIs key on it "livesAt": { "repository": "<owner>/<host>", "path": "<name>" }, // where it sits TODAY "version": "0.1.0", "needs": ["<the harness it instantiates>"], "directories": [ /* only directories that exist, each with its graphTypologies */ ] } . | repository differs from livesAt.repository — that difference is what makes the directory a staged layer, and it is what the separation guard and seed:ready read. Nothing lists the staged layers by hand. | The directory may sit anywhere — a root sibling is the convention, but the tools read livesAt.path, so folio/<name>/ works the same. | Scaffold it with init-folio --staged <path>: . bun run cat init-folio --staged <path> --title "<title>" \ --repository <owner>/<name> --needs <harness> # --host-repository when origin cannot say . It writes exactly two files, <path>/<name>.json and an empty <path>/platform.ts, and nothing at the host’s root; init-folio-staged.test.ts snapshots the whole host tree to hold that. Never --instance inside a host: it writes a repository’s worth of scaffolding (AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a work items store, a session hook; 15 files, measured with --dry-run). --instance is for stage 8’s repository. | Declare a directory with its files, in one commit: a declared-but-absent directory is scanned as empty and reported clean. | . 3 · Push generic down — before the seam, not after . Move everything generic into the harness below, consolidate what the sub-KG needs into its own harness, and only then seed. The other order copies generic code into a repository that has to give it back. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data, not only in imports: a skill definition naming a package one layer up, a dependsOn, a publication target enumerated in an input schema, prose links, a needs edge to an empty layer. So run all three direction checks, not one. 4 · One import seam: <name>/platform.ts . Every symbol the sub-KG uses from the platform is re-exported from one file, and nothing else in the directory climbs out of it. On the day it leaves, re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit instead of a sweep. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/instance-separation-imports.test.ts is the guard. It covers every layer whose repository differs from its livesAt.repository, not only those that opted in, because an opt-in guard is silent for exactly the layer that has no seam. Layers other layers build on are an explicit, checked exemption, and a layer that still climbs has a ceiling that may only fall. Create the seam at stage 1, not here. It costs one file on day one, and every later climb is a reroute. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive, so a red guard after one is the expected signal to reroute, not a regression. 5 · Rehearse self-contained — run the gates, do not scan . bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . It copies the layer and what it needs into a scratch workspace of sibling directories and runs the tests there. It is a run rather than a reading because: . | a static import scan misses files the gates load at run time — a JSON code list read by URL, for one; | renaming the directory can change every generated page, when a URL prefix or a chrome lookup keys on the directory name. Take the identity from the declaration’s name, never from the path, and check for that before seeding into a different directory name. | . 7 and 12 · The two confirmations . Both are userTasks in the administrator lane, marked relaxable="false", and both follow deletion-requires-confirmation: the agent reports what would happen, how large it is and how it is undone, then waits. Silence is not a yes. The questions are numbered, four options at most, the recommended one first, with a stated default: . Before stage 8: . <name> is staged and rehearses green: N files, M MB, history of K commits. Creating <owner>/<name> is visible outside this repository and is not undone by a revert. May it be created? . | Yes — you create it, and tell me when it exists (recommended) | Yes — I create it (only if this session has that permission) | Not yet — keep it staged here | . Default if you do not answer: 3. Nothing is created. Before stage 13: . <owner>/<name> is green from a fresh clone and the host consumes it. The in-repo copy is N files. Deleting it is one commit, revertable. | Delete the in-repo copy now (recommended) | Keep it until the new repository’s first release | Show me the file list first | . Default if you do not answer: 2. Nothing is deleted. When the repository must be created by someone with credentials this session lacks, the hand-over is agent-handoff: one work item, one sentence for the person to relay. 9 · Copy the staged contents in, with history . The staged directory becomes the new repository’s content with its history: git subtree split --prefix=<name> in the host, then git subtree add (or a merge of the split branch) in the new repository. It goes in on a branch, as a draft PR, never straight to main. The new repository’s own root files — its declaration at the root, its config, its README — are a second commit in the same PR, so the copy itself stays byte-identical and reviewable. Ready to seed? comes first, at seed time, because the tree has moved since the rehearsal: every open PR touching the layer when the copy is taken is orphaned. Its criteria and thresholds are in kg-separation §”Ready to seed?”, and not restated here. 10 · Re-point the declaration . | what changes | how | . | livesAt | removed in the new repository — absent means “sits at the root of repository” | . | the seam | platform.ts points at wherever the platform now is: a remote-mounted path, or a sibling checkout | . | the host | remote mount if the host imports code from the sub-KG — a source.remote layer in the host’s root index.config.json (remote-mount; never a submodule); subscription (kg:subscribe) if it only reads its content | . | pins | the host pins a commit while staging, a version once released (upstream-version-adoption) | . | its site | the new repository publishes and previews itself (feature-staging, Which site): "site": { "agentRun": true } in its index.config.json when an agent publishes it, plus whatever workflow its publisher layer’s own creation skill requires (an IG’s AST-cache refresh, for one) | . | its checks | .github/workflows/harness-pr-checks.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml, so its gates run on every pull request | . | its QA record | when it declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, cat/cat-harness/qa-reports, keyed by commit): .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, so every push to main and every pull request publishes its results to its own qa-reports branch, and test/results/ in .gitignore. A host reads them at the commit it pins. Without the job, the declaration names a store nothing writes | . | .gitignore | the mount block, written by the mount tool between its own markers. Never typed: a hand-written marker makes remote-mount.ts refuse (markers unpaired) | . Copy these from a sibling repository of the same kind; never type them. A repository scaffolded by hand misses them, and its site cannot be built until each is copied in. The host keeps its own copy through this stage. The re-point is additive. 11 · Verify on a fresh clone . bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <seeding branch> --text # exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 unknown . The Tool sub-kg-verify-clone clones the new repository into an empty scratch directory with its submodules (and each --sibling beside it), installs, and runs its own gates script, else its test script. An empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a test that climbs out (Cannot find module '../../../<harness>/…') fails here. A rehearsal in the host’s scratch space is not this check; it shares the host’s node_modules and network. The new repository’s own site is part of this check: bun run cat stage:local --repo . --dry-run from the fresh clone must build. A refusal names what stage 10 left out.

135dbcea725f.title: Stage 13: the frozen copy
135dbcea725f.content: After cutover the host keeps a frozen copy in fsh-guts, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion. Step 12 asks (1) move to fsh-guts now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first, default (2). Step 13 deposits the directory into the PARENT’s fsh-guts as a verified archive (not plain trees, which CI would audit as live content), then removes it from main. The deposit is the one state:seed --cutover makes for a state graph: an archive that must extract to the exact tree being removed, plus a provenance note (movedFrom, movedOn, sourceCommit, tree), and the removal commit is made only once it has landed. A separation targets the parent’s fsh-guts rather than the departing layer’s, which --cutover does not yet do. The live copy is the remote mount (index.config.json source.remote), npm package retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm), or subscription (kg:subscribe) from stage 10; the frozen one is never refreshed and never rendered. How checks treat a frozen subtree . This is the one place the rule is stated; scanners point here. A frozen subtree is one retired item, and its sibling note is the node that answers for it. Every reader of fsh-guts — the fsh-guts.jsonld export, the fsh-guts page, the render-pipeline and bean-reference tests, check:materialized-fixity — reports the note and does not enter the directory. The page shows it as one row in the via sidecar state. | Recognised by declaration, never by path. A directory is frozen because <name>.md beside it declares $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1 and kind: separated-instance (isFrozenSubtree in schemas/kg/fsh-guts.ts). A copy dropped in with no note, or under a note of another kind, is walked like any directory, so its files fail self-declaration loudly rather than vanishing from every check. | The note must carry all four stage-13 fields — movedFrom, movedOn, repository, matchesCommit — because it is now the only thing any check reads about thousands of files. Those beyond the common set are exported under the node’s data. | Materialization records inside are not judged. They claim bytes in the repository the graph now lives in, which the copy deliberately does not carry. | The note’s bean: resolves against main’s work plan, with no pending escape. So the deposit lands on the fsh-guts branch in the same step that merges the PR carrying that work item, never before it; a deposit pushed ahead of its PR turns every PR’s CI red. | .

36d9491346ae.title: Anti-patterns
36d9491346ae.content: . | Creating the repository first. It is the one irreversible step; everything that can be done in place is done before it. | A seed with no history. A one-commit seed severs blame for every line, and the history is cheap to keep. | Re-pointing by sweep. If more than one file changes when the platform moves, the seam was skipped. | Reading the rehearsal as the fresh-clone check. They catch different things: the rehearsal catches climbs, the fresh clone catches everything the host’s environment was quietly supplying. | Deleting the in-repo copy because the new repository is green. Green is the precondition for asking, not the answer. | Committing mounted directories to the host repository. Remote mounts populate layer directories locally. If .gitignore does not ignore the mounted paths, external files pollute downstream git status. index.config.json must generate gitignore entries for all remoteMounts. | Breaking dependents when dependencies fold. If a dependency layer folds into another (e.g. cat-openapi into cat-harness), downstreams that still reference the folded layer fail unless FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES maps them. | Separating before resolving withheld asset clearance. If library items are withheld or unpermitted in the separated repository (as with the IRIS replica), materialization results in broken links. Clearance must be verified at seed time. | .

ed2b57feb78e.title: A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository
ed2b57feb78e.content: Process_SubKgLifecycle · strict · 11 step(s) . Create a knowledge graph inside a harnessed repository as a layer of its own, grow it there, and when it should leave, stage it for separation and move it whole into a new repository. Declared in place with a planned repository and a livesAt saying where it sits today; staged by one import seam (<name>/platform.ts), the separation guard and a self-contained rehearsal; then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, the repository is created, the staged contents are copied in with their history, the declaration is re-pointed, a fresh clone is verified, and the in-repo copy is frozen in the kept trashcan. The light sibling of kg-separation, which splits a graph into a content and a tools repository; this moves a data layer whole, and shares kg-separation’s seeding gateway and decision table. DRAWN IN PHASES (owner, 2026-11-08, Q-B1-3 A): it keeps its own grow-in-place and staging steps, and calls the authorise, move and cut-over phases it shares with kg-separation. i i i i i i i i i i i Actors: Authoring agent · Platform authoring agent · Build pipeline · Administrator (owner) .

28664dd608df.doc: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
28664dd608df.title: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
28664dd608df.content: Process_SubscribeKg · strict · 11 step(s) . Subscribe a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph pinned to a full commit SHA, then take each chosen part from referenced to materialized through materialize-remote and instantiate each chosen harness once its needs are held, so the harness appears in the subscriber’s navbar. A SUBSCRIPTION IS NOT A NEW MECHANISM, and this diagram is where that claim is kept honest. Every byte that arrives does so through Process_MaterializeRemote, called once per chosen subgraph or asset; every held copy is refreshed through Process_RefreshMaterialized. Neither is re-described here. What this process adds is only the walk: pin, validate, choose, and then carry each chosen part from referenced to materialised one at a time. A SUBSTRATE is a repository whose root declaration meets bootstrap’s schema requirements and declares at least one harness. Both are answerable from the declaration file alone, so validating one never needs the whole repository. WHERE IT LIVES: library/processes/, beside Process_MaterializeRemote and Process_RefreshMaterialized, which it calls, naming the kg-subscription and materialize-remote skills in library/skills/large-datasets/; every ref stays inside the harness. STRICT. The pin and the five gates are the reason: an unpinned subscription is how two subscribers see two graphs under one name, and a gate that only warned is a gate nobody fails. i i i i i i i i i i i Actors: Subscriber (the folio's owner) · Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) .

The schema refuses anything else (SubscriptionSchema.ref), and this step exists so the refusal is met while choosing rather than at commit time. A tag replaces the SHA only once the substrate publishes releases. | . | Fetch and validate the pinned declarationTask_Validate | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | A sparse, shallow fetch of the substrate’s root declaration only. Two questions: does it parse as bootstrap’s KnowledgeGraphDeclarationSchema, and does it declare at least one harness? could not fetch is a third answer and is never read as conforms. | . | Record why it is not a substrate; write no entryTask_Refuse | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | No subscription entry is written for a repository that is not a substrate. What is recorded is the reason (non-conforming, no harness, or unreachable) and the pin it was asked at, so a later attempt at a different commit starts from what failed. | . | Write the entry and cache the declarationTask_Record | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | The subscriptions entry in the subscriber’s layer declaration — id, repository, ref, and nothing chosen yet — plus a cached copy of the substrate’s declaration at the pin. The entry holds the choice and the pin, never state: whether a part is held is answered by its materialisation record, and a second answer here would be free to disagree with it. | . | Refresh the held partCall_Refresh | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Refresh materialized remote contentmaterialize-remote | The shared refresh, called, not re-described: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both did. Whatever that process decides — refreshed, kept divergent, or deferred — is the part’s new state; this loop only moves to the next part. | . | Move the entry’s ref and re-cache the declarationTask_RePin | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | Only after every held part has been through the refresh. Moving the ref first would make the records of parts not yet refreshed describe a commit the entry no longer names. The cached declaration is replaced so the review that follows shows what the NEW pin offers, including subgraphs that did not exist at the old one. | . | Review what the substrate offersTask_Review | Subscriber (the folio’s owner) | kg-subscription | Every subgraph, asset class and harness the cached declaration names, each with its current state — referenced, materialised, unknown, stale, or refused by a gate. Choosing is not holding: a chosen subgraph is still referenced until the gates below let it through. Choosing nothing is legitimate — a subscription with no parts chosen is a pinned reference, the case associatedHarnesses covers today. | . | Materialise the partCall_Materialize | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Materialize remote content: the shared subprocessmaterialize-remote | The ONLY way bytes arrive. Purpose first, then the five gates — size, restrictions, copyright, retention, source loss — then fetch with fixity, or stay referenced with the refusing gate’s basis recorded. Both ends of that subprocess return here and the walk continues: one part refused is not the subscription refused. | . | Instantiate the harness: write its configTask_Instantiate | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscriptionindex-config | Write <harness>.config.json at the repository root, plus the state directories the harness declares, and — where the checkout has a root index.config.json — add the harness to its instances[] (kg:instantiate does both), because the index, not the file, is then what reads as INSTANTIATED (index-config skill); a root config the index does not list fails check:landing-instance. 8b9d06ebc5f1.title: Surprise to corpus — notice it, filter it, then ask
8b9d06ebc5f1.content: Skill surprise-to-corpus: What was unexpected in that task, and does it belong in the corpus? Logical surprise is the detectable kind, recurrence is the filter that stops this generating noise every turn, and the agent PROMPTS — it never writes corpus guidance unasked. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: surprise-to-corpus · Package: folio-core . When something unexpected happens during a defined process that runs often, it may be worth a new skill, guidance or tool refinement: prompt the person to add it to the corpus. Three clauses: notice, filter by recurrence, prompt. The first alone is a diary; the first two are an agent rewriting the corpus on its own authority; the third without the second is a prompt every turn until people stop reading them.

69a2512d559c.title: 1. What counts as a surprise
69a2512d559c.content: Ask it as an after-action review asks it: . What did you expect to happen, what actually happened, and why the difference? . This makes the surprise articulable BEFORE you know whether it matters. “Something felt off” is not reviewable; “I expected the tracer to read the mask as ink and it read the ground” is. The filter in §2 then operates on a statement rather than on a feeling, so it can be applied consistently. Only LOGICAL surprise is detectable. Statistical surprise implies a base rate, and the corpus carries none — nothing records how often a gate fires, a merge conflicts, or a selector breaks. Do not claim a statistical surprise: it would assert a distribution nobody measured. Logical surprise needs no baseline. It is any of: . | A premise turned out false. You believed something about the system, acted on it, and the system disagreed. | A gate fired for a reason nobody predicted — including a gate that passed when you expected red. | A command failed and the failure was invisible, because whatever ran next produced plausible output anyway. | Two things that looked like one thing, or one thing that turned out to be two. | . Examples of the general shapes . | the surprise | the general shape | . | potracer treats ZERO as foreground — the inverse of what the name suggests | a library whose convention is the opposite of its name | . | Image.crop past the edge pads with BLACK, which a tracer reads as ink | a default that is invisible until another tool interprets it | . | a CSS class used as an IDENTITY is reused by a second button as a box class, breaking every selector at once | a name doing two jobs, discovered when the second arrives | . | an id sliced one character short fails silently behind a tail -1 | a truncated identifier that still LOOKS like an identifier | .

211eff731ad3.title: 2. The recurrence filter — the part that stops the noise
211eff731ad3.content: A surprise inside a one-off is an anecdote. The same surprise inside a process that runs often is a defect in the process. Without this filter the rule fires every turn, because every non-trivial turn contains something somebody did not expect. With it, the question is narrow and answerable: . Did this happen inside a defined process that runs often — and would the next agent running that process hit it too? . Both halves. A rare process can still be worth guarding if its failure is expensive, but then say that rather than claiming a recurrence you have not seen. “The next agent would hit it too” separates a fact about the system from a fact about your own mistake. Three ways a candidate fails the filter, all of which end in silence rather than a prompt: it happened once, in a process nobody runs twice; it was your own slip and the system behaved as documented; or the corpus already says it and you had not read that part. The third is the common one, and checking costs one grep. Read the slip blamelessly . A finding is about the SYSTEM rather than about the person. “My own slip” fails the filter only when the system behaved as documented AND nothing about the system made the slip easy. Where the system DID make it easy, would the next agent hit it too is true, and the candidate passes. A mis-copied id is not just a slip: a truncated id is still a well-formed id, and a | tail -1 hides a non-zero exit — both properties the next agent meets unchanged.

91d060d2a465.title: 3. PROMPT, never write
91d060d2a465.content: The agent proposes; a person decides. This is deletion-requires-confirmation pointed the other way: that skill governs removing a durable artefact on your own initiative, this one governs ADDING durable guidance on your own initiative. The corpus is read by every future session, so the person who has to live with a line in it should be the one who agreed to it. What a good prompt contains — the same parts interaction-modality §4.1 binds every handed-over decision to, and the test is identical: can the reader answer without opening anything? . | What happened, concretely, with the measurement or the error text. | Which process it happened in, named. | Why it will recur — the filter above, argued rather than asserted. | What you propose: a new skill, a line in an existing one, or a tool change. Say which, and where it would live — where-does-this-go is how you answer that. | Your recommendation, marked as such. | What happens if they say nothing: nothing gets written, and the candidate is filed as a work item so it is not lost. | . A work item is the third state — recorded, unactioned, findable — so silence is not expensive and an unanswered prompt is something the next session can pick up rather than rediscover.

979b2d8580b5.title: 4. When to run this
979b2d8580b5.content: At the end of a task, not continuously: one pass over what actually happened. Most turns produce nothing and should say nothing — a loop that reports “no surprises” every turn is a loop people stop reading. It pairs with turn-reporting (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), which governs the shape of the report you were already writing.

8a1dfe11b277.title: What this skill deliberately does not do
8a1dfe11b277.content: . | No severity scale. Ranking surprises would invite filing the low ones, which is the noise the recurrence filter exists to prevent. A candidate either passes the filter or is worth a work item at most. | No automated corpus change. A mechanism that could write guidance would be used to write guidance. | No timeline reconstruction. The agent was present for the whole turn, and the transcript is the timeline. | No routing method. Where a surprise goes is where-does-this-go, which needs an index rather than a taxonomy at its size. | .

42222f23d60f.title: Role
42222f23d60f.content: Extract the personas a layer’s BPMN diagrams put in swimlanes as a SKOS concept scheme, and keep the retirement ledger that lets a dropped term be told from an accident. Not the paper glossary. glossary-build walks a paper’s blocks and writes a LaTeX chapter from defines[]. This walks a knowledge graph and writes JSON-LD. Different corpus, different output, different consumer. Whether they ever converge is undecided, so do not merge them on your own initiative.

22546ed43bf5.title: When to invoke
22546ed43bf5.content: . | A user mentions: swimlane glossary, defined-terms index, SKOS concepts, glossary-export, the glossary ledger, retiring a term. | After adding, renaming or removing a role in a layer’s scenarios/roles.json, or a lane in any .bpmn under it. | Before believing any count of “how many terms does this repository define” — the generator’s report is the answer, never a number in prose. | .

29ec38033196.title: Tools
29ec38033196.content: | Command | Purpose | . | bun run cat glossary:export | Build cat-harness’s glossary → _kg/, and refresh its ledger | . | bun run cat glossary:export:bootstrap | The same for bootstrap, as a SECOND RUN | . | bun run cat glossary:check | CI gate — non-zero if the committed ledger is stale | . | bun run cat glossary:check:bootstrap | The same for bootstrap | .

39a445cad9a5.title: A concept is a ROLE, not a lane name
39a445cad9a5.content: There are far more lane names than roles, so a concept per lane name would duplicate roles.json. Re-derive any count before quoting it: bun run cat check:lane-documentation for the lane count, bun run cat glossary:export for the rest. build-pipeline is named many ways — “CI/CD Pipeline”, “Scheduled log sweep”, “Graph audit (system)”, and more. A concept per lane name would copy one authored definition onto each of them. Those names are skos:altLabel. That is what altLabel is for, and it is what makes “Reviewer / SME” findable as the same term as “Reviewer” rather than a rival entry.

de533247adeb.title: Three predicates, three sources, and each answers a different question
de533247adeb.content: | SKOS | source | answers | . | prefLabel | the role’s title | what is this called | . | altLabel | every distinct lane name binding it | what else is it called | . | definition | the role’s description | who is this persona, everywhere | . | scopeNote | the lane’s <bpmn:documentation> | what is this lane accountable for in this process | .

bcaab3ddbc90.title: scopeNote goes on the USAGE, never on the concept
bcaab3ddbc90.content: A lane name that appears in several diagrams carries different documentation in each, and should. Hanging those notes, unattributed, off one concept asserts apparent contradictions about one word. So each appearance is a LaneUsage node carrying the process, the label that process gave the lane, and the note. The note is stored VERBATIM. Lane documentation is extracted to .pot as its own msgid, so a note stored exactly as the diagram wrote it already has a translation slot in every locale. Wrapping it — In "<process>": <note> — reads well in English and produces a string no catalogue contains.

44361f5c882e.title: Never mint a second name for one thing
44361f5c882e.content: A concept’s @id is the IRI kg-export already mints for that role (makeIri(docIri, "role", id)), imported rather than re-spelled. The graph’s performedBy links point at exactly those IRIs; a parallel cat-harness:reviewer would leave the glossary unjoinable with the graph it describes.

eee2552b8324.title: The ledger is the memory, and it is the only durable part
eee2552b8324.content: The document is derived and rebuilt every run, so it has no memory: delete a role and its concept simply stops appearing, which is what “never existed” also looks like. Retirement and accident must not look alike (deletion-requires-confirmation), so the one non-derivable fact — this term was once minted — is committed at <instance>/glossary/glossary-ledger.json, declared as graph typology swimlane-glossary (holds: "state"; glossary-terms’ glossary/ page reads this ledger as one source). Three rules for it: . | Keyed on the IRI’s local part, never the absolute IRI. The publication base is a deploy-time variable; a stored absolute IRI would rot the day it moved and take every retirement record with it. | An already-retired term keeps its own retiredOn. Re-stamping it erases when the term actually went. | A term that comes back is un-retired, and reported. Leaving the flag on reports a live term as gone for ever. | . Usages are not ledgered: a usage is an occurrence, regenerated wholesale, while a concept is a term somebody may have cited; ledgering every occurrence would bury the records that matter.

98b83bc49a90.title: Run it once per layer — never widen the scan
98b83bc49a90.content: --instance <root>, the shape kg-export and translate-bpmn already use. Widening cat-harness’s scan to reach bootstrap’s diagrams is the leak instance-graph-isolation.test.ts exists to stop.

6fe00d1c0d0d.title: What it reports and never acts on
6fe00d1c0d0d.content: . | Declared roles no swimlane draws. They are still concepts — omitting them would leave the glossary silently short of the vocabulary it claims to index. The report says which walk found nothing (“no swimlane in <instance>/ draws”) and splits the list: a role a lane in ANOTHER layer binds (partitionElementRef) is named with that diagram (drawnElsewhere), apart from roles no diagram in the repository draws, because unsplit, a role drawn in another layer reads like one drawn nowhere: a fact about the walk phrased as a fact about the corpus. Reporting it is not widening the scan: nothing outside the layer is bound or emitted. | A lane binding naming a lane no diagram contains. Distinct from a role whose lane exists but holds no task, which is not a defect. | A lane whose binding is dangling, contradictory or unbound. | . A lane declaring <bootstrap.processes:role variable="true"/> is none of these. It emits a concept with a scope note and no definition, which is true — see role-model. laneBinding() is the only route from a lane to a concept for exactly this reason: variable must never be reachable as unbound.

16efa29bbb30.title: Running a SWOT scan
16efa29bbb30.content: Skill swot-analysis: Running a SWOT situation analysis — the activities of swot-analysis.bpmn, what each step must produce, and the one thing the technique must never be used for. The method itself lives in the methodology graph and is not repeated here. Named by: SWOT situation analysis . The method is not in this file. It is the swot node in the methodology graph, rendered from an ingested source, and this skill is the instruction for performing it (methodology-adoption’s split). The method’s text lives once, so two skills quoting it cannot drift apart. Read methodologies/swot.md first — in particular §”What this platform adopts, and what it refuses”. Ask the methodology graph for it rather than assuming the path.

25fa7794e301.title: The one refusal, before anything else
25fa7794e301.content: A SWOT never decides. It produces the raw material a decision is made from. If you find yourself choosing between options inside a SWOT, you have left the methodology: stop, and go to options-analysis, which selects a decision methodology by context. swot-analysis.bpmn has no path that decides. If a scan seems to need one, you are in the wrong process.

b2b734e4c071.title: What each step must produce
b2b734e4c071.content: | step | produces | the trap | . | Name the subject and the level | one sentence: what, and at which level (individual, organisational, national) | skipping it — quadrant criteria depend on the level, and a country is not a company | . | Scan the environment | opportunities and threats, worked through the source’s six categories of change | free-associating instead of working the checklist | . | Scan the subject | strengths and weaknesses, worked through the source’s seven business functions | recording a strength as a fact; it is a claim, and where evidence exists, cite it | . | Pool knowledge | the lists reviewed by more than their author | treating this as optional politeness rather than the method’s own bias control | . | Record what did not classify | the factors sitting in two quadrants or none | forcing every factor into one quadrant, which reports a cleanliness the method does not have | . | Cross the axes | SO, WO, ST, WT candidate strategies | stopping at four lists, which is the source’s own central criticism of SWOT | . External is scanned before internal. That is Weihrich’s argument as the source reports it — opportunities and threats are outside the subject and largely beyond its control, and must be managed using its strengths and weaknesses.

1073216844ae.title: Two things you will want to do, and must not
1073216844ae.content: Do not rank or score the factors. SWOT has no priority mechanism; the source is explicit that “quantity does not mean quality”. A scored list asserts a ranking the technique did not produce. When ranking is genuinely needed, use a methodology adopted for ranking — not a weighting invented here. Do not blend in another method to patch the gap. The source surveys a long line of quantitative extensions (AHP, ANP, fuzzy variants, SMART, SMAA-O, MADM, TRIZ). None is adopted; blending one in is the composite methodology-adoption forbids, a house method that cites nobody while claiming everybody’s authority.

642d8d73d794.title: When SWOT is the wrong tool entirely
642d8d73d794.content: Ask methodology-adoption’s selection question. SWOT is situation analysis, and it is the answer to none of those four questions — it is what you do before them. If the task is choosing among options, grading evidence, recording a decision, or computing a recurring branch, you want a different methodology.

cdcee1257713.title: SWOT situation analysis
cdcee1257713.content: Process_SwotAnalysis · advisory · 7 step(s) . Situation analysis over two axes — internal/external and helpful/harmful — producing the raw material a decision is made from, and NEVER the decision. THE ONE STRUCTURAL CLAIM THIS DIAGRAM MAKES: there is no path through it that decides anything. Every completed run ends either at a recorded situation or at a handoff into options-analysis, which selects a decision methodology. That is not a modelling preference; it is the swot methodology’s stated refusal drawn so it cannot be skipped. Gürel and Tat’s conclusion is that SWOT gives “the raw material needed to perform more in-depth strategic analysis” but “cannot show them how to achieve a competitive advantage”, and that it must not become “an end in itself”. A diagram with a decide-here activity would contradict the methodology it implements. WHY EXTERNAL IS SCANNED FIRST: Weihrich (1982), reported in the source, holds that the only logical starting point is opportunities and threats — they are outside the organisation and largely beyond its control, and must be managed using its strengths and weaknesses. The order is his argument, rendered; it is not a house preference. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not rank the factors it finds. The source is explicit that SWOT has no way to prioritise — “quantity does not mean quality” — and the long list of quantitative extensions it surveys (AHP, ANP, their fuzzy variants, SMART, SMAA-O, MADM, TRIZ) is NOT adopted here. An activity that scored or weighted factors would be inventing the part of the method that does not exist. i i i i i i i Actors: Business analyst · Stakeholder .

5eef893389ab.title: How it connects
5eef893389ab.content: . | Called by: no call activity names this process | Calls: none | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Skill: swot-analysis | Running instances: none recorded | .

e74cb7ccc93d.title: Lanes — who acts
e74cb7ccc93d.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Business analyst | business-analyst | Performs the scan and the crossing. This lane owns the analysis and owns nothing else: it does not authorise, and it does not choose between options. Its deliverable is four lists, the four matched strategies, and an explicit record of what could not be classified. | . | Stakeholder | stakeholder | Consulted, in a lane of their own because the source names group discussion as a property of the method rather than as good practice around it: SWOT “promotes group discussion about strategic issues” and pools knowledge through participatory techniques. It is also the mitigation for the limitation the source states most sharply — that a list of strengths is “bound up with aspirations, biases, and hope of the individuals involved”. A single analyst producing four lists alone has performed the technique’s shape without the part that checks it. | .

d526ddf31671.title: Steps
d526ddf31671.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Name the subject and the levelA_FrameSubject | Business analyst | swot-analysis | One sentence naming WHAT is being analysed and at WHICH level — individual, organisational, national, international. The source requires this before anything is listed: “the classification of a variable also depends on the purpose of the practice”, and the criteria for assigning a variable to a quadrant “may be more difficult to clarify if the methodology is not used for a company but for a country”.It also bounds the known limitation that SWOT “is rarely deployed at lower than the organization level”, where one scan drives strategy for units its factors do not hold equally for. Naming the level does not remove that risk; it makes it visible in the record. | . | Scan the environment opportunities and threatsA_ScanExternal | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The external axis, first, per Weihrich. Work the source’s categories of environmental change rather than free-associating: societal, governmental, economic, competitive, supplier and market changes, each item recorded with what it impacts.An opportunity is an external element that gives benefit; a threat is one that could cause trouble. Both are outside the subject and largely beyond its control — that is what puts them on this axis, not whether they feel good or bad. | . | Scan the subject strengths and weaknessesA_ScanInternal | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The internal axis. Work the source’s functional checklist rather than a blank page: marketing, research and development, management information systems, management team, operations, finance, human resources.A strength gives advantage over others in the field; a weakness places the subject at a disadvantage relative to others. Both are attributes OF the subject. The source’s warning belongs to this step specifically: listing strengths on paper “is very different from testing the organization and experiencing the strengths at work”, so a strength recorded here is a claim, and where evidence for it exists it is cited. | . | Pool knowledge across participantsA_GroupReview | Stakeholder | swot-analysis | The four lists are reviewed by more than the person who wrote them. This is the method’s own answer to its own bias limitation, and it is a distinct activity rather than advice attached to the scans, because an activity can be recorded as not performed and a recommendation cannot.Disagreement about which quadrant a factor belongs in is an OUTPUT of this step, not a failure of it — it feeds A_RecordAmbiguous. | . | Record what did not classify cleanlyA_RecordAmbiguous | Business analyst | swot-analysis | Factors that sit in two quadrants, or in none, are written down as such. The source states this as inherent rather than as analyst error: “the same factor can be fitted in two categories. A factor can be a strength and a weakness at the same time.” It adds the two drifts — strengths not maintained become weaknesses, and opportunities not taken but taken by competitors become threats.A scan that silently forced every factor into one quadrant would report a cleanliness the method does not have. This is the same third-state discipline the rest of this repository applies to “could not determine”: an unclassifiable factor is a finding, not a blank. | . | Cross the axes into SO, WO, ST, WTA_Cross | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The TOWS matching step, and the only step that produces anything actionable. Strengths and weaknesses across, opportunities and threats down, and each cell names the strategy the pairing implies: SO — achieve opportunities that greatly match the strengths; WO — overcome weaknesses to attain opportunities; ST — use strengths to reduce vulnerability to threats; WT — prevent weaknesses, to avoid becoming more susceptible to threats.A SWOT that stops at four lists is the failure the source names as its central one. This step is what the process exists to reach.It produces CANDIDATE strategies, not a chosen one, and they are not ranked — see the process documentation on why no scoring activity exists. | . | Hand the candidates to a decision methodologyA_HandOff | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | The candidate strategies go to options-analysis, which selects the decision methodology by context and applies it. SWOT does not make that selection and does not make the decision.What is handed over includes the ambiguities from A_RecordAmbiguous and the fact that the candidates are UNRANKED. A receiving methodology that assumed an ordered list would be reading a priority SWOT never established. | .

4e2c839fa5be.title: Decisions
4e2c839fa5be.content: Every one of the 1 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Does a decision follow?GW_DecisionFollows | Is this scan feeding a choice that has to be made now, or is it standing situation analysis?DELIBERATELY NOT DMN-BACKED. Whether a decision follows is a fact about the caller’s intent, not a function of the analysis’s contents, so there is nothing recurring for a table to compute. dmn’s own test — would the same inputs have to produce the same branch next month — fails here, and a table would assert a repeatability this does not have.Both branches are completed runs. Neither is a skipped step. | yes → Hand the candidates to a decision methodologyno → Situation recorded; no decision in play | .

7af937714005.title: Task authorization — four questions before every task
7af937714005.content: Skill task-authorization: The check every BPMN task execution runs before anything is recorded: is the actor authenticated, assigned to the role the lane binds, authorized by an ODRL policy to perform the task, and allowed access to the content it acts on? One generic check in the engine rather than a step drawn in some diagrams; strict, with GitHub as the authenticator. Also how the HTTP routes ask the same policies. Triggers on: may this actor, who may perform, authorization, authentication, access rights, permission check, RBAC, rbac.ts, workflow_complete refused, not eligible for role. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Hand back to the discussion . Before an actor performs a task or answers a decision, the BPMN executor asks: who is this, may they act in this lane, does a policy let them do it, and may they touch this content? .

d8b1f49db68b.title: The four checks, in order
d8b1f49db68b.content: | # | question | answered from | a “no” | . | 1 | Authenticated — who is the actor, and how do we know? | the executor’s Principal (src/core/access.ts) | recorded as a finding | . | 2 | Assigned — may this actor take the role the lane binds? | ActorDef.roles in cat-harness/scenarios/actors/; the lane’s roleRef | refuses | . | 3 | Authorized — may they perform-task in this process, for this task, as this role? | ODRL policies in policies/*.jsonld | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . | 4 | Access — the same, on the content (target) the task acts on | the same policies, rule target | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . It is one function, authorizeTask in src/workflow/authorize.ts, run by the interpreter’s complete() and by workflow_gate. It is not drawn as a task in any diagram. A check drawn into some processes is a check missing from the others. The verdict is written into the instance history (HistoryEntry.authz) and the task-end log line, so the record of a step says who did it and on what authority, not only that it happened. Why checks 2 and 3 stay separate . A role is what the actor is acting as; a permission is what the actor may do (role-model §”Three questions about an actor”). An actor permitted to perform-task everywhere still cannot sit in a lane its roles do not include. So the role check does not wait on the policy and cannot be overridden by it.

35524e47fa0e.title: One action for every task
35524e47fa0e.content: A task always asks for perform-task, scoped by cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints and by target. A step needing a narrower right gets it as a constrained rule in a policy, never as a new attribute on the diagram: . { "assignee": "content-reviewer", "action": "perform-task", "constraint": [{ "leftOperand": "cat-harness:role", "operator": "odrl:eq", "rightOperand": "reviewer" }] } . Remember the direction of includedIn: a grant of a broader action covers a narrower one. perform-task sits under odrl:execute, so granting adjudication (which is included in perform-task) does not grant perform-task. It is the other way round.

a0951127e281.title: Authentication is the executor’s job, and GitHub is today’s authenticator
a0951127e281.content: Whoever executes a process (the MCP workflow tools, a script, a swarm orchestrator) must say how it knows who the actor is. A Principal carries authenticatedBy: . | value | meaning | today | . | github | GitHub authenticated the caller | a GitHub Actions run (GITHUB_ACTOR, set by the runner) | . | http-gateway | the auth-gateway’s OAuth session, as headers | the HTTP routes, once deployed (deployment-auth) | . | asserted | an actor id the caller typed | every local agent session | . | none | nobody named | a step recorded with no actor | . The second half of GitHub as access control needs no code: the KG data store is a git repository on GitHub. An instance file, a work item or a content change becomes durable only through a push GitHub has authorised. The in-process check decides whether the step may be recorded; branch protection and push rights decide whether the record lands. Do not treat asserted as authenticated. Report it as asserted. policies/ never holds identity.

a458309c9254.title: Asking who you are: the auth_whoami Tool
a458309c9254.content: The user-auth Tool node (MCP auth_whoami, src/tools/auth.ts) answers three questions in one call: . | Who am I? It asks GitHub (src/core/github-auth.ts). With a person’s own token, GET /user gives the login and the permissions block of GET /repos/{o}/{r} gives their role. In an Actions job the token is the workflow’s, not the person’s, so it asks GET …/collaborators/{GITHUB_ACTOR}/permission instead. | What does GitHub let me do? That role, mapped onto the gateway actors policies/http-gateway.jsonld already grants: admin → owner; maintain and write → collaborator; triage and read → viewer; none → nobody. A GitHub caller and an HTTP-gateway caller therefore get the same answer from the same policy, and no login is written into the repository. | What does policy let me do here? The ODRL answer for an action, or the full four-check verdict for a BPMN step when process and task are given. | . It answers in three states: authenticated, unauthenticated, and unknown (GitHub could not be asked). unknown is never shown as a pass. A role that cannot be read stays unknown and maps to nobody; it is never guessed. An actor you name is reported as claimed, because GitHub vouched for the login, not for the BPMN actor. One resolver for preferences and permissions, two thresholds. The same identities feed both, through resolveIdentities (cat-harness-tools/src/core/identity.ts): GitHub’s answer is the one auth_whoami gives, and the other providers — GitLab CI, the agent host’s account, the user-level store, the git author — are listed beside it, each marked vouched or self-asserted. A preference may follow a self-asserted identity (interaction-modality §3.1). A permission never does: only an identity GitHub vouched for maps to an actor, and a self-asserted one maps to nobody. There is no login-to-actor table. A personal-account repository has exactly three GitHub permission levels, and they are the whole mapping (PERSONAL_ACCOUNT_LEVELS in src/core/github-auth.ts): . | GitHub level | GitHub role | actor | . | owner | admin | owner | . | collaborator | write | collaborator | . | anyone else, public repository | read | viewer | . | anyone else, private repository | none | nobody | . The consequence is stated in every auth_whoami answer: there is no read-only or triage collaborator on a personal-account repository, so every collaborator can write the whole graph. Telling an author from a reviewer is left to the per-lane ODRL rules. The actors are owner, collaborator and viewer, and nothing finer is mapped from a login. At the GitHub level author, reviewer, adjudicator and release manager are all collaborator; sign-off stays with owner by the merge, as the CRDM process has it. Access granularity is a property of the tool that holds the data, not of the actor: a GitHub-backed write is all or nothing for the whole repository, and a different tool, such as a future data store in front of the graph, may give the same actor finer grain.

80b14da89547.title: GitHub as the auth layer: what it is good at, and where it stops
80b14da89547.content: The knowledge graph’s data store is a git repository on GitHub, so GitHub is the authenticator and the outermost access control. That choice has real strengths and one structural weakness, and every answer auth_whoami gives ends by restating the weakness. Strengths . | Real identity at no extra cost. Accounts with two-factor authentication, organisation SSO where it is configured, per-repository fine-grained tokens, and a runner-set GITHUB_ACTOR in Actions. There is no second identity system to run. | Access to the graph is access to the repository. One place to grant, and revoking a collaborator takes effect on the next request. | Every write is attributable. A change lands as a commit with an author, and PR reviews and merges are recorded. That is the durable half of the audit trail that the PROV-O report (below) reads. | Write governance exists. Branch protection and rulesets can require reviews and passing checks before a merge, and CODEOWNERS makes review requirements path-scoped. | . The weakness: all of the knowledge graph, or none of it . | Read is whole-repository. Anyone with read sees every sub-graph, every node and every file. GitHub cannot say “the glossary, but not the unpublished chapters”. | Write is whole-repository too. write lets a person push to any path on any unprotected branch. Path scoping exists only for reviews (via CODEOWNERS), and it binds merges into protected branches, not pushes. | No query-path control. GitHub serves files, not queries. It cannot authorize a traversal that starts in a sub-graph you may read and reaches a node you may not, because it does not know the edge exists. | Five roles, no actions. admin, maintain, write, triage and read are its whole vocabulary. Authoring, adjudicating and releasing are all just write. The ODRL profile’s actions cannot be expressed in it. | Once read, it is copied. A clone or a fork keeps the data after access is revoked. Revocation stops the next read, not the last one. | A login is not an actor. GitHub says who pushed, not which lane or role they were acting in. | . What follows from that . | Where a boundary must hold against a reader, it is a repository boundary. Sub-graphs with different read audiences belong in different repositories. | Everything finer is ODRL, enforced in process. The engine’s four-check verdict and the HTTP routes govern callers that go through them. They are not a security boundary against someone who can clone the repository. Do not describe a scoped ODRL rule as protecting data from a GitHub reader. | Real per-node or per-query enforcement needs a data store in front of the graph (the auth-gateway, and later a relationship engine such as OpenFGA). The policies do not change when it arrives. Only the place that evaluates them does. | .

1309592068fd.title: The engine is strict
1309592068fd.content: policies/http-gateway.jsonld grants perform-task to owner and collaborator in every lane; viewer gets nothing beyond the anyone floor. The principal is the one GitHub vouches for (githubPrincipalFor), not an actor name the caller types. Together these are what make strict mode workable: without a permit in every lane and an authenticated principal, strict would stop every process. workflow_gate and workflow_complete run in strict mode (ENGINE_MODE in src/tools/workflow.ts). Strict refuses deny, a role mismatch, unknown, an asserted identity, nobody, and an undeclared actor. The actor a caller passes is still written to the history, as what it said it was acting as; it does not decide anything. With a GitHub-authenticated principal, every task and gateway in processes/ is allowed for owner and collaborator and refused for viewer (unknown) and for nobody. scripts/tests/task-authorization-strict.test.ts pins this. What strict costs: if GitHub cannot be asked (no token, no network, rate limit), no step can be recorded; that is the price of authentication being real rather than typed. authorizeTask itself still defaults to advisory, so a reader that re-checks history (the PROV-O report below) is not strict by accident.

324c26b4882e.title: The HTTP routes ask the same policies
324c26b4882e.content: src/core/rbac.ts asks the ODRL policies: . | a route names the action it performs: allows(req, "content-authoring"); | the gateway’s three sessions are three declared actors (viewer, collaborator, owner), and what each may do is policies/http-gateway.jsonld; | at the HTTP boundary unknown refuses. A route is a door, and a door nobody has decided about stays shut. That is the one place the two callers differ. | . | route | action | . | edit content, revert content, upload documents, save glossary curation | content-authoring | . | delete feedback | review-comments | . | adjudicate a relevance verdict | adjudication | . Every gated route allows collaborator or owner, and task-authorization.test.ts pins that.

0300505ef577.title: When a step is refused
0300505ef577.content: . | Read the verdict line: it names which of the four checks said no. | Role mismatch: you are acting as the wrong actor, or the lane binds a role you do not hold. Hand the step to an actor who may take the role (process-state). Do not edit your actor’s roles to get past it; that is actor-role-administration.bpmn, and it belongs to the administrator lane. | deny: a prohibition was written on purpose. Ask the user; never remove it yourself (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

85d8e70b701d.title: The engine writes its own PROV-O record
85d8e70b701d.content: complete() attaches a prov:Activity to each history entry it records under an authorization context (src/workflow/prov-record.ts, HistoryEntry.prov): . | prov:agent is the actor GitHub vouched for, not a typed name; | prov:hadRole is the lane’s role, and prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>; | cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy in force, because decide evaluated every one; | prov:used is the target, when the step names one. | . It is written at the moment it is true, which the after-check below cannot do from a name alone. The same no-invention rule applies: a refused step, a step with no actor, or a step in a lane that binds no role gets no activity.

ef2cc9f0b3ad.title: The after-check: the PROV-O QA/QC report
ef2cc9f0b3ad.content: The engine checks before a step. An agent swarm acts first, so the same policy is checked after, from the record (docs/source/concepts-agentic-harness/bpmn-execution.md). scripts/prov-qaqc.ts reads every instance in beans/workflows/, including its subprocesses, and for each history entry on an activity or decision: . | writes one prov:Activity (schemas/content/prov.ts): prov:agent is the entry’s actor, prov:hadRole is the role the lane binds (laneBinding), prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>, and cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy evaluated. One log per instance goes to docs/assets/prov/<instance>.prov.jsonld; | re-runs authorizeTask itself. For an entry recorded under a verdict it re-checks the principal that verdict recorded (the actor GitHub vouched for); for an entry that records just a name, it uses that name, asserted; | emits the engine’s own prov:Activity when the entry carries one, and derives one only for an entry without one. | . Findings: unknown, deny, not-eligible, undeclared-actor, a recorded authz that disagrees with the recomputed one (authz-disagrees), and gaps in the record itself: no-actor, no-role, node-not-in-model, source-moved and source-missing. An entry with no actor, or in a lane that binds no role, gets no prov:Activity, because the schema requires both and a guessed value is fabrication. It gets a finding instead. bun run cat prov:qaqc # write docs/prov-qaqc/index.md and the logs bun run cat check:prov-qaqc # CI: fail when they are stale . It is advisory, unlike the engine: findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page and never fail the build. check:prov-qaqc fails only on stale outputs, a prov:Activity that does not validate, or an internal error. Quote the counts from a run, not from the page you remember.

b30b69981988.content: . | A bug was found — write a regression test before fixing. | A new script or config file is added — test its contract. | A LaTeX macro is changed — test extraction still works. | A Lean project is added — auto-discovered, but verify. | The editor skill detects a potential error — it will ask the user whether to write a test. 9be863960a45.title: How to write a test
9be863960a45.content: // In scripts/tests/<suite>.test.ts import { describe, test, expect } from "bun:test"; import { REPO_ROOT, LEAN_DIR, ... } from "./helpers"; describe("Feature under test", () => { test("specific behavior", () => { // Arrange // Act // Assert expect(result).toBe(expected); }); }); . Conventions . | One test file per concern: lean-projects.test.ts, latex-lean-coverage.test.ts, infrastructure.test.ts. Create new files for new concerns. | Use helpers.ts: Don’t hardcode paths or re-implement discovery. | Informational vs. blocking: Tests that report data quality (sorry count, coverage gaps, label mismatches) should log and pass. Tests that verify contracts (JSON validity, required fields, file existence) should fail. | Comment the failure point: Each test should document what bug or failure it prevents. | Types from folio-assistant/schemas/qou-types.ts: Use TestResult, TestReport, CoverageEntry etc. when generating structured output. | . Adding a new Lean project . When a new Lean library is added to lakefile.toml (e.g., Unital): . | discoverLeanProjects() in helpers.ts auto-discovers it | lean-projects.test.ts automatically tests it (directory, files, sorry audit) | No manual test registration needed | . Test categories (from TestCategory type) . | Category | What it tests | . | lean-compile | .lean files exist, have imports, are non-empty | . | lean-library | Toolchain, lakefile, dependencies declared | . | lean-sorry | Sorry count per project/file | . | latex-lean-coverage | \lean{} tags resolve, theorem coverage, \leanok consistency | . | latex-structure | Labels, cross-refs, environments | . | schema-validity | JSON manifests match their schemas | . | infrastructure | MCP config, scripts, deploy, .gitignore | . | content-validation | Content objects pass Zod + constraint + AST checks | . Content-object tests . Test content objects using the validation pipeline: . import { validateObjects } from "../../content/pipeline/validate"; describe("Content objects", () => { test("all objects pass schema validation", async () => { const result = await validateObjects("folio/quantum-observable-universe/quantum-universes/"); const errors = result.issues.filter(i => i.level === "error"); expect(errors).toHaveLength(0); }); test("rendered LaTeX passes AST validation", async () => { // The validation pipeline includes AST checks automatically const result = await validateObjects("folio/quantum-observable-universe/quantum-universes/"); expect(result.valid).toBe(true); }); }); .

7197fa6eb870.title: Theme art intake
7197fa6eb870.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

e55dc630ec79.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
e55dc630ec79.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

6a340a51a36a.title: The constraints
6a340a51a36a.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

d9f4e0385932.title: Refuse, report, or neither
d9f4e0385932.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

6e0382c37a40.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
6e0382c37a40.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

15d54ef4246b.title: Reading the report
15d54ef4246b.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

33daad5fc3f1.title: Adding a constraint
33daad5fc3f1.content: . | Name the failure it answers. No failure, no constraint. | Decide refuse vs report by the line above — can the art do its job? | Write the remedy before the detection. If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . The stages of theming, and which owns which question, are in theming.

5dded5d91849.title: What is NOT here
5dded5d91849.content: The theming code — schemas/ui/themes.ts, schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts, scripts/check-theme-art.ts, scripts/gen-themes-css.ts, scripts/gen-avatars-css.ts — stays where it is. This is the kg graph: the instructions an agent follows, not the implementation. A skill and the code it describes are different node kinds, and moving code beside its documentation would make the partition meaningless.
