2d3ee627352e.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
2d3ee627352e.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

ef109d31de01.title: What it reviews
ef109d31de01.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the layer’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

da62f59ada70.title: What this gives up — accepted
da62f59ada70.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

5b04cf9b5c3e.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
5b04cf9b5c3e.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

c65b131bced9.title: Measure; do not assert
c65b131bced9.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

f7cac9b3e977.title: Branding is a question about the LAYER, not about taste
f7cac9b3e977.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the layer’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

b38c6fce72d6.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
b38c6fce72d6.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

ae282d23c1a4.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
ae282d23c1a4.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

771754291102.title: What this does NOT cover
771754291102.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

0da9802dc071.title: Both viewports, always
0da9802dc071.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .

a5c17065e3cc.title: Installing beans (fresh sandbox / cloud container)
a5c17065e3cc.content: beans is the hmans/beans Go binary — a flat-file issue tracker storing issues as markdown under .beans/. Cloud sandboxes do not ship it, so reinstall on demand (Go ships in the sandbox): . scripts/install-beans.sh # idempotent; installs into a PATH dir # equivalently, the one-liner it runs: GOBIN="$HOME/.local/bin" go install github.com/hmans/beans@latest . Note: the npm package named beans is an unrelated abandoned tool — do not npm install beans. Verify with beans list && beans check.

5a378d95ff3f.title: Core Directives for Sessions
5a378d95ff3f.content: . | Every session is a Bean: At the start of your session, you MUST create a parent bean (--type milestone or --epic) that represents the session and its goals. beans create "Session: <Branch/Goal>" --type milestone | Every todo is a Child Bean: All tasks, probes, and action items planned for the session MUST be created as child beans (--type task) and linked to the session bean. beans create "<Task Title>" --type task beans update <child-id> --parent <session-id> | No manual .md checklists: Never use session-beans.md or raw Markdown - [ ] checklists to track global tasks. Always use the beans CLI to prevent namespace pollution and maintain the official project tracking. | Check before you create: beans create is not idempotent. Run the existence check below before every beans create — no exceptions, including the session milestone. | .

9620c9880b0b.title: Check before you create — beans create is not idempotent (STRICT)
9620c9880b0b.content: beans create mints a fresh random ID on every call and dedupes on nothing. Re-running a work-plan step is therefore not a no-op — it creates a second bean. Before every beans create, check whether the bean exists: . T="Prove Foo.bar" beans list --json --search "title:\"$T\"" | python3 -c ' import json, sys t = sys.argv[1] m = [b for b in json.load(sys.stdin) if b["title"] == t] print(f"{len(m)} exact match(es)") [print(" ", b["id"], b["status"]) for b in m]' "$T" . | ≥ 1 match → do not create. Claim the existing bean instead: beans update <id> --status in-progress --body-append "Claimed by <branch>" | 0 matches → beans create "$T" --type task | . --search is a fuzzy Bleve query, so the exact-title comparison inside the pipe is load-bearing — do not drop it and trust --search alone. Why this is STRICT. On 2026-08-04 one agent context re-ran its 15-bean session work-plan ~980 times back-to-back (median 19 s per cycle, ~16 h wall). Because create is unconditional, that produced 14,688 duplicate beans — 92 % of every open bean in the repo. The damage was not just clutter: . | the session-start sweep and the idle-backlog policy (§4 of the AGENTS.md work-plan policy) were reading mostly noise; | 980 copies of an already-proved core sat at todo (JucysMurphy.seminormalVector_base_exists, discharged in SeminormalBaseExists.lean); | the duplicates collided with the IDs of 15 real beans, making beans update <id> ambiguous for those; | they corrupted a later agent’s own corpus-grep — 4,928 .beans files matched “specht” across just 36 titles, inflating 14 real corpus files into an apparent 54 and nearly landing a false correction in a PR body. | . The runaway loop is not something a doc can prevent; an unguarded create is. Cleanup + full triage: bean qou-2ryn.

2939c37ee1fb.title: Working with Beans
2939c37ee1fb.content: 1. Finding Tasks Use beans list to find beans you should work on. Look for todo or in-progress beans that match your current scope/branch. 2. Setting Dependencies You can map out sequence blockers using: beans update <id> --blocked-by <blocker-id> beans update <id> --blocking <blocked-id> . 3. Updating Status & Adding Comments . | When starting work: beans update <id> --status in-progress | When completed: beans update <id> --status completed | To add notes or discussion: beans update <id> --body-append "Your note" | .

5a9e5b500de7.title: Stalled-claim takeover — a claim is not forever (STRICT scope)
5a9e5b500de7.content: Agents stall: containers get reclaimed, sessions die, a branch is abandoned mid-task. Standing policy (AGENTS.md work-plan §2, 2026-08-15): a bean at in-progress whose backing branch has had no commit for > 3 h is presumed abandoned and may be taken over. This is the sole exception to “never resolve/claim a sibling’s bean”. Scope — read this or you will clobber live work. The > 3 h rule applies ONLY to the branch backing a live in-progress bean. It is NOT a licence to resurrect the thousands of long-idle claude/* branches — most are months old and permanently stale; age alone makes none of them a takeover target. Detect (the claimed branch is recorded in the bean’s claim note): . beans show <id> # find "branch `claude/...`" in the body git fetch origin <branch> git log -1 --format='%cI %h' origin/<branch> # last-commit ISO time + sha # stale iff (now − that time) > 3h. A running CI/lake build is NOT a stall — # check the PR for an in-flight job or a recent comment before deciding. Take over safely: . | Re-claim, recording the handoff: beans update <id> --status in-progress --body-append "Taken over <date> by <yourbranch>; prior claim <oldbranch> stale since <time> (last <sha>)." | Continue from the stale branch’s tip if its partial work is worth keeping (git checkout -b <yourbranch> origin/<oldbranch>); otherwise branch from main. | Never force-push the sibling’s branch. Open your own branch and leave theirs as the record; if they resume, the bean body shows the handoff. | For high-blast-radius work, drop a one-line note on the sibling PR that you have taken it over (per the AGENTS.md sibling-coordination rules). | .

f5d4bf5ecbec.title: Status Display Format
f5d4bf5ecbec.content: When the user asks “status” or “show beans”, run beans list and display the hierarchy: . ## Session Beans - [epic-123] Session: 1ppq-qbeta (in-progress) - [task-124] Task A (completed) - [task-125] Task B (in-progress) - [task-126] Task C (todo) .

871fb9f96387.title: Translation adjudication — the review loop
871fb9f96387.content: Skill translation-adjudication: A person’s word on a translation, carried from the translation review page or a block’s 🌐 pane to the record: anyone proposes text, which joins the ranked candidates; an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates, by accepting a catalogue or choosing one string’s translation with a reason; it is filed as a translation-adjudication/v1 issue; a workflow checks the author and the catalogue’s hash, writes the records, re-runs the auto-pick and opens a PR; a maintainer merges it. Use for “review the translations”, “this string is mistranslated”, “why was my review not recorded”, and when wiring a layer for review. Locale sign-off is a separate act, not this one. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Review task, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . Skill id: translation-adjudication · Package: library-core . The process is translation-review-adjudication.bpmn; this page is what each lane of it needs to know. translation-manager is the reference for every term used here (catalogue, msgstr, fuzzy, translation node, official).

0cf0a7b35e75.title: What it records, and what it never does
0cf0a7b35e75.content: What one person said about one catalogue, against the exact bytes they saw. Who they are decides what it counts as: anyone proposes; only an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates, and that is read from the issue event’s author_association, never from the body. | what was filed | by | what is written | . | a suggestion | anyone | appended to the catalogue’s candidates sidecar as a human candidate (id: github:<login>, by, issue, its msgidHash and placeholder QA), beside every other candidate; never refused for a changed catalogue | . | a suggestion with Choose as the translation (choose: true, reason) | a collaborator | the suggestion is also the string’s msgstr, not fuzzy, and the sidecar entry’s chosen records how: adjudicated, by, at, issue, reason and which candidate | . | the same | anyone else | refused as a choice, with a comment; kept as their proposal | . | acceptable | a collaborator | the catalogue’s translation node gets signedOffBy / signedOffAt, and each fuzzy string in it is adjudicated as it stands; the review page shows it reviewed, and stale once its bytes change | . | acceptable | anyone else | refused, with a comment | . | any of the above | — | an entry appended to the catalogue’s translation-qa attestation, criterion human-adjudication (or human-proposal), naming the issue and the hash the person saw | . After the writes, every string nobody has adjudicated is auto-picked by rank (below). It never makes a translation official. The PO header X-Folio-Official and the locale’s status.json are left alone: locale sign-off is the translation coordinator’s act in human-translation-workflow (Task_Signoff), checked by check-translation-officiality. A reviewed catalogue is evidence for that sign-off, not a substitute for it.

05a6ff4fe9e0.title: Candidates are never a barrier to having a translation
05a6ff4fe9e0.content: A string may have several candidate translations, from several sources; they live beside the catalogue in <locale>/<catalogue>.candidates.json (translation-candidates/v1), and translation-candidate-source is how they are produced. The rule that binds every writer: . | the .po keeps one msgstr; the sidecar keeps the rest; | when a string’s msgstr is empty, the writer also puts the first candidate there, marked #, fuzzy — the page always has something to show, the status page counts it as needing review, and it stays the default until a person adjudicates; | an existing msgstr is never replaced by a candidate, only offered beside it; | a candidate is never a verdict, whoever produced it. | .

847e4aded32d.title: The rank, and the default pick
847e4aded32d.content: When no collaborator has chosen, a string shows its best-ranked candidate. The rank is one function, rankCandidates: the tool that writes the strings projection ranks with it, the 🌐 pane restates it for a bare candidates sidecar, and a test holds the two equal, fixture for fixture. | tier | score | . | official — an official publication’s text | 0 | . | human-adjudicated — the text a collaborator chose | 1 | . | human-proposed — a person’s proposal | 2 | . | platform — a translation platform (Weblate, Crowdin, Transifex) | 3 | . | agent — an agent model | 4 | . | mt — open machine translation, or a machine-translation web service | 5 | . A QA failure (glossary, placeholders, round trip) adds 10. A check not run is not a failure. Ties go to the newest source.at, then the order recorded. A stale candidate — its msgidHash is not the string’s now, because the source text changed — is listed after every other and is never auto-picked. The auto-pick fills an empty msgstr, or replaces one that is itself an earlier auto-pick; it never overwrites a collaborator’s choice, or text whose provenance is not an auto-pick. It is written fuzzy and unofficial (chosen.how: auto), except an official candidate whose sourceText is the msgid exactly: whitespace, case and punctuation included. That one is written without fuzzy, as auto-official.

9c816d0a4f75.title: The reviewer’s lane
9c816d0a4f75.content: There are two ways in, and both file the same issue. | The review page (review.html, beside the translation status page): a layer’s catalogues × locales. A cell is machine, flagged, stale or reviewed when it can be adjudicated; none, empty and official cannot. | A block’s 🌐 pane, in the block’s 📣 panel, on every page — source-language pages included. It lists every locale’s current translation of the block: its status (official, adjudicated, proposed, agent, mt, missing, stale, unattributed) and how it came to be (chosen.how, chosen.by). On a translated page that page’s locale comes first and the others are collapsed. It reads assets/translation-status/review.json and each catalogue’s strings projection (folio-translation-strings/v1), which every site build publishes wherever the checkout has translations. | . Then: . | Read the strings against their source. ✎ Fix translation shows, per locale, each string’s candidates as a ranked table: the text; the source’s kind, id and version; who, linked to the issue it came from; the date; the QA results; a stale mark; whether an official source’s English matched exactly; and which one is the default. | Either mark the catalogue acceptable, or, for each wrong string, pick a row (its text fills an editable box, and its source is recorded while the text is unedited) or write your own text. | If you are an owner, member or collaborator and mean it as the translation, tick Choose as the translation and say why. Anyone else may tick it too, but only a collaborator’s choice is recorded; anyone else’s becomes a proposal. The help text says so. | Submit. The page opens GitHub’s new-issue form prefilled with a readable summary — per string, whether you propose or choose — and the translation-adjudication/v1 JSON block, labelled translation-adjudication and titled [translation review] …; when the record is too long for a URL, it copies the body for you to paste. Filing the issue is the act of proposing or, for a collaborator who chose, of adjudicating, under your own login. | . Do not edit the JSON block by hand. It carries the hash of each catalogue you saw, and a hand edit that changes what you reviewed is a record of something you did not read.

a67077c60941.title: The workflow’s lane — and every refusal
a67077c60941.content: layer-translation-adjudication.yml (a reusable workflow; a layer’s caller is a few lines) runs translation:adjudicate on the issues event. It reads the event file and parses the body only as JSON. It refuses rather than guesses, and says why on the issue: . | refusal | why | what to do | . | already recorded | the issue’s branch exists | nothing: one issue, one record | . | could not determine (exit 2) | no event, no issue author, or no declaration | the run FAILS; it is never read as “nothing to record” | . | an acceptable or a choice from an author who is not an owner, member or collaborator | identity comes from author_association, never the body | nothing: their suggestions are recorded as proposals; a collaborator can choose among them | . | invalid record, wrong repository, wrong translations directory | the record is not for this layer | file it from this layer’s page | . | a choice or acceptance against a catalogue that changed since the page showed it | the poHash no longer matches | reload the page and choose again; the proposal is kept | . | a choice whose current text is no longer the catalogue’s | the string moved under you | reload and choose again; the proposal is kept | . | node or attestation will not parse | the attestation is append-only and never overwritten | fix the file; nothing is recorded for that catalogue | . Proposals are never refused for a moved catalogue: the pins bind adjudication only. When every item is refused, nothing is written and no PR is opened (exit 3). When some survive, those are recorded and the refusals are listed beside them in the PR body and the issue comment — never a partial record dressed as a whole one.

9fa200e57cdd.title: The maintainer’s lane
9fa200e57cdd.content: The workflow commits on translation-adjudication/issue-<n>, authored by the issue’s author, and opens a ready PR. A PR opened with the workflow’s token starts no other workflows, so the layer’s checks run once a maintainer pushes to it or re-opens it. The maintainer judges whether the PR writes down what the issue decided and nothing else — not the translation, which was the reviewer’s verdict. Closing it records nothing.

9b02524ac6b5.title: Tools
9b02524ac6b5.content: Every Tool here is one concrete way of doing a step; another forge or another engine is another Tool satisfying the same skill. | step | Tool | . | produce candidates | any translation-candidate-source Tool: translation-candidates-agent, or the open machine-translation engines through translation:candidates | . | build the review page | translation-status-viewer (translation:status writes review.html) | . | read and submit a verdict | translation-review-page, or a block’s 🌐 pane (cat-harness site-chrome/assets/js/translation-review.js) | . | publish what the pane reads | publish-translation-review.ts, run by every site build | . | carry the issue, run the workflow, hold the PR | github | . | the workflow itself | translation-adjudication-workflow | . | plan and write the records | translation-adjudicate | .

215eb28a34aa.title: Do not
215eb28a34aa.content: . | Do not treat reviewed as official, or sign a locale off from this loop. | Do not accept a catalogue whose suggestions you just wrote: they are fuzzy until somebody else reads them. | Do not paste an issue body into a shell or an expression: it is untrusted text, read only as JSON from the event file. | Do not let a candidate’s source stand in for a verdict: an agent model’s candidate is as unreviewed as an open model’s. | Do not treat a high rank as a review. The auto-pick is a default to show, fuzzy and unofficial, not a choice anyone made. | Do not let a source change block a pull request on its translations: the strings go stale and re-enter this process. | .

290792548f64.title: Translation candidate source — one interface, many engines
290792548f64.content: Skill translation-candidate-source: The one interface every candidate-translation engine meets: for a layer’s catalogues, append candidate translations per string to the translation-candidates/v1 sidecar, each carrying its source, and seed an empty msgstr with the first candidate marked fuzzy. An agent model and the open machine-translation engines (OPUS-MT, LibreTranslate / Argos) are interchangeable behind it. Use when adding an engine, choosing one, or producing candidates for review. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Review and publish a folio, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . Skill id: translation-candidate-source · Package: library-core . A candidate is a translation somebody or something proposes for one string. This skill states what producing candidates means, independent of the engine. A Tool that satisfies it runs one engine or several — the open machine-translation Tool picks its engine by flag — and which engine produced a candidate is recorded on the candidate. The reviewer’s choice among candidates is a step of translation-adjudication.

acb201b82984.title: The contract
acb201b82984.content: What makes engines interchangeable is what they WRITE, not how they are called: every Tool of this skill walks a layer’s catalogues for the locales asked and leaves the same two things behind. |   |   | . | input instance | the layer root whose catalogues to propose for | . | input locales | the target locales; absent means every locale the layer declares | . | output candidates | translations/<locale>/<catalogue>.candidates.json, translation-candidates/v1, appended to | . | output catalogues | the .po catalogues whose empty msgstr got the first candidate, #, fuzzy | . Engine-specific inputs (which engine, a server’s URL, a model) belong to the Tool that runs that engine. Each Tool states its selection — when to reach for it, where it stops, what it costs — so an agent can choose among them. The sidecar holds, per string (msgid, with msgctxt when there is one), a list of candidates and, once there is one, the chosen translation. | field | what it says | . | text (forms for a plural) | the translation | . | source.kind | official, agent, open-mt, web-service or human | . | source.id | the model, service or publication (opus-mt-en-fr, a model id, weblate); a person as github:<login> | . | source.version, source.at | when known; at breaks ties in the rank, newest first | . | source.by, source.issue | who proposed it, and the issue it came from: every proposal filed from the review page or a block’s 🌐 pane, by any GitHub author, is appended as a human candidate | . | msgidHash | sha16 of msgctxt U+0004 msgid U+0000 msgid_plural when the candidate was made; when it no longer matches, the candidate is stale and never auto-picked | . | sourceText | for an official candidate: the English as the publication prints it. Only an exact match with the msgid makes its auto-pick official | . | qa | glossary, placeholder and round-trip results; a failure costs it 10 in the rank | . | basedOn | a person’s proposal that repeats another source’s candidate names it | . chosen is { text, how, by, at, issue, reason, candidate }: how is adjudicated (a collaborator chose it), auto-official (an exact-match official candidate) or auto (the best-ranked candidate, fuzzy). How they are ranked is translation-adjudication.

a80e45e88adf.title: The rules every engine keeps
a80e45e88adf.content: . | Append, never overwrite. Another engine’s candidates stay. | Seed an empty msgstr, marked fuzzy. Candidates are never a barrier to having a translation: when a string has no translation, the first candidate also goes into the .po as its msgstr with #, fuzzy. An existing msgstr is never replaced. | Keep what must not be translated. Placeholders, code, math, URLs and tags shielded by extraction must survive; the deterministic gates of translation-manager judge the .po after any engine has written to it. | Say what you are. A candidate without a source is refused by the sidecar’s schema; an engine that cannot name its model and version names what it can. Record the msgidHash of the string you translated, so a later change to the source text shows your candidate stale. | A candidate is never a verdict. Nothing an engine writes makes a catalogue reviewed or official, and no engine writes chosen with how: adjudicated: only the adjudication workflow does, for an owner, member or collaborator. | .

6309debbd48a.title: Adding an engine
6309debbd48a.content: A new engine is either a new value of an existing Tool’s engine flag — the open machine-translation engines are one Tool, translation:candidates --engine opus-mt,libretranslate — or, when it is a different mechanism (a person, an agent, a paid service), a new Tool node under tools/<id>/<id>.json that satisfies this skill, writes the outputs above, states a selection, and — when it reaches a host — requires.network: true with a remedies entry naming what to do when that host is refused. Nothing in the process changes: the process names this skill, never an engine.

610bd166cc46.content: The authoritative documentation is docs/guides/translation-support.md. Read it before using this skill. This file is the operational checklist, not the architecture.

0b3d76d20a44.title: The two-axis model
0b3d76d20a44.content: A content node varies along two axes: . | Format — .md (Markdown), .lean (Lean 4), .tex (LaTeX), .bpmn, .dmn, etc. | Language — BCP 47 locale tags (en, fr, es, ar, zh, ru). | . The format axis is handled by companions. The language axis is handled by the PO/POT pipeline with TranslationNode manifests in translations/<locale>/.

b74a086cb5dc.title: TranslationNode — .po/.pot files as KG nodes
b74a086cb5dc.content: Each .po/.pot pair is wrapped by a .ts manifest that makes it a first-class node in the knowledge graph: . import type { TranslationNode } from "../../schemas/translation"; const node: TranslationNode = { label: "trans:fr/index", locale: "fr", sourceFile: "docs/index.md", potFile: "translations/fr/index.pot", poFile: "translations/fr/index.po", status: { locale: "fr", official: false, generatedBy: "agent" }, coverage: { translated: 37, total: 37, pct: 100 }, }; export default node; . The manifest carries the status, coverage, and QA results inline — no separate status.json or .qa.json files.

9ea244dbaeb3.title: PO source resolution (fallback behavior)
9ea244dbaeb3.content: Content blocks can declare explicit PO sources via poSources[] on BlockBase. When not declared, the pipeline resolves by convention: . | Block-level: translations/<locale>/<block-stem>.po | Chapter-level: translations/<locale>/<chapter-slug>.po | Folio-level: translations/<locale>/global.po | Dependency walk: walk <name>.config.json dependencies depth-first | . When poSources is declared, only the listed files are consulted (no fallback). Later entries override earlier for the same msgid.

47aa8e63748f.title: What is translatable
47aa8e63748f.content: | Content | Translatable? | Notes | . | Block titles | ✅ | From .ts manifests | . | Prose bodies (.md) | ✅ | Segmented by paragraph | . | Chapter/section titles | ✅ | From chapter.ts / section.ts | . | Kind headings | ✅ | “Definition”, “Theorem”, etc. → locale catalogue | . | LaTeX math | ❌ | Universal notation | . | Block labels | ❌ | Structural identifiers | . | Code blocks | ❌ | Programming language content | . | Lean companions | ❌ | Formal mathematics | . | FHIR resources | ⚠️ | Use FHIR’s own designation system, not gettext | .

6aa4b3359a1c.title: The exported GRAPH per locale
6aa4b3359a1c.content: The graph a machine consumes is translated per locale, not only the rendered page: bun run cat kg:locale writes it (kg:locale:bootstrap for the nested layer, kg:locale:check in the gate set). Four rules; an implementation breaks the first by default. 1. The core graph must not reference its translations. No hasTranslation, no availableLocales, no translationOf, no per-locale @id, no locale key in the @context. The obvious implementation hangs a pointer off each node; that grows the core by an edge per locale per node and makes bootstrap’s graph reference artefacts it does not own and cannot validate. The arrow runs one way — a per-locale document references the core, never the reverse — and the core is complete with no translation existing. The same relation board-diagram-interchange states for a board and its folio. localeDocumentsUnreferenced checks it rather than trusting it. 2. A translated node keeps its @id. A translation is not a new term. Locale-suffixed IRIs are ruled out by that, not chosen against. 3. The language tag rides the VALUE, never the document. A blanket "@language": "fr" would assert French over every string that fell through — and fall-through is the normal case, because parsePo takes only non-empty msgstr and skips fuzzy entries. A translated value is {"@value": …, "@language": …}; a fall-through stays a plain string under the document’s declared sourceLanguage. Fall-through is then visible in the data rather than inferable from a coverage number. 4. A catalogue is scoped to the asset it was extracted from. Merging every .po under a locale lets a docs page’s "yes" → "oui" translate every BPMN gateway branch label — output that looks right while no diagram catalogue exists, so it can only be caught by provenance, not by reading the output. So a .po is read only when its stem names an asset the graph projects. A residual is accepted and named: a msgid from diagram A applies to an identical string on a node from diagram B — not a new assumption, since kg-export already dedupes lane-derived Role nodes by lane name across every diagram. What the gate is not. kg:locale:check says nothing about how much is translated. Where a diagram template has no .po in a locale, the exporter writes nothing and reports the locale saying so. A locale with nothing to say is reported, never a missing file a reader cannot tell from a broken build; --all-locales emits a source-language copy per locale for the other reading.

f6334f7c46f5.title: Workflow
f6334f7c46f5.content: 1. Extract (POT generation) . bun run pipeline/pot-extract.ts [--chapter <dir>] [--block <label>] . Or use the translation_extract MCP tool. Produces .pot files at the configured granularity. 2. Build the locale term base, and review it . Before translating, build the term base for the target locale from the layered glossaries, review it, and translate with it. See The locale term base for where each layer’s glossary is and the precedence rule. The term base is the merge translation:glossary:check checks against, so build it the way that check does, not by hand from one layer. Review it before you use it: a term the more authoritative layer has fixed is not re-translated, and a term with no fixed form in any layer is a decision you make once, here, not again in every block. 3. Translate . Translate with the term base open. Options, in order of preference: . | Existing .po from SMART Base — if the DAK already has translations from Weblate/Crowdin, use them. | Open machine translation, as candidates — bun run cat translation:candidates --instance <root> --engine opus-mt (OPUS-MT, Helsinki-NLP Marian models, CC-BY 4.0, run locally), or --engine opus-mt,libretranslate --url <yours> to add a self-hosted LibreTranslate as a second source. The Tool is translation-candidates. Each source’s text for each empty or fuzzy string is a CANDIDATE, appended to <locale>/<catalogue>.candidates.json (translation-candidates/v1). A candidate whose placeholders or markup do not round-trip is not recorded. Candidates are never a barrier to having a translation: an EMPTY msgstr gets the first good candidate, #, fuzzy. A non-empty msgstr is never overwritten, and official is never set. --init starts a .po from a template that has none. No hosted freemium API is used. The DeepL / Google Translate route through po-translate is no longer recommended, because it needs a quota and sends the text to a third party. Paid services (DeepL, Google Cloud Translation, Azure Translator, Amazon Translate) are deliberately not candidate sources here. | Agent translation — LLM translation of .pot → .po. Also tagged unofficial. An agent’s text can be recorded as a candidate with source.kind: "agent" through the same writer. | Human translation — the gold standard. | . A candidate is a draft, never a verdict. Candidates reach a person through the translation review page (review.html, beside the status page) and through a block’s 🌐 pane, on every page. There a reader picks one candidate per string, accepts the default, or types their own text. Anyone’s text is recorded as a proposal, a human candidate beside the others. An owner, member or collaborator who ticks Choose as the translation adjudicates it, and the issue names the source of the picked candidate. Until someone adjudicates, each string shows its best-ranked candidate, fuzzy (the rank is in translation-adjudication). A catalogue whose author wrote DO NOT MACHINE-FILL in its header (the viewer’s kg-viewer.po) still gets candidates for a reviewer. Its .po is never machine-filled: the tool refuses that, and so does an agent. Modal strength: a recommendation stays a recommendation . A lowercase should is a recommendation, and its translation is the locale’s recommendation form, never its obligation form. Turning it into “must” strengthens the claim, and in a guide it then reads as a conformance rule. Lowercase must, shall and needs to are obligations. The uppercase BCP 14 keywords (RFC 2119, RFC 8174: MUST, SHALL, SHOULD, MAY) keep the fixed renderings the locale’s term base gives them. | locale | should (recommendation) | must / shall (obligation) | . | ar | ينبغي، يُستحسن | يجب | . | es | debería, se recomienda | debe | . | fr | devrait, il est recommandé de | doit | . | ru | следует, рекомендуется | должен | . | zh | 应当, 宜, 建议 | 必须 | . A brief may not normalise one into the other, for consistency or anything else. A lexical round-trip screen cannot see this shift either: the words of a back-translation overlap whether it says “should” or “must”. So the adjudicator reads every string whose source has a modal (see “What counts as drift”). 4. Inject (PO → translated Markdown) . bun run pipeline/po-inject.ts --locale <locale> [--chapter <dir>] . Or use the translation_inject MCP tool. Reads .po files and produces translated .md in docs/<locale>/ for docs pages, or in the content directory for content blocks. 5. Create TranslationNode manifest . After injection, create or update the .ts manifest: . # The pipeline does this automatically, or create manually: translations/<locale>/<stem>.ts . The manifest carries status, coverage, and round-trip QA results inline. Validate with TranslationNodeSchema from schemas/content/translation.ts. 6. Round-trip QA . After injection, run round-trip translation QA: . bun run pipeline/translation-qa.ts --locale <locale> . Or use the translation_validate MCP tool for coverage and staleness. Semantic verification is per block and lives in the sidecar, not in a node-level summary field: TranslationNode.roundTripQA was removed with the numbers it held. See §”Per-block translation QA” below, and route drift to a human reviewer. 7. Glossary consistency . After translating, check that every glossary term was translated the way the term base fixes it, and the same way everywhere: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> . The check enforces a fixed term wherever the source uses it in its glossary sense; see The locale term base for how the sense is decided. It exits 1 on an in-sense use whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation. A use still pending adjudication is listed and fails nothing. To have the pending uses ruled on, list them for the adjudicator and record the answers: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --pending --json bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --record <verdicts.json> . Fix each violation in the .po, not in the injected output, and re-inject. Then include the check’s glossary section in the KG QA report, so the reviewer who signs off sees it. That section lists violations, exceptions, pending uses and other-sense uses. A violation the translator believes is right is not fixed by editing the term base in the layer: a term a lower layer fixes is changed in that layer, or it goes to the adjudicator. 8. Sign-off . A human reviewer signs off at the desired level: . bun run pipeline/translation-signoff.ts --locale <locale> --level <block|section|chapter|folio> [--path <content-path>] . Or use the translation_signoff MCP tool. Updates the TranslationNode manifest with sign-off metadata and source hash. Before sign-off: review and adjudication, catalogue by catalogue . A reviewer who reads one catalogue and finds it acceptable, or finds a mistranslation and picks a candidate or writes their own text, records that through the review page, a translation-adjudication/v1 issue and a PR — the loop in translation-adjudication, drawn as translation-review-adjudication.bpmn. Anyone may propose; only an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates, by accepting a catalogue or choosing a string’s translation with a reason. It marks a catalogue reviewed, or a string adjudicated, and never official: the sign-off above stays a separate act. A string nobody has adjudicated shows its best-ranked candidate, fuzzy and unofficial, unless an official source’s English matches the msgid exactly. Candidate translations from any engine — an agent model, OPUS-MT, LibreTranslate / Argos — are produced through translation-candidate-source, and an empty msgstr gets the first candidate, marked fuzzy: candidates are never a barrier to having a translation. 9. Staleness watch . On every content change, the pipeline checks whether any official translation’s sourceHash no longer matches the source .md. Stale translations are flagged in the viewer and in translation_status output. Per string, the same holds: a candidate records the msgidHash of the source text it translated, so when the source changes, the candidate and any translation chosen for the old text show stale in a block’s 🌐 pane. A stale candidate is never auto-picked, and the string re-enters translation-adjudication. A source change is never held back for its translations: the pull request that changes the source merges, and the translations catch up.

d8ebc691a6eb.title: Translating into several locales as a team
d8ebc691a6eb.content: The workflow above is one catalogue’s life. When several locales are produced from the same source at the same time, by several translators, the steps are the same and the order around them matters more. The process is multi-locale-translation.bpmn, with its round trip in translation-round-trip.bpmn and its upkeep in translation-refresh.bpmn, whose steps the translation-refresh skill gives as commands. Five lanes: the owner (scope, merge window, sign-off), one source-language lead, one locale translator per locale, a back-translator and a round-trip adjudicator. Extract once, and merge the source first . The source-language lead extracts every template once: the pages, the diagrams (translate-bpmn --extract, which writes this harness’s own diagrams into its own translations/) and the glossary schemes. All of them go into one source PR to main, and it merges before any locale starts, so every translator branches from the same main. A translator never re-extracts. A locale that seems to need a different template has found a defect in the extraction, and that is reported to the lead. Each locale is its own PR to main . Each locale lands as its own PR, based on main and targeting main. Never into the source branch: a PR into an unmerged branch lands only when that branch does, and a branch that has merged and then receives more commits carries work main will never see. Once a source PR has merged, its branch receives nothing more; a later source fix is a new PR. What a locale contributes . | translations/<locale>/**.po, mirroring the templates’ layout. | A translation-node manifest beside each catalogue, official: false, generatedBy: "agent" (or "human"). No status.json: status is a property of the manifest, and officiality is a person’s sign-off, never the translator’s. | FHIR terms as CodeSystem supplements, one file per locale, holding the locale’s designations for every code system it translates. Never an edit inside a resource: an inline designation is a change to the source, every locale’s edits then collide in the same file, and the supplement is the mechanism FHIR has for exactly this. The supplements must compile with no SUSHI error and pass their structural checks (each one names the code system it supplements, at its version, and carries only codes it defines). | Source-text errors are reported, never fixed in the translation. The translator renders the source as it stands and notes the location; the lead files every such note as one issue on the source. A fix to the source is a source PR, and the next refresh carries it to every locale. | . The deterministic gates . Before any round trip, every gate passes: . | gate | command | . | templates current | translate-bpmn:check, and the layer’s page and glossary template checks | . | every catalogue matches its template | translation:drift:check --instance <root>, translation:obsolete:check --instance <root> | . | coverage | translation:status --instance <root>; a published page has its catalogue: translation:catalogue:check | . | placeholders, tags and URLs preserved | translation:page-qa --instance <root> (translation-terms-preserved) | . | officiality agrees | check:translation-officiality | . | the graph per locale | kg:locale:check | . | translated links resolve | translated-links:check | . | supplements compile | the layer’s supplement build: 0 SUSHI errors, structural checks pass | . The untainted round trip, as run . The discipline is untainted-verification and §”The agentic round trip” below; this is how it was run across several locales. | The sample, chosen by the translator before any result is seen: every diagram label, every persona and scenario string, and a seeded random fraction of the rest, with the seed recorded so the sample can be drawn again. A refresh samples only the strings it changed. | The back-translator gets the target strings alone, keyed by an opaque id, and renders them into the source language with no tools. | A mechanical pre-screen over every (source, back-translation) pair flags a pair whose negation, modal, quantifier, number or code tokens differ, and a pair whose word overlap is low. It only orders the reading. | The adjudicator reads every flagged pair in full, with the source and the back-translation and never the target, and rules each drift or not drift with its reason. | Both halves are stated. Drift: a claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed; a term of art swapped for one that means something else; a named entity, number or quantifier moved. Not drift, and the cases that came up most: inflection; a purpose clause rendered in the subjunctive (Russian чтобы + past tense reads back as “so that … would”); an acronym left uninflected in a language that inflects nouns; an acronym spelled out with the acronym kept beside it. | Each drift is fixed on the locale’s PR, and the fix is noted beside the ruling. When two separate parties cannot be dispatched, the producer records “could not dispatch” with the reason: never a pass. | Each ruling is keyed by content, never by position. A ruling on a catalogue string is pinned by field_hash.msgid, the hash of the source it judged, and field_hash.msgstr, the hash of the translation; a reader pairs strings with rulings by those hashes. Its index is only an order for reading. So: . | the catalogue | what follows | . | gains a string | no ruling is found for it, and the report fails loudly: run the round trip on that string | . | changes a translation | its ruling’s msgstr hash no longer matches: reported stale, never counted as a pass; run the round trip on that string | . | loses or reorders strings | nothing is invalidated, and no agent is re-run; once the removal is on main, the layer’s prune command (who-iris: translation-qa:prune) drops the removed strings’ rulings and renumbers the rest | . Rulings may be recorded before the PR whose strings they judge merges (they live on a state branch, the strings on main), so a ruling no string claims is not an error. The prune command is a dry run until --write, drops only rulings whose string main once held and no longer does, and never changes or invents a verdict. Run it after the removal merges, never on the removing branch: the state branch serves main too. | . Glossary precedence, and sense checks . The term base is layered, in this order: the normative reference glossaries first (the standards bodies’ own term lists the layer declares), then each layer in the order the index config lists it, and the layer’s own glossary last. A later layer adds terms; it never overrides a translation an earlier one fixed in the same subject area. translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> checks a locale against that merge. A platform term found in text of another subject area (the harness’s policy, say, in a health guide’s prose) is a sense check for a person to read, not a violation. It fails nothing. The QA report, one per locale . Each locale’s report goes under test/results/translation-qa/: beside the per-catalogue sidecars translation:page-qa writes, a report that names coverage, each gate’s result, the round trip (sampled, flagged, drift, not drift, and every drift ruling with its fix), the glossary violations and sense checks, and the source errors reported. The lead reads it before merging the locale’s PR, inside the owner’s merge window. Harness commands for another layer’s catalogues . Every command here reads a layer through its own declaration, so one composed checkout serves every layer it mounts: . | --instance <dir> on translation:drift:check (each locale’s .po against the .pot beside it, in the layer’s translation-sources directory; a layer with no site has its catalogues compared and its pages reported unreadable), translation:obsolete:check (msgids a catalogue carries that its source no longer yields; exits 2 when the layer declares no catalogue directory), translation:index:check (the layer’s own site; exits 2 when it declares no Jekyll site) and translation:status (prints the per-locale table, writes nothing; exits 2 without a translation-sources declaration). | translation:page-qa (translation-block-qa.ts --catalogues): every <translations>/<locale>/<rel>.po with its .pot beside it, not already measured as a block or page, is measured against its template, with a sidecar at test/results/translation-qa/translations/<rel>.<locale>.translation-qa.json in the layer’s QA tree. --instance <dir> sweeps another layer. | po-inject takes its units from segmentMarkdown in pot-extract.ts, the same segmentation the extractor writes the catalogue from, so a wrapped paragraph, list item or blockquote is looked up as the one msgid it was extracted as. | translation:glossary:check is the glossary-consistency command named above. | . Exit 2 from any of them is “could not determine”, and is reported, never read as clean.

adb69daca632.title: Per-block translation QA, and the agentic round trip
adb69daca632.content: Two sweeps, two subjects, and confusing them is how a site reports a translation nobody measured. | translation-qa-sweep.ts measures the docs site: how much of each page exists in each language. It writes docs/_data/translation-qa.json and feeds the badge under a page title. | translation-block-qa.ts measures a block, one sidecar per (block, locale): <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, in the block-qa/v1 entry shape, which is what the per-block TR icon opens. | . bun run cat translation:block-qa # write the sidecars bun run cat translation:block-qa:check # fail if any is stale . What a script may claim, and what it may not . Three criteria are deterministic and carry a script witness: translation-coverage, translation-terms-preserved (acronyms, numbers and URLs that must survive translation and did not — the class a fluent mistranslation passes) and translation-not-echo (a “translation” identical to its source; a warn, because that is right for a proper noun and wrong for a sentence). translation-semantic-roundtrip is written with no entry. A round trip asks whether the MEANING survived, and that needs a translator that has not seen the original. The only back-translation available to a script here is the PO’s own msgid→msgstr map read backwards, which returns the source exactly, always: a perfect similarity score measuring the lookup table. Do not fill this criterion mechanically. A green tick nobody should trust is worse than a gap that says it is a gap — a reader who sees the tick stops asking. This was not hypothetical. translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator” — a measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the translation. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. The agentic round trip — an INSTANCE of untainted verification . The discipline is generic and lives in untainted-verification: the two parties, why neither may see what would let it shortcut, the TOOLS_USED declaration that is recorded rather than assumed, which party rules, how both are written as witnesses, the model / model_source rule, and the two traps — a sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself, and a verdict is hashed to what it was about. Read that first. This section is only what translation adds. The round trip was where that discipline was first written down, and generalising it turned up a defect in the generalisation: the spine’s UntaintedDispatch was typed over CompanionRole, and po is deliberately not one — a PO is a companion of a (block, locale) pair, not of a block. So the founding case could not be expressed in the type taken from it. The abstraction was widened rather than the case bent; untaintedPartitionDefects now takes its artefact universe as a parameter. The declaration . ROUNDTRIP_DISPATCH in pipeline/translation-block-qa.ts: . | party | sees | never sees | . | back-translator | po — the target text, and nothing else | md, ts | . | adjudicator | md — the original, plus the back-translation | po | . Disjoint, which is the whole rule in one line. Shown the source, a back-translator writes the source back and the check passes vacuously — measuring the lookup table rather than the translation. That is not a warning here any more: untaintedPartitionDefects reports it, and a test asserts it. What counts as drift, and what does not . Both halves, always. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and every translation fails. Synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift. A claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is; so is a term of art swapped for something that means a different thing, and a named entity or quantifier moved. A modal is a claim’s strength: “should” read back as “must”, or “may” as “should”, is drift, however close the words are. This is the part that does not generalise — the spine requires a drift statement and checks only that one exists, because “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the defect the whole mechanism exists to stop. Recording it . bun run pipeline/translation-roundtrip.ts --payload <file.json> . Where it lands: translation-block-qa writes translation-semantic-roundtrip: [] on every run, and before mergeCriteria an unrelated re-run deleted a round trip a pair of agents had produced — silently, with nothing in the output to say so. That incident is why the spine carries the replace-only-your-own rule. Staleness is per locale here: the entries hash the .md, the .ts and the .po, so editing the source stales every locale’s round trip and editing one translation stales only that locale’s. The instrument, not the translation . translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator”. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject.

5b00752e1692.title: Automatic badge rendering
5b00752e1692.content: Translation badges are automatically rendered on every docs page by docs-ui.js. There is no need to manually add badge includes or front matter. How it works . | head_custom.html publishes a <script type="application/json" id="fa-translation-meta"> block on every page, reading from page front matter | docs-ui.js reads that block and auto-injects into the page title: . | 🌐 Language coverage badge — 0/5 languages (grey), 1/5 (amber), 5/5 (green) | ⚠️ Unverified warning — auto-injected when translation_status: unverified | . | . Front matter for the translation pipeline to stamp . The translation pipeline stamps this front matter on generated pages: . # Source pages (English): lang: en available_locales: ["en", "fr"] # every locale the page can be read in # Translated pages: lang: fr translation_status: unverified # or "official" translation_source: index.md # source file available_locales: ["en", "fr"] . The locale term base . A glossary term must be translated the same way on every page, and the same way in every layer that uses it. The term base is the one place that says how. Where the terms come from. Each layer’s glossary is the directory it declares with the glossary graph typology in its <instance>.json (a *.glossary.json SKOS scheme per file); a layer without that declaration has no glossary of its own and inherits its dependencies’. The terms’ translations today are the per-scheme catalogues translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po written from those schemes, and the pins in translations/<locale>/glossary.po below. Subject areas. Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Each glossary scheme declares the subject area its translations bind in, as subject (dcterms:subject, a local id such as harness-vocabulary or digital-health-trust); a term may override its scheme’s. A term with no subject, on itself or its scheme, binds only within its own scheme. Precedence applies within a subject area. The term base for a locale is the glossaries of the layer and every layer it needs, merged in layer order: within one subject area, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation; a layer only adds. A layer may add a term no layer below defines, and may fix its translation. It may not give a term a lower layer has fixed, in the same subject area, a second translation; that is a violation, reported by translation:glossary:check, never an override. A term used in sense keeps its fixed translation. Owner, 2026-11-07: if a glossary term is used in the narrative in the correct context, the translated narrative uses the glossary translation. The same word is not always the same concept. The harness’s policy is fixed as 策略 (an access policy), but a health guide’s “policy” is 政策. So the sense of each use is decided by rule first, then by an agent: . | By rule. A use in a page or catalogue whose subject area is the term’s own is in sense automatically. | By an adjudicator. Any other use is pending until an untainted adjudicator agent rules on it. The agent is given the term, its skos definition and the source sentence. It rules in-sense or other-sense with a one-line reason. Alternatively it records an exception: in sense, but the fixed term is wrong here because of a reason it gives. | What the check does with each state. An in-sense use (by rule or by verdict) whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation is a violation, and the check fails. A pending use is listed and fails nothing. An other-sense use is not checked. An exception passes and is listed. | Keeping the English term. A msgstr that keeps the English term verbatim renders it only where the term is part of a code or resource name. The same term left in English in prose does not render it. | Where verdicts are kept. They are stored durably in the layer, in a committed file beside its catalogues. Each is keyed by the term’s id and a hash of the msgid. Sense is a property of the source, so one verdict serves every locale and each use is asked about once. A changed msgid invalidates its verdict, and the use is asked again. | Who decides. Each verdict names who decided it, an agent or person id, never a model. The check itself never asks a model. | . How a fixed translation is recorded. It is derived, never flagged: a term whose status is authored and whose scheme catalogue (translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po) holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel is fixed. There is no #, fixed flag and no translated label in the glossary JSON, so the catalogue stays the one place a translation lives. Whether a person has signed it off is the term’s translationStatus, per locale, official or unofficial (absent means unofficial). A pinned msgstr in glossary.po below is a QA hint, not a term base entry. The terminology glossary — translations/<locale>/glossary.po . translation-terms-preserved can see that a source term is absent from a translation. It cannot see whether that is a correct localisation or a silent loss: WHO missing from a French sentence is either OMS or a dropped term, and guessing either way is worse than saying so. The glossary is how a folio tells it which. | entry | meaning | when the term is absent | . | msgstr "OMS" | the expected form, pinned | fail — the glossary said what it should be | . | msgstr "FHIR" (identity) | must survive verbatim | fail | . | #, localised | rendered in the target language, form NOT pinned | pass | . | no entry | unknown | warn | . #, localised exists so a glossary needs no translated content. Pinning a form means authoring target-language material; the flag says the one thing the checker needs — this term gets localised, I am not pinning how — and it is reviewable by someone who reads only English. Pin a form when you want the stricter check. It is a reading rule and cannot become a mute button, which is the property to preserve if you touch it. localised only converts a would-be finding about that term into a pass: it never reaches strict tokens (a URL or a number consults no glossary — nothing localises a 3), it cannot act on a term it does not name, an entry with neither a form nor the flag is unfinished rather than permission, and each locale’s file is read alone, so marking a term in French says nothing about Arabic. Every one of those is a test in translation-block-qa.test.ts. The file is hand-authored and has no POT — schemas/content/translation.ts declares that slot, and TranslationNode.potFile is optional for exactly this. Work item he0e. available_locales includes the SOURCE language, and that is not a formality. It is the list a reader’s language bar and coverage badge are computed from — “which languages can I read this page in” — and the page is certainly readable in the one it was written in. It is not the list of translations that exist, which is what availableLocales() in pipeline/po-resolve.ts returns by resolving translations/<locale>/<stem>.po; that lookup can never name the source language, because there is no translations/en/ and there never will be. Use localesAvailableFor() in pipeline/translation-index.ts to go from one to the other. Both halves of the corpus — generated and hand-authored translated pages — must stamp the same meaning, or a badge reads a numerator larger than its denominator. Do not stamp qa_translation_* keys: stamped from a node-level round trip, they publish every string nobody back-translated as semantic drift. Per-block QA is the record: the TR icon beside each block opens <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, where a verdict names the witness that reached it. docs-ui.js injects the unverified-translation warning itself, from the page’s own front matter. There is no include to add: buildLanguageBar renders the six UN languages and greys out the ones not yet translated. Do not add a translation-warning.html, language-selector.html or qa-translation-badge.html include.

b9be788f99a0.title: The navbar filters by locale
b9be788f99a0.content: Translated pages are labelled as translated content in the graph and are not shown in the navbar unless their locale is selected; with no translation, the navbar falls back to the source language. Three rules, and each is enforced somewhere different because each can break somewhere different. 1. A page is a translation because the PAGE says so . Three fields in its own front matter, and nothing else anywhere: . lang: fr # this page is French nav_exclude: true # keep it OUT of the static nav translation_source: index.md # which page it expresses . pipeline/translation-index.ts walks the site and reads those. A page with no lang is the layer’s source language — absent means the default, not unknown. Never match a directory name against a list of language subtags. A layout coincidence is not a contract, and it is wrong in both directions: a folio with a no/ chapter (Norwegian, or the English word) is silently hidden from its own navbar, and a pt-BR/ or translated-fr/ directory is silently shown as source. Neither announces itself — the navbar simply has the wrong entries in it. Put the French page at accueil-fr.md beside its source and it is indexed correctly; put an English page in a folder called fr/ and it is left alone. There is deliberately no translated-content graph typology. A declaration per locale subtree restates what every page already says and grows as O(locales × subtrees). What is translatable is a node’s content (Markdown, BPMN, …), not its schema: translatability is a property of a format within a content type. Each layer that owns a content type declares, under contentTranslations in its own <instance>.json, which formats have an extract/inject pair, and schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects them — Markdown, LaTeX, PlantUML, SVG, ArchiMate, Excel, BPMN, FSH, FHIR JSON — and isTranslatable(contentType, extension) is the predicate. The index asks it rather than inventing a second answer, so a .json beside a page is data and never a language. translations/ is declared, as translation-sources. That one earns a kind: a .po catalogue is not content in any language, so no file inside it can declare one. There is no nav_order on a translated page. It stands where its source stands, because it replaces that item rather than joining the list. A nav_order beside a nav_exclude is two facts that contradict each other, and the check refuses it. 2. nav_exclude is the half that JavaScript cannot do . just-the-docs builds the navbar at build time, from front matter, on a static site serving the same HTML to every reader. It cannot know which locale anybody chose, so a translated page left in the nav is in it for everybody. A script can swap a nav item; it cannot un-render one without a flash of the wrong nav first. So the translations leave the static nav entirely, and a reader with no JavaScript gets the source-language navbar — the correct degraded answer rather than an arbitrary one. 3. The swap, and the fallback that is not a code path . pipeline/translation-index.ts writes docs/_data/translations.json; _includes/head_custom.html publishes it into every page as #fa-translation-index; mountNavLocale in site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js reads it. With a non-source locale selected, each nav item that has a page in that locale is rewritten in place — same position, same parent, translated title, translated href, and its own dir so an Arabic item inside an English column is not laid out backwards. Fallback is the absence of a rewrite. An item with no page in the selected locale is not touched, so it keeps its source-language title and link. There is deliberately no branch for it: a fallback implemented as its own code path is a code path that can be wrong, and this one cannot be. Which locale is “selected”, in precedence order: ?lang= on the URL, then the page’s own lang when the page is a translation, then the remembered fa-locale, then the source language. A locale the index has never heard of is not honoured — labelling the navbar tlh while every item is in English is a claim the page cannot support. Three states, and the third is why the index is published as null . | data-fa-nav-index | when | what the navbar does | . | ok | the index parsed and holds pages | filter it | . | empty | it parsed and holds none | nothing to swap; every item is source language | . | unknown | no island, unparseable, or index: null because the data file was absent at build time | left exactly as built | . empty and unknown produce the same navbar and are not the same answer: one is “this folio has no translations”, the other is “this build could not tell”. A build that could not determine the translation set must never render as a folio that has none — so translation:index exits 2 rather than writing a partial index over a complete one, and the deploy fails rather than publishing it. Adding a locale . | Write the pages, each carrying lang, nav_exclude: true and translation_source. Where they sit is up to you — the convention here is <dir>/<locale>/<page>.md, and nothing depends on it. | bun run cat translation:index and commit docs/_data/translations.json. | . There is no third step and no declaration to remember. The thing that IS easy to forget is nav_exclude, which is why translation:index:check fails without it: a translated page left in the static nav is in it for every reader, whatever locale they chose, which is the bug this section records.

fc56fec15ffd.title: translations/ directory rules
fc56fec15ffd.content: The translations/ directory contains only three file types: . | .pot — POT templates (extractable strings) | .po — PO translated strings | .ts — TranslationNode manifests (KG nodes) | . Do not put .md, .qa.json, or status.json files in translations/. Rendered output lives in docs/<locale>/; QA and status are properties of the TranslationNode manifest. A layer with no translations directory of its own is hosted. translationsHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts its templates in the extracting harness’s translations/<locale>/<stub>/ — cat-harness/translations/<locale>/bootstrap/processes/*.pot for bootstrap’s three diagrams — rather than inside the layer, which holds no translation machinery. The templates are extracted from the bootstrap the harness has pinned; when bootstrap is its own repository they stay here, since a template is the harness’s work over bootstrap’s text, not part of it (kg-separation §”The pair”).

3d0f487efb0f.title: A layer that defines its own translator
3d0f487efb0f.content: A layer built on this one may define its own translator actor and translation subsystem. Then the rule is load it; never vendor it: the subsystem is invoked from that layer’s checkout, not copied here, and that layer’s skills say how. This skill names no layer above it.

13c01fa83244.title: IG Publisher i18n
13c01fa83244.content: For FHIR IG folios, the IG Publisher’s own i18n system is used in parallel: . | i18n-default-lang in sushi-config.yaml — source language. | i18n-lang — target languages. | translation-sources — path to input/translations/{lang}/ containing per-resource .po files. | Run with -generation-off -validation-off flags for fast translation-only builds. | . The prose translation pipeline (this skill) and the FHIR resource translation pipeline (IG Publisher) are complementary and independent.

db975dd0577c.title: Do not
db975dd0577c.content: . | Do not manually add badge includes. docs-ui.js renders them automatically from front matter. The include it replaced is deleted, not deprecated — an include that still exists is one somebody adds back. | Do not publish a semantic-QA number a script cannot establish. A back-translation from this repo’s own PO map, or from a word-substitution table, scores the table rather than the translation — and a string with no back-translation at all scores 0 and reads as drift. If no independent back-translator has run, the criterion has no verdict, and saying so is the honest output. | Do not infer a locale from a directory name. docs/fr/index.md is French because it says lang: fr. A subtag match is wrong in both directions and neither failure announces itself — see The navbar filters by locale. | Do not add a graph typology for translated content. It is the same kind of thing as the page it translates, differing by a field the file declares. Translatability is a property of a FORMAT within a content type — schemas/library/translation-tools.ts and isTranslatable — not of a directory. | Do not leave a translated page in the static nav. nav_exclude: true is what keeps it out, and no amount of client-side work substitutes for it: the nav is built once, for every reader, before anybody has chosen a locale. | Do not put non-PO files in translations/. Only .pot, .po, and .ts manifests belong there. Rendered .md goes in docs/<locale>/. | Do not vendor SMART Base translation scripts. Load from checkout. | Do not translate math, labels, or code. Exclude in extraction. | Do not auto-sign-off. Official status requires a human. | Do not re-extract per locale. Templates are extracted once, merged to main in one source PR, and every locale starts from them. | Do not open a locale PR into the source branch, and do not push to a branch whose PR has merged. Each locale is its own PR to main. | Do not fix the source in a translation. Report it as one issue. | Do not edit a FHIR resource to translate it. Its terms go into the locale’s CodeSystem supplement. | Do not re-translate a term a lower layer fixes in the same subject area. Translate with the locale term base, and fix a violation where the term is fixed. A use in another subject area is enforced once an adjudicator rules it in sense; until then it is pending, not a violation. | Do not treat staleness as “wrong”. A stale translation is still useful; it just needs re-review. | Do not conflate FHIR resource translation with prose translation. They are different pipelines with different tooling. | Do not auto-remove staging previews. Require staging:cleanup label. | .

79cc6e263a81.title: Content-type-specific translation tools
79cc6e263a81.content: Each content type declares what formats it can translate and what scripts handle each format. The declaration belongs to the layer that OWNS the content type, under contentTranslations in its <instance>.json; schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects every present layer’s profiles and refuses a content type declared twice. A module or diagram path in a profile resolves from the declaring layer, then down its needs chain. The profiles: . | Content type | Formats | RTL | . | document | Markdown | ✅ | . | paper | Markdown + LaTeX | — | . | dak (WHO L2) | Markdown + PlantUML + SVG + ArchiMate + Excel + BPMN | ✅ | . | ig (WHO L3) | Markdown + FSH + FHIR JSON | ✅ | . The generic pipeline (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts) handles Markdown. Adapter-specific tools extend it with format-specific extractors. The Python originals from SMART Base live in scripts/translation/ and are referenced in the registry. RTL support . Arabic (and Hebrew, Farsi, Urdu) pages are detected at load time by docs-ui.js and get dir="rtl" on <html>. The CSS in docs-ui.css provides smooth 0.4s transitions for sidebar and content layout: . | Sidebar slides to the right side | Content flows RTL | Mermaid diagrams and badges stay LTR | BPMN diagrams need re-rendering with translated labels | . Staging review . When presenting translated content for review, use the staging-review skill to provide before/after URL comparison tables. See schemas/sdlc/staging.ts for the StagingComparison schema.

0d157b0d41fd.title: Staging links

Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.
