149f242b922a.title: uses[] Editorial Review
149f242b922a.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

12cdc9452143.title: The relation you are auditing
12cdc9452143.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

2df0f182bfdf.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
2df0f182bfdf.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

9ec21c291d36.title: The prime directive
9ec21c291d36.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

45f9ae404ad0.title: Workflow
45f9ae404ad0.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

e7dda76c3d0c.title: Verdict rubric
e7dda76c3d0c.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

638d5eb05161.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
638d5eb05161.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

efac311c3fba.title: Declaring the second case
efac311c3fba.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

cdf79b4c3f1a.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
cdf79b4c3f1a.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

0dccc021fcbb.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
0dccc021fcbb.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

d568e5c7e38b.title: One reading is not the standard
d568e5c7e38b.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

92bed16e0914.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
92bed16e0914.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

c02590ad818d.title: Interaction with other skills
c02590ad818d.content: | Skill | Interaction | . | content-graph | Owns the graph the mechanical checks read | . | prepare-merge | Runs the uses axis as part of the content gates | . A content type’s own skills that consume or extend this relation are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this skill.

c6ce47b6a182.title: uses-editorial-review (skill)
c6ce47b6a182.content: The skill uses-editorial-review as its source file cat-harness/skills/authoring/authoring-core/uses-editorial-review.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

fc566b0964b1.title: Voice editorial review
fc566b0964b1.content: Skill voice-editorial-review: Adjudicate a voice-* finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-voice.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

1e7169286fd3.title: The axis you are adjudicating
1e7169286fd3.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

c1cf8a9796f6.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
c1cf8a9796f6.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

e811f330984f.title: What the criterion cannot know
e811f330984f.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

f078ba9e06d3.title: Adjudicating one finding
f078ba9e06d3.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

414d0ecfab58.title: Where the open findings are
414d0ecfab58.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

7af32033cc3b.title: Do not
7af32033cc3b.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

d1eef6c833b6.title: voice-editorial-review (skill)
d1eef6c833b6.content: The skill voice-editorial-review as its source file cat-harness/skills/authoring/authoring-core/voice-editorial-review.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

cea60de568b3.title: Voice overlay review
cea60de568b3.content: Skill voice-overlay-review: Review a block against the active voices’ rules and record the verdict on its QA sidecar. The human/agent half of the voice overlay; the mechanical half is whatever patterns and terminology a rule carries. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Narrative review, Review task, Voice overlay review, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate .

b78690f07af5.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
b78690f07af5.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

0c9747d1c88e.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
0c9747d1c88e.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

e941bf730485.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
e941bf730485.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

6232d6ced718.title: A mechanical match is a question
6232d6ced718.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

2f5ca985ae48.title: Recording the verdict
2f5ca985ae48.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

3cfcb4c37824.title: Do not
3cfcb4c37824.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

b3f8d929a7e3.title: Voice overlay review
b3f8d929a7e3.content: Process_VoiceReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . The voice axis: load whichever editorial voices are active, run each rule’s mechanical half, and decide — for each finding — whether the prose is wrong, the rule does not apply to this content, or this block is a stated exception. You are in this process after the base voice has been adjudicated, and only if a voice is active at all: the first gateway ends the process honestly when none is, rather than reporting a clean review of nothing. Three outcomes, all legitimate, and the third is the one that needs recording: an exception without a reviewer entry is indistinguishable from a rule nobody ran. There is also a fourth path the diagram draws deliberately — if the rule’s own citation does not support it, the RULE is the defect, and that becomes a bean rather than a finding against the prose. i i i i i i Actors: Narrative reviewer .

At each citation, this lane also has to route the defect to the right place: a rule its own citation does not support goes to Task_RuleIsWrong as a finding against the VOICE, never into Task_Adjudicate, which only ever judges the block. | .

c19b0ee1324d.title: /watch — background watcher with integration check
c19b0ee1324d.content: Skill watch: Background-watch a branch (default origin/main) or a GitHub PR for new activity while you work, and on every event report whether to integrate / whether it conflicts with the current branch / whether it lets you simplify exposition / proofs / computations . Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome . A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and pull requests (subscribe via the GitHub MCP). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user. Merge Steward vs Sibling Watcher Routing (STRICT): . | If you hold the active merge-steward lane watching the merge queue, follow folio-assistant/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-manager-watcher.md, merge-queue.md (Process_MergeTrain + merge-overlap), merge-to-main.md (Process_MergeToMain), and prepare-merge-auto.md — never poll in an intra-turn loop. | If you are a sibling-session watching your submitted Ready PR in the queue, follow merge-queue.md §”After submitting: do not spend CI you do not need yet”: never self-merge onto main, and stand still (do not churn rebases on non-overlapping main advances) unless your PR conflicts or the merge-steward notifies you that your PR is in the next train. | .

d29c88cb8cb4.title: Invocation
d29c88cb8cb4.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | mcp__github__subscribe_pr_activity (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

7f23cf205367.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
7f23cf205367.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . git fetch origin <BRANCH> 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: . mcp__github__pull_request_read(method="get", pullNumber=N, owner=..., repo=...) # stash result["head"]["sha"] .

90853bffe079.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
90853bffe079.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — GitHub MCP subscription . Use mcp__github__subscribe_pr_activity directly. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

7cbb0df9cd56.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
7cbb0df9cd56.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (qou-v0t8: Contended Tree-Measuring Audit Witnesses) . 🛑 qou-v0t8 RULE (OVERRIDES OLD REGEN-ON-BRANCH ADVICE): Tree-measuring audit witnesses count properties across the whole working tree and are regenerated on main’s own cadence. NEVER regenerate or commit any of the contended tree-measuring audit witnesses from a feature branch — doing so either walks a drain-only ratchet backwards (if behind main) or immediately re-acquires a merge conflict on the next main landing: . | computations/audits/q0-anchor-consistency-audit.witness.json | computations/mpf-float-source-audit.witness.json | computations/mpf-import-time-dps-audit.witness.json | computations/never-raises-dps-audit.witness.json | computations/witness-float64-padding-audit.witness.json | computations/witness-raw-float64-audit.witness.json | computations/q0-value-drift-audit.witness.json | computations/no-free-parameter-certificate.witness.json | computations/codata-truncation-audit.witness.json (plus witness-value-copy-audit, compute-audit-scan, derivation-chain-audit, e0-calibration-audit) | . The recipe when git rebase origin/<BRANCH> halts on any contended audit witness (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # 1. If the conflicting commit ONLY touched contended audit witnesses, drop/skip it: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '(q0-anchor-consistency-audit|mpf-float-source-audit|mpf-import-time-dps-audit|never-raises-dps-audit|witness-float64-padding-audit|witness-raw-float64-audit|q0-value-drift-audit|no-free-parameter-certificate|codata-truncation-audit|witness-value-copy-audit|compute-audit-scan|derivation-chain-audit|e0-calibration-audit)\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. If a mixed commit accidentally included a contended audit witness alongside real work, # take origin/main's copy (--ours during rebase onto origin/main) so your commit drops the diff: git checkout --ours -- <contended-audit-witness.json> git add <contended-audit-witness.json> git rebase --continue . And whenever you run scripts/compute-qa.py or scripts/precision-gates.sh locally on a feature branch, always revert any dirtied contended audit witnesses before staging (git checkout -- computations/audits/ computations/*.witness.json). For .qa.json sidecar conflicts during rebase, resolve script entries to origin/main and restore agent verdicts mechanically via: python3 scripts/qa-sidecar-agent-union.py --against <pre-rebase-ref> --apply. Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a witness other than the three audit witnesses above (e.g. markov-trace-axiomatic-multi-atom.witness.json has a substantive numerical drift — that means a CI-run script on main produced different numerical output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting). | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For witnesses specifically: if upstream regenerated *.witness.json files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging the JSON. Witness drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply the four reuse questions from prepare-merge.md §2a: . | Definitions / lemmas / simulators / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / \cite{} and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a calc chain, or close a sorry? Apply via local/proof-simplifier (narrative) + local/lean-build-fix / local/lean-completeness-audit (Lean). | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through local/scientific-accuracy / local/readability-editing. | Computation — does a new script or witness in computations/ supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the witness JSON. (See §2a for the routine compute-audit-scan / derivation- chain-audit / e0-calibration-audit drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its .lean sibling), delegate to local/compute-integration-watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. The watcher runs the I1–I12 wiring checklist and returns a verdict (WIRED / PROBE-ONLY / NOT-WIRED) plus a concrete fix recommendation. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether .claude/skills/local/*.md (or .claude/skills/<pkg>/*.md) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" \ -- '.claude/skills/local/*.md' '.claude/skills/*/*.md' . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision in the watcher’s ledger (.beans/<watcher-name>-ledger.md for integration-watcher children, or chat-only for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only (.claude/skills/local/*.md and .claude/skills/<pkg>/*.md). Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

7fad2244a8a6.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
7fad2244a8a6.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise call mcp__github__unsubscribe_pr_activity. | .

38fad4e57c6a.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
38fad4e57c6a.content: . | Witness drift: upstream regenerated *.witness.json while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Lean version bumps: a Mathlib hash changed in lakefile.toml → check cat .lake/packages/mathlib/lean-toolchain aligns with our branch’s lean-toolchain before continuing the Lean build. | Schema migrations: if folio/schema/ changed, run cd content && bun run migrate-lean-refs and bun run validate before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

de68d1b4bfe8.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
de68d1b4bfe8.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare current baseline against actual main HEAD git fetch origin main 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches the failure mode where a focused work session (axiom discharge sweep, content authoring marathon, witness regeneration loop) silently lets main move 10+ commits ahead while the watcher is timed out.

535462be864a.title: 6.  Output style
535462be864a.content: Match user-accessibility note in AGENTS.md: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .

41b6285ba731.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Declare the web-app directoryA_Declare | App author | web-apps | The layer declares a directory of kind web-app in its <name>.json and puts a web-app.json (web-app/0.1.0) at its root: id, title, description, how it builds, the languages it ships (the site’s six UN languages: ar, en, es, fr, ru, zh), the layer directories it reads at build time (contentFrom), a size budget, and for a copied app its licence and source. 49bcda0e304c.title: Web apps — an app is content, the harness publishes it
49bcda0e304c.content: Skill web-apps: Interactive web apps as knowledge-graph content: a layer holds an app’s source in a directory of kind web-app (one web-app.json), its UI strings go through the harness’s translation process like any template, and the harness’s apps visualiser (Tool web-app-build) builds it at publish and writes it to its own route with no site chrome, loaded only when a reader opens it. Read before adding an app to any layer, before writing a publish script for one (do not), and when an app’s build or translations fail. Named by: Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route . Skill id: web-apps · Package: ui-core · Kind: web-app · Tool: web-app-build (bun run cat web-apps:build) · Process: web-app-publish .

bbc90a91918e.title: The rule
bbc90a91918e.content: A layer that carries an app declares it; it does not publish it. Owner, 2026-11-11 (cards Q-GAME-5 A and Q-GAME-7 A): a content layer with an app (a WHO onboarding game was the first) must not become a harness to ship it, and the one-off route VaxLink used (web/ + its own publish.sh + site.build.keep) is retired. The kind and its visualiser are the harness’s, so every layer that mounts cat-harness gets them. Before writing an app at all, ask whether it is a journey: a walkthrough of people and steps is a user-scenario and a workshop drawn by the journeys-viewer, not an app. An app is for what a page cannot be: a game, a simulation, a 3D world.

452eed3246b2.title: Declaring one
452eed3246b2.content: . | Put the app’s source in a directory of the layer, with its package.json and a lockfile (package-lock.json for npm, bun.lock for bun): the build installs exact versions only. | Declare the directory in the layer’s <name>.json with "graphTypologies": ["web-app"]. | Put a web-app.json (web-app/0.1.0, the schema the Tool web-app-build reads) at its root: | . { "$schema": "web-app/0.1.0", "id": "onboarding-game", "title": "Join the Network", "description": "A country onboards to the GDHCN, one choice at a time.", "build": { "installer": "npm", "script": "build", "outDir": "dist" }, "locales": ["en", "ar", "es", "fr", "ru", "zh"], "i18n": { "catalog": "src/i18n/en.json", "out": "public/i18n" }, "contentFrom": ["business-processes", "glossary"], "sizeBudgetMB": 45, "license": "Apache-2.0", "source": { "repository": "https://github.com/carlsbox/gdhcn-onboarding-game", "commit": "bd4c34c" } } . | field | rule | . | id | lower-case kebab; the route segment. Two layers claiming one id is a declaration error naming both. | . | build | defaults npm / build / dist. The app must build with relative asset paths (Vite base: './'), since its route is computed, not chosen. | . | chrome | always none (the default): the app draws its own frame. | . | locales | the first is the source language. A WHO layer ships the six UN languages: ar, en, es, fr, ru, zh. Arabic is right to left: the app sets dir="rtl" for it. | . | contentFrom | the layer’s own directory ids the app reads at build time. An app reads the layer’s content (its BPMN, glossary, actors, instances) at build time rather than copying it into code, so it cannot drift. | . | sizeBudgetMB | the index flags an app over it; the site size review reads it. | . | license, source | for a copied app: keep its LICENSE and a NOTICE naming the source commit. | .

22825942a111.title: Where it is published, and why it loads only when opened
22825942a111.content: | route | what | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/ | the index, in the site’s chrome: one entry per app, its languages and size | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/<id>/ | the app’s build, every page marked <meta name="folio-navbar" content="none"> and rendered-by: web-app-build | . The route is computed by visualiserRoute, as for every visualiser (harness-tiles). No other page embeds an app or loads its scripts: a tile, an IG page or a journey links to it. So a reader downloads an app only by opening its route. Inside the app, put heavy parts (a 3D engine, films) behind a dynamic import() or preload="none" so the first screen paints first. Lazy on screen, complete in print . Defer what a reader may never reach (owner, 2026-11-14: “do lazy load content and libs”): images with loading="lazy" and decoding="async", libraries behind a dynamic import() on first use, a hidden panel or a closed <details> drawn on its first open, a popout built when it is opened. Every deferral has a print path (owner, 2026-11-14: “make sure printing loads all of the content before it renders the PDF on the browser”). On beforeprint, and in a Print button that waits before it calls window.print(): switch lazy images to eager and wait for them, build and open what is built on toggle, and write out text that only a popout shows. afterprint closes again what the preparation opened. The library entry page (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, docPrintPrep) is the worked example.

d9170c52f465.title: Translating an app — the harness’s process, not a second one
d9170c52f465.content: An app’s UI strings are one more template to the translation process (translation-manager, translation-refresh, multi-locale-translation.bpmn): . | Source catalog. i18n.catalog is a flat JSON object { key: text } in the source locale. Placeholders are {name}. Nothing else is translatable: no strings hard-coded in components. | Templates. bun run cat web-apps:build --extract writes translations/<locale>/apps/<id>.pot in the declaring layer, one ui-string entry per key with the key as msgctxt. Name this command in the layer’s AGENTS.md §Translations as the app’s “refresh the templates” step, so the watcher runs it. | Translation. Translators fill translations/<locale>/apps/<id>.po exactly as for pages and diagrams: one PR per locale, the fixed terms, the untainted round trip, officiality as the layer declares it. | Injection is the build. Before building, the Tool writes each locale’s translated strings to <i18n.out>/<locale>.json. The app loads its locale’s file and falls back to the source text per string. | Gates. web-apps:build --check fails on a stale template, a translation that drops or adds a {placeholder}, or a translation for a key the catalog no longer has. Untranslated strings are reported, never failed. | . Media that speaks (narration, films) is not a string: list each clip per locale in the app’s own data, and say in the app when a locale has captions only.

b3d1b51d2d7b.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

81add79c9dbe.title: 1. Intent
81add79c9dbe.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

f3afb03cd68a.title: 2. Candidates
f3afb03cd68a.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

ca6e65b47b4a.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
ca6e65b47b4a.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

73f28e59c9ff.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
73f28e59c9ff.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

91c019c3d9b6.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
91c019c3d9b6.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

401ba143cd39.title: Staging links
401ba143cd39.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

94e5f49d9197.title: Showing it to the requester
94e5f49d9197.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (feedback-deep-links, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

de2b1907b5c5.title: Refresh computation witnesses
de2b1907b5c5.content: Process_WitnessRefresh · strict (defaulted) · 6 step(s) . Bring qou’s computation witnesses back in line with the producers that write them, without a witness ever being rewritten that the owner did not approve. Owner, 2026-10-04: “all witnesses tools will need to go into the KG”; this is the process those Tools run in. A WITNESS IS CONTENT HERE. Its numbers are what the paper quotes, so the owner’s rule that a migration changes no mathematics applies to it, and so does the ask-first rule for refreshing one. That is why the decision sits in the owner’s lane between the measurement and the re-run, and why nothing before it writes a file: the dry run and the parity check both work on the committed tree or a scratch copy of it. THE PLAN IS run_pipeline.py --dry-run --content-only, UNCHANGED. The process does not re-derive staleness; it calls the pipeline’s own answer through the witness-refresh-plan Tool, so the list a person approves is exactly the list the pipeline would act on. No rendered diagram — run bun run cat render:bpmn.

d8ea143842da.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | List stale producers (pipeline dry run)Task_Plan | Compute agent | — | Run python3 computations/run_pipeline.py --dry-run --content-only (the witness-refresh-plan Tool). It lists every content-linked producer whose witness is stale (script changed, a dependency changed, or a stale q0) in dependency order, and writes nothing. | . | Classify each: does a re-run reproduce it?Task_Parity | Compute agent | — | Run the platform’s witness-parity Tool on the listed witnesses. It re-runs each committed producer in a scratch git worktree and reports pass, fail (with the differing paths) or unknown (environment mismatch, stale script, error, timeout). The owner sees, for each candidate, whether a refresh would change numbers or only provenance. | . | Approve which producers to re-runTask_Approve | Owner (the paper’s author) | — | The owner picks the producers whose witnesses may be rewritten, from the classified list. Saying nothing approves none. A witness whose re-run changes numbers needs a decision about which result is right before it is approved. | . | Re-run the approved producersTask_Run | Compute agent | — | Re-run exactly the approved producers, in dependency order. A producer that writes sibling witnesses outside the approved set is reported, and those files are restored to their committed state rather than committed. | . | Precision gates; keep audit output outTask_Gates | Compute agent | — | Run scripts/precision-gates.sh --changed. A red that names one of the refreshed witnesses stops the process at the producer. A red that predates the change does not, but it is reported. The gate scripts rewrite their own audit-report witnesses as a side effect; those are restored, never committed. | . | Commit the refreshed witnessesTask_Commit | Compute agent | — | Commit only the approved witnesses, naming the producers, the fields that changed and the gate result, and re-run witness-parity on them, expecting pass. | .

64f5c874f933.title: State in a running process
64f5c874f933.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

8677423a0f25.title: Which store answers which question
8677423a0f25.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

3000ef28b445.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
3000ef28b445.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

a18eaf7f57b7.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
a18eaf7f57b7.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

8f4299b403e0.title: What state does NOT buy you
8f4299b403e0.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

4337ac605cd4.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
4337ac605cd4.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

2a5483ef050f.title: Reading the state you did not write
2a5483ef050f.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
